en: Having bowed to the noble Mañjuśrī— the moon of primordial wisdom who pervades the three times— and likewise to his *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which possesses profound and vast qualities, [Vilāsavajra/Viśvarūpa composes] the *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*.
Having examined the Yogacaryā, Kriyā, and Caryā Tantras, as well as the Pāramitā system, the Sūtra and Abhidharma Piṭakas, and other treatises;

having likewise considered the Jātakas, the Itivṛttakas, and the opinions of the authors of hymns; and having recollected the entirety of the Vijñānavāda, the Madhyamaka, and the worldly sciences transmitted through the succession of gurus, and having remembered the oral instructions—now, at the request [of others], I [compose this].
An explanation is being composed for that [work], which proceeds in a profound and noble manner, with a mind moistened by compassion for sentient beings of dull intellect.
Now, the structural arrangement of this *Nāmasaṃgīti* is set forth. It is as follows: the request, the reply, and the survey of the six families.

The sequence of the awakening through the *māyājāla*: the *bodhicitta* by way of Śrī Vajrasattva is the *suviśuddhadharmadhātu-jñāna*; by way of Mahāvairocana’s own nature is the *ādarśa-jñāna*; by way of Akṣobhya is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*; by way of Amitābha is the *samatā-jñāna*; by way of Ratnasaṃbhava is the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*; and by way of Amoghasiddhi’s own nature is the praise of the gnoses (*jñānastuti*). [These are] the body, the meaning, the benefits, and the arrangement of mantras—thus, there are fourteen topics of the body.

Therein, beginning with "Then Vajradhara... and continuing up to "...standing before him with body bowed," there is the request made in sixteen verses. Then, beginning with "Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni... and continuing up to "...it is well, Blessed One," there is the reply in six verses. Then, beginning with "Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [beheld] all... and continuing up to "...the great family of the Great Uṣṇīṣa," there is the survey of the six families in two verses.

Beginning with the verse "imāṃ ṣanmantra... and continuing up to "arapacanāya te namaḥ," the sequence of awakening through the *Māyājāla* is indicated by these three verses. Beginning with "tad yathā... and continuing up to "mahāyānanayottamaḥ," the designation of the Vajra of Awakening Mind (*bodhicittavajra*) is expressed by means of the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu through these fourteen verses.

Beginning with "Mahāvairocana Buddha" and ending with "Vajrāṅkuśa, the Great Noose," there is praise by means of twenty-four and a quarter verses through the nature of the *suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna* (the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena). Beginning with "Vajrabhairava, the Terrifier" and ending with "Ghoṣa, the Best among those who possess sound," there is praise by means of fourteen and a half verses through the nature of the *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom).

Beginning with "Suchness, reality, selflessness," and so forth, up to "the flame of gnosis, most radiant," there is praise by means of the gate of discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) in forty-two verses. Beginning with "The supreme accomplisher of desired aims," and so forth, up to "the great jewel, the crest-jewel of gems," there is praise by way of the nature of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) in twenty-four verses.

Beginning with "The one to be awakened by all the perfectly awakened ones" and ending with "Mañjuśrī, the best among the glorious," there is praise by means of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) in fifteen verses. Beginning with "Homage to you, the supreme vajra-granter of boons" and ending with "Ognis of knowledge, homage be to you," there is praise of the five wisdoms by way of the five Tathāgatas in five verses.

This is the praise of the benefits, beginning with "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara," and so forth, up to "the King of Dharma. The praise by means of mantra begins with "Oṃ sarvadharmā... and so forth, up to "...dharmadhātujñānagarbha Āḥ. Then, the concluding praise begins with "O Vajradhara," and so forth, up to "taught by all the Perfect Buddhas. Thus, in one place, the complete praise consists of one hundred and sixty-two verses and one hundred and fifty lines of prose concerning the benefits.
And this is the summary meaning of the *Nāmasaṃgīti* of the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Being Mañjuśrī, who is the wisdom-body of all Tathāgatas.

In this regard, since those who proceed by first engaging in conceptual investigation—driven by doubt concerning the meaning of the words and by the influence of the connection, the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojanasya prayojana*)—enter [this work], the connection and so forth of this *Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti* must also be stated. Thus, its connection and...

If the subject matter (*abhidheya*) were not taught, those who first entertain doubts—fearing that it might be as disconnected and meaningless as the words of a madman—would not listen. Therefore, its connection (*sambandha*) and subject matter must certainly be stated.

Since those possessed of faith engage [with the teachings] precisely by taking the word of the Blessed One as authoritative, what need is there to mention the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth? Why is it unnecessary to mention them? Because they engage through mere faith alone. In this context, the subject matter is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). This is also stated in terms of its qualities, as it has been said:
"The two dharmas..."

It is said: "The teaching that one should grasp the names for the purpose of grasping the well-purified [reality] is as follows. The "expresser" (vācaka) is the *Nāmasaṃgīti* (Chanting of the Names). "Recitation" (*pāṭha*) means utterance; thus, the names that are perfectly uttered are the "Perfect Utterance," which is the *Nāmasaṃgīti*. As for the "names," they pertain to the Yoga Tantra, the Kriyā Tantra, the Carya Tantra, and... [29a2] ...the [other] tantras.

All the sūtras of the excellent speech, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya; all that is mundane and supramundane, and all that is moving and unmoving—their true enumeration is not the primary [reality], but remains as something secondary and not ultimate. As for the conventional: "The root of existence is completely severed; all these are merely names."

This is according to such reasoning. These constitute the relationship characterized by the signifier and the signified, or the relationship characterized by the means and that which arises from the means. Furthermore, the purpose is the devotion of those bodhisattvas who practice by way of secret mantra.

Through two types of mental engagement with suchness, one primarily realizes all phenomena individually: first, by means of non-conceptual wisdom, one analyzes; second, by means of actualizing through faith, one attains the non-dual gnosis of phenomena. Furthermore, one should apply this to the ultimate purpose, which is the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata through the supreme perfection of cultivation.
Now, the meaning of the words shall also be explained: "Then" refers to what was spoken with reference to the Vajradhara, for that is the occasion when the request itself has arrived.

From the chapter on the Net of Samādhis within the Noble *Ṣoḍaśasāhasrikā-māyājāla*, a Mahāyoga Tantra, spoken by the Blessed One Śākyamuni: "The Blessed One Vajradhara makes this supplication for that which is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī-Jñānasattva’s *Paramārthanāmasaṃgīti*."

It is for the sake of guiding sentient beings of dull faculties. Alternatively, regarding the expression "then" (*tataḥ*) used [in the phrase] "then," the word "then" signifies immediate succession. Then, together with Vajradhara, Bhṛkuṭī, and the others, the Lord Buddha...

"O Bhagavān! Having prostrated to the Tathāgata and joined his palms, he sat before him and spoke thus"—this is the connection. Because he holds the vajra, he is Vajradhara; by this word, the direction [of the teaching] is explained. Śrī is the goddess; he who possesses her is Śrīmān. By this, his vastness is expressed.

What is it that will be taught here? It is the Blessed Lord Vajradhara, whose nature is skillful means and wisdom, who is thus revealed. This very point is stated in the *Śrī-Samvaratantra*: "The glorious Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, pervading the expanse of all space. Those who are to be disciplined through suffering are those difficult to subdue, such as Maheśvara and others.

Their discipline is taught by him, because he is the Vajradhara who disciplines them. Since he is the most excellent among those such as Īśvara and the rest, the Vajradhara is supreme. Regarding the "three worlds," these are the world below the earth, the world upon the earth, and the world above the earth.

Because he possesses this disposition of victory over those [three], he is "Victorious over the Three Worlds" (*trailokyavijayin*). Alternatively, the three—the one who causes victory, the one who produces honey, and the one who accomplishes all aims—are the "Three Worlds. Because he possesses this disposition of victory over them, he is "Victorious over the Three Worlds."

For that very reason, the Blessed One Vajradhara is the Hero (*vīra*), because he cannot be overcome by others. Regarding "Vajreśvara": *vajra* is the five-pronged vajra; its *īśvara* is the lord, and Vajreśvara is the Blessed One Vajradhara.

From the *Śrī-tattvasaṃgraha*, the Five Secrets are proclaimed: "In whatever way beings may be tamed, according to their very nature, for the sake of those beings, one should act through the purity of passion and the rest. For the benefit of all beings and as a cause for the Buddha's teaching, even if one were to kill all sentient beings, one would not be stained by sin."
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, if one steals the wealth of others in order to bring them into union with the Buddha-body, [there is no fault].

He is not defiled by sin. There is no pleasure like that of passion; he offers it to the Victors. For the sake of sentient beings, by relying on other women, he attains merit. For the benefit of all sentient beings, because it is the cause for the Buddha’s teaching, by performing all such actions, he acquires manifold merit. Thus it is said.

Because he is the king of those five secrets, he is the "King of Secrets" (*guhyarāja*). Alternatively, because he is victorious over the secret ones, he is the "King of Secrets. Regarding the phrase, "Having joined the palms, standing before him, one should speak thus," this should be applied as a connective formula to all subsequent passages that follow. As for "white lotus," it refers to a white *padma*.

"Expanded" (*phullita*) means blossomed. "Eye" (*netra*) means the eye. As for the grammatical construction of this term: it is both a white lotus (*pundarīka*) and it is expanded; therefore, it is a "blossomed white lotus. One who possesses such eyes is described as such. Regarding the phrase "face with a fully blossomed lotus": "lotus" (*padma*) is simply the lotus itself. "Fully blossomed" (*praphulla*) means well-opened.

"Face" means countenance; he who possesses a face resembling a fully blossomed lotus is thus addressed. "Holding it with the hand from the center of the vajra, turning the vajra upward again and again" refers to: "Twirling the supreme vajra repeatedly with one's own hand. This is connected with the phrase "he spoke as follows."

From the *Śrī-vajrapāṇy-abhiṣeka-tantra*, the five hosts of wrathful deities, such as the venerable Vajradhara’s attendant Bhṛkuṭīkrama and others, are proclaimed. This is connected with the statement that the Blessed One Vajradhara, having prostrated together with them, spoke these words.

Since those wrathful verses also have infinite meaning, it is said: "O Vajrapāṇi, you who are infinite! Just as the Vajradhara [subdues], they too subdue infinite beings; and just as the Vajradhara subdues those difficult to tame, it is therefore said: "The subduer of those difficult to tame."

For that very reason, he is a hero (*vīra*), because he cannot be overcome by them. Therefore it is said: "a hero. What is his excellence? It is the conduct of a hero. What is his form? A terrifying form. For that very reason...

It is said: "The heroic one who is terrifying," it says. Regarding "the vajra tip radiating intensely": this refers to the tip of a vajra that radiates intensely; that which possesses such an initial portion is "the vajra tip radiating intensely. As for "wielding," it means brandishing upward. By what? By one's own hand.

What is their essential nature? They possess an essence that accomplishes the welfare of beings through great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means; thus, they are those who accomplish the welfare of beings through compassion, wisdom, and skillful means. In that regard, they are "compassionate" because they possess compassion; they are "compassion" because they bring about the cessation of suffering.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the cessation of one's own happiness through suffering caused by the suffering of others. Because it does not increase one's own happiness, it is "compassion" (*karuṇā*), and because it is also "great" (*mahatī*), it is "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), owing to its nature of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the thorough discernment of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Skillful means (upāya) consists in accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings according to their respective capacities, by way of demonstrating all supramundane meditative concentrations (samādhi) without exception. "The world" refers to those belonging to the three realms; "their welfare" refers to their purpose. Therefore it is said: "Through great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, one performs the supreme benefit for the world."

For that very reason, since those wrathful ones are sublime (*dam pa*), they are supreme; therefore it is said, "supreme" (*mchog*). What is their nature? It is the nature of a joyful, delighted, and glad disposition. In that regard, "joy" (*dga'* ) is from the perspective of the mind's intention; "delight" (*mgu*) is from the perspective of the body; and "gladness" (*rangs pa*) is by way of the intellect. Its meaning is as follows:

Those who possess a mind of joy and contentment are said to be "possessing a joyful and contented disposition. For that very reason, "delight" (*rangs pa*) means "enthusiasm," because of acting for the benefit of sentient beings. This is precisely what is stated: "delight. The "form of the body" refers to the form of a wrathful deity (*krodha*). What is the nature of this form of the wrathful body? It is the Great Terrifier (*Mahābhairava*).

With a fierce laugh, many heads, arms, and feet; with unattractive eyes, brown hair standing erect, yellowish-brown eyebrows, a frowning brow, and being adorned with garlands of skulls, snake ornaments, and a lower garment of tiger skin.

That which possesses those [qualities] such as these is one endowed with the form of the body of a wrathful deity; therefore it is said: "endowed with the form of the body of a wrathful deity. The activity of the Buddhas is the Buddha-action (*buddhakarma*); to perform it is to carry it out, as it is said: "performing the Buddha-action. For that very reason, he is the Protector (*nātha*).

Because he performs the enlightened activity (*phrin las*) of the Teacher, the Buddha, he is therefore called the Protector (*mgon*). "By those who have bowed their bodies" means having prostrated; this is connected with the request that follows below, made together with those who have prostrated to the Blessed One Vajradhara. Having done what? Having paid homage. To whom? To the Protector.

Because he instructs those in the world who are without a protector, the Principal One (īśvara) is the Protector (nātha). If one asks what kind of protector this protector is, it is said: "the Tathāgata. In that context, "thus" (tathā) refers to suchness (tathatā). Because he knows that, he is the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, he is called the Tathāgata because he has come and gone in the same manner as all the Tathāgatas have come and gone. In what way? The term "Bhagavān" refers to the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because he possesses perfect fortune (*bhaga*), or because he conquers the four Māras. As it is said: "Afflictions, karma, and likewise birth; likewise, the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations."

The Blessed One (Bhagavān) is so called here because he has conquered whatever phenomena constitute the discordant factors; thus, by way of this etymological sequence, he is the Blessed One due to his conquest of the afflictions and so forth. Alternatively, it is because he possesses qualities such as sovereignty (īśvara) and the rest. As it has been said: "Sovereignty, beauty of form, fame, glory, and supreme excellence..."

Then, it is explained that he is endowed with wisdom and diligence, as well as the six [perfections]. Furthermore, what is the nature of the Protector? "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksambuddha) means one who has attained complete and perfect awakening, because he is not a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. "Having prostrated" connects to what precedes. "Having joined his palms" means...

As for "sitting before [the Lord]," the Blessed One Vajradhara spoke these words for the sake of my benefit and so forth: "O Pervasive Lord, for my healing; for my healing" means for my benefit—that is, for the sake of my very healing in the future. "For my purpose" means for my necessity. "For me" means for my own sake; O Pervasive Lord, out of compassion for me.

"For the sake of benefiting [others], may I attain [this] through this very sequence. If one asks, "By what means is it to be attained? it is said: "Through the manifest perfection of the net of magical illusion (*māyājāla*)."

"In what way shall I attain awakening?"—this connects with the subsequent verb "may I attain" the stage called the "Manifestly Perfect Awakening of the Net of Magical Illusion. O Blessed One, please explain how this may come to pass for me. As for what those sentient beings are like: "Their minds are agitated by the afflictions..."

These are the six afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus it is taught in the *Abhidharma*: "Pride, views, doubt, attachment, aversion, and delusion. Those sentient beings whose minds are thoroughly agitated by these afflictions are those "whose minds are disturbed by the afflictions."

Therefore, it connects with the request: "I pray that the Blessed One may explain this for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed fruit. Furthermore, what kind of distinction characterizes these sentient beings? It is said: "Physicians for all sentient beings who are submerged in the mire of ignorance. In this context, "ignorance" refers to *avidyā* (unawareness); it is so called because it is the very locus of obstruction.

Because it is difficult to escape, it is like mud; thus, it is "mud. This connects with the words, "Please explain for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings who have sunk therein. Regarding the phrase, "In order to attain the unsurpassed fruit": the unsurpassed fruit is buddhahood itself. To attain that is to acquire it thoroughly. Its purpose is "for the sake of attaining that."

Regarding the phrase "Blessed One, please explain," and so forth, the term "Perfect Buddha" (Sambuddha) refers to him from the perspective of permanence. The term "Teacher of the World" (Jagadguru) means the teacher of all beings because he is the preceptor of the world; this refers to him from the perspective of Ratnasambhava. The term "Instructor" (Śāstṛ) means one who instructs the world.

32a1 || From the perspective of Akṣobhya: "Samaya" refers to the Blessed One Vajrasattva; since he is both "great" (*mahā*) and "samaya," he is the "Great Samaya" (*mahāsamaya*). His "reality" (*tattva*) is the "Reality of the Great Samaya. Because he knows that, it says: "He who knows the reality of the Great Samaya"—this is from the perspective of Amitābha. 32a2 ||

"Faculties" (*indriya*) refers to those who are dull, middling, and sharp; their "intentions" (*āśaya*) are their mental dispositions. Because he knows these, he is called "the Knower of the Intentions of the Faculties," by way of accomplishing the purposeful goal (*arthasiddhi*). Thus, because the Blessed One is the supreme among the five Tathāgatas, he is the "Exalted One" (*parama*); this connects with the phrase "please explain. Then:

Regarding the phrase "the wisdom body of the Blessed One" and so forth, it connects with the words that follow later in the text: "O Blessed One, I shall uphold this *Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva-sambandha-nāmasaṃgīti*. What kind of distinction does it have as a "wisdom body"? It is a wisdom body because it is the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*).

That is the body of primordial wisdom (*jñānakāya*); it is [so called] by way of the mirror-like primordial wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding "the great uṣṇīṣa" (*mahauṣṇīṣa*), the "great crown" (*mahamuṣṇīṣa*) is the "great uṣṇīṣa"; that is the great uṣṇīṣa. It is [so called] by way of the primordial wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Because it is the nature of the empowerment of all the Tathāgatas, it is the great uṣṇīṣa.

Regarding the term "Lord of Speech" (*vāgīśvara*): "speech" (*vāk*) refers to sound; "lord" (*īśvara*) means sovereign; thus, he is the Lord of Speech. He is the Lord of Speech by way of the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Regarding the term "Wisdom Body" (*jñānakāya*): since wisdom itself is the body, it is the Wisdom Body. This is by way of the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Regarding the term "Self-Arisen" (*svayambhū*): he is self-arisen because he has arisen by himself.

This is the meaning of "arisen from the power of meditation. As it is said in the *Śrīparamādya-tantra*: "The self-nature of Samantabhadra is manifest enlightenment. Therefore, he is called "self-arisen" (svayambhū) by way of the wisdom of the utterly pure dharmadhātu.
If one asks how it is said that this will occur: Mañjuśrī, the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) possesses the five wisdoms.

The possession [of qualities] has been shown. Regarding "Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva": he who is gentle (*mañju*) and endowed with glory (*śrī*) is Mañjuśrī. As for "jñānasattva," it is because he dwells in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas. Since he is both Mañjuśrī and that very jñānasattva, he is Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva.

He is not a bodhisattva who is a sovereign of the ten stages. If one asks who he is then, it is that very non-dual gnosis, the perfection of wisdom, which is Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*). For this very reason, the venerable Diṅnāga said: "The perfection of wisdom is non-dual; that gnosis is the Tathāgata."

Thus it is said. This connects with the statement: "I shall uphold this *Mañjuśrījñānasattvasambandha-nāmasaṃgīti*, which is the very nature of the five wisdoms. If one asks what its specific characteristics are, it is stated: "The supreme recitation of names," and so forth; the meaning of that has already been explained.

Regarding the term "profound meaning" (*arthagambhīra*): it is profound and it is also the meaning; therefore, it is "profound meaning," which is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because that [teaching] possesses both meaning and profundity, one says, "I shall uphold it. Regarding the phrase "vast in meaning" (*arthavaipulya*): it is the meaning of being extensive. That which possesses this is "vast in meaning."

"Great purpose" (*mahārtha*) refers to that which is great in meaning; it is "greatness of purpose" itself because it completely fulfills all the intentions of the entire realm of sentient beings without exception. "Incomparable" (*asama*) refers to that which is without equal; it is "the incomparable. Why is it incomparable? Because its very nature is the *dharmadhātu*.

"Utterly peaceful" (*rab zhi*) is because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have been completely stilled. "Virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end" refers to attaining enthusiasm, joy, and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) during the stages of hearing, reflection, and meditation; this is connected with the thought, "I shall uphold these three virtues. Furthermore, what is its other specific quality?
It is said: "That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past," and so forth. This means:

that which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, that which will be spoken by the future perfectly enlightened Buddhas, and that which is spoken again and again by the present Blessed Buddhas. By this, it will be spoken as follows:

Because the Tathāgatas of the three times have spoken this *Mantra-samyak-gāthā* (Chanting the Names), this Dharma discourse is taught to be like space. As it has been said: "Whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear, the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains ever-present. Furthermore, what is it like?

Regarding the passage beginning with "From the Great Tantra of the Net of Magical Manifestation" (*Mahāmāyājālatantra*) and so forth: it is connected to the statement, "I shall uphold that which was joyfully sung as a true song by immeasurable great Vajradharas who hold the great secret mantra within this Great Tantra of the Net of Magical Manifestation. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Protector of all Perfect Buddhas" and so forth:

"O Protector, just as you are, please explain so that I may become one who holds the secret of all the perfect Buddhas"—this connects with what precedes. "To hold" (ādhāra) is a technical term of the Dharma. Until [I attain] definitive emergence, I shall uphold this with firm intention.

"Thus" means: until I have attained the definitive emergence (*niṣkramaṇa*) from this *Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṃgīti*, I shall uphold it. "Definitive emergence" refers to nirvāṇa. How should it be upheld? With a firm intention (*āśaya*). "Intention" is the mental inclination; "firm" means unshakable. One who possesses that is one with a firm intention.

This connects with what follows: "Having realized it exactly as it is, I shall explain it according to the specific inclinations of all sentient beings. For whose sake? It is said: "In order to eliminate all afflictions without exception and to abandon all ignorance without exception. (33a7)

In that context, "afflictions without remainder" refers to the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The meaning of their exhaustion is the complete elimination of those afflictions. "Ignorance without remainder" refers to the ignorance of things without exception; its destruction is for the sake of abandoning ignorance without exception. It is with this purpose that I request [the Buddha] to explain it.

"It is connected to the activity. 'I wish to explain it to sentient beings according to the distinctions of their intentions' means that, having realized it as it truly is, I wish to explain it thoroughly to all sentient beings according to the distinctions of their respective intentions. "By Guhyendra, Vajrapāṇi" means:

In this context, "Secret" refers to the yakṣas who dwell in the palace called Alakāvatī. Because he is their king, he is called the Lord of Secrets (Guhyādhipati). Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata spoke thus": it means that in such a manner, the Blessed One, the Lord of Secrets Vajrapāṇi, addressed the Tathāgata. Having thus addressed him, what did he do?

"Having joined the palms and bowed the body, one should stand before [the Buddha]" means that one should remain standing before him with the body bowed. "Having first performed acts of veneration, one who seeks the goal" refers to making a formal request; "veneration" consists of prostrations and the like.
From the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā* titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokana*, this is the first chapter on the stages of request, consisting of sixteen verses.

Then, immediately after the request was made, he spoke: "Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni," and so forth. In this context, "then" means that immediately after the request was made, he spoke again. "Blessed One" has already been explained. He is "Śākyamuni" because he is the Sage (*muni*) of the Śākya clan. Furthermore, he is a "Sage" because his body, speech, and mind are subdued. He is the "Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds."

Thus, the Perfectly Enlightened One has been explained. "Two-legged" refers to gods and humans; "supreme among them" means the most excellent. "From his own mouth" means from the very mouth of Śākyamuni himself. "The fine tongue" is like a conch shell coiled to the right and is the locus of all phenomena (*dharma*). Having extended it long and wide—

This means that he performed the emanation of his own tongue, which was long and wide, from his own mouth, in order to summarize [the teaching]. What did he do? It is connected as follows: "Illuminating the three worlds," and so forth;

having displayed a smile that illuminates and clarifies the three worlds—the subterranean, the terrestrial, and the celestial—he spoke again to Vajrapāṇi. Furthermore, regarding the specific qualities of the smile...

If one asks what it is like, it is said: "The subduer of the four Māra-enemies. The four Māras are the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputramāra*), and the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). These very ones are the enemies.

The phrase "their discipline" connects with the statement: "Having displayed a smile that subdues and humbles them through a conformable discipline, he spoke again to Vajrapāṇi. Regarding the phrase "having displayed the smile that purifies the three lower realms of sentient beings," the "three lower realms of worldly sentient beings" refers to the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.

This indicates the smile that performs purification; it connects with the statement, "He spoke again to Vajrapāṇi. When the Tathāgatas teach the Dharma, there are three signs, namely: the smile, the gaze, and the stimulation by light rays. In some instances there is one, in some two, and in some three, as follows:

In the *Śrī-māyājāla-tantra*, two [signs] are taught: smiling and looking. According to some, there are three, as follows: from the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, [the signs are] looking at Maitreya, a smiling face, and the emission of light rays. According to others, there is one, as follows: from the two [versions] of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*.

Regarding the phrase "having displayed a smile," that smile is of four kinds: radiating from the limbs and digits, radiating from the pores of the skin, radiating as natural light, and radiating from the faculty of the tongue. Here, it is a sign preceded by the demonstration of the miraculous power of the faculty of the tongue. As for what kind of words [were spoken]:

"Voice of Brahmā" means that it is the voice of Brahmā because it possesses the sound of Brahmā. "The sound of Brahmā" is a synonym for greatness and great qualities, as it is said: "Possessing Brahmā, merit is excellently produced. [This occurs] from many thousands [of verses].

The term "thousandfold" should be understood as referring to the great trichiliocosm world-system; it indicates the mandala that has the nature of many thousands. As it has been said: "the great trichiliocosm world-system."

It is said that it fills with sound. Just as it is heard within, so too is it known without. In that regard, what is "within" refers to those who dwell in this great trichiliocosm; "without" refers to other world systems as well. Therefore, because of its greatness, it is the Brahma-voice.

Alternatively, "Brahmā" refers to the Blessed One Śākyamuni. These very words of that Brahmā constitute the speech of Brahmā. "With pleasant [sound]" means because it is inherently delightful to hear. "Filling all the three worlds,"...

This refers to his activity: by means of the single voice of Brahmā, which completely pervades the three worlds, he spoke again to Vajrapāṇi. As it has been said: "Though the voice that destroys existence is but one, through its differentiation in teaching the various vehicles, in whatever way all beings [perceive it]..."
"Flawless and clearly manifest, it becomes the cause for realization. Regarding the passage beginning with "Because you have come to possess great compassion," [it says]: "Vajrapāṇi, well done!"

"O Youthful Śrīvajradhara, for whatever purpose you strive to hear from me this *Saṃgīti* of the Names associated with the body of Mañjuśrījñānasattva—for that very purpose, O Lord of Secrets, it shall be well explained. This connects to the question: "For what purpose have you asked me?"

"For the sake of benefiting beings" means that one has become endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in order to provide assistance to the world. If one asks what kind of specific characteristics the *Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṃgīti* possesses such that one strives to hear it, [the text says]: "It purifies and removes evil. In this context, "purifying" means auspiciousness.

"Dispelling evil" means destroying non-virtue. "Listen with a one-pointed mind" means that he will say this: it is not suitable [to listen] like an overturned vessel, a cracked vessel, or an impure vessel; such is the meaning. If one asks, "Then how? it is said: "Listen well."

Immediately after the Blessed One himself had spoken, Vajrapāṇi requested: "Blessed One, it is well," which means that the Blessed One is Śākyamuni; [Vajrapāṇi] said, "I shall listen to it in that manner. Well.

This means that I have heard it exactly according to the sequence in which it was spoken. From the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā* titled *Nāmaguhyamantrārthaviniścaya*, this is the second chapter on the sequence of what was further spoken, consisting of six verses.

Now, immediately following what was said, the section on the sequential observation of the six families is taught, beginning with: "Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni... and so forth. In that regard, the phrase "all the great families of secret mantra" is a general introductory statement; here, he gazes upon each of those [families] respectively.

This connects with the subsequent phrase: "The Lord of Speech, Mañjuśrī, spoke this verse concerning the unborn nature [of phenomena] in connection with the Wisdom Being (jñānasattva). Regarding the phrase "the family of mantra-holders and vidyā-holders," they are called "vidyā-holders" because they hold the vidyā-mantras.

Since he is both the essence of secret mantra (*guhyamantra*) and the holder of the vidyā-mantra (*vidyādharin*), the "holder of secret mantra and vidyā-mantra" is the essence of the grasper. His lineage is the lineage of the holder of secret mantra and vidyā-mantra; this is the meaning of the "action lineage" (*karmakula*). He beholds the three lineages.

This means that because it is the very nature of body, speech, and mind, it is the family of Vairocana. Regarding the phrase "the worldly and the supramundane families": it is called "worldly" because it views the world; its family is the "worldly and supramundane family," which is to say, the Lotus family. And the great family that illuminates the world...

The phrase "illuminating the worlds" refers to Akṣobhya, who is the essence of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) that brings light to the worlds. His family is described as "the great family that illuminates the worlds," which is the Vajra family. The phrase "the supreme family of the Great Mudrā" refers to the Bodhisattva Vajra family; for that very reason, it is called "supreme."
Because it is the very nature of the bodhicitta of Vairocana and the others; its lineage is the supreme lineage of Mahāmudrā. Having beheld the great Uṣṇīṣa of the great lineage...

As for the phrase "thus," because he has been consecrated as the sovereign of the three realms by all the Tathāgatas, he is the Great Uṣṇīṣa; his lineage is the Great Uṣṇīṣa lineage, which means the Jewel lineage. The meaning of "Great Vision" has already been explained above.

From the *Extensive Commentary on the Noble Mañjuśrī-nāmasaṃgīti*, titled *The Vision of the Meaning of the Secret Mantra of the Names*, this is the third chapter, the section on the vision of the six families, and the second verse.

Now, the stages of the manifest awakening of the glorious *Māyājāla*, transmitted from one master to another, will be explained. Furthermore, this [text] has emerged from within the sixteen thousand chapters of the glorious *Māyājāla*. Regarding that, first of all, having entered the gateway of mantra and engaged in the conduct,

Bhagavān Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, this crest-jewel called the *Samantabhadra-nāma-saṃgīti*, the non-dual ultimate reality that is the crown of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas—any bodhisattva who desires to manifest this [jewel] possesses the intention to completely liberate the entire realm of sentient beings, without exception or remainder.

Endowed with the mind that aspires for great enlightenment and the nature of skillful means and wisdom, one should gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction and generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. One should also speak these words: "May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas turn their attention toward me."

I, who am called [name], from this time forth until I abide at the heart of enlightenment, shall generate the unsurpassed mind of supreme awakening. Just as the Protectors of the three times have generated the unsurpassed, sublime, and certain bodhicitta for the sake of awakening itself, so shall I generate it. Furthermore, regarding the training in ethical discipline...

I shall firmly and individually uphold the ethical discipline that gathers virtuous qualities and accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings. From this day forward, I shall take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—the unsurpassed and supreme Triple Gem—and never forsake them at any time. From now on, I shall steadfastly maintain the vows that give rise to the application of the Buddhas.

One should grasp [the vajra]; with that very same [purity], one should individually grasp the mudrās of the vajra and the bell of the great supreme Vajra family. One should also grasp the preceptor (*ācārya*). Having performed these six acts, one should daily bestow the four kinds of gifts. This is the joyful commitment (*samaya*) of the great supreme Ratna family. [It consists of] the outer and secret three vehicles.

I shall also uphold the sublime Dharma, which arises from the Great Awakening of the pure and supreme Lotus family. Regarding the great and supreme Karma family, I shall correctly undertake all the vows; I shall also perform acts of worship to the best of my ability within the great and supreme Karma family. [I shall maintain] the unsurpassed mind of awakening.

Having thus generated [the aspiration], I shall undertake all the vows without exception for the sake of all sentient beings: I shall cross over those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated; I shall bring breath to those who have not found their breath; and I shall establish sentient beings in nirvāṇa. One should generate the mind of awakening preceded by the undertaking of the vows.

One should meditate through this sequence of the five stages of manifest enlightenment. First of all, one should meditate by means of the application of the reflection of mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*).

Just as the cognitions of objects belonging to their respective places and times appear individually upon the surface of a perfectly pure mirror, so too does the realm of sentient beings—distinguished by differences of migrations, locations, and births—appear within the great bodhicitta, which is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the utterly pure dharmadhātu.

One should also look upon that mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) which is utterly stainless, and thereafter generate compassion directed toward sentient beings, thinking: "Alas! These sentient beings are without a protector and without a refuge."

For the sake of those who are suffering from being without a protector and are sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra, one should deliver them from suffering in every way and in all respects, just as one would for oneself; and just as one would for a sentient being in pain, all sentient beings should be made to appear conventionally within mirror-like gnosis (ādarśajñāna).
Then, having cultivated conviction in the wisdom of equality, through the application to the equality of the selflessness of all phenomena, one [realizes] how phenomena are empty.

Having thus meditated that self and [intrinsic] nature are empty and without self, one should grasp all phenomena as being without self. As it has also been said: "Just as I am, so should one know all sentient beings; just as all sentient beings are, so should one know all phenomena," and so forth.

Then, having realized that all phenomena are by nature selfless, one should generate compassion focused on phenomena through the wisdom of equality. Then, having recited the mantra: *ākāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt*, the mantrin, having meditated upon the meaning of the mantra in its entirety and in brief, together with non-referentiality— 36b3.

One thoroughly meditates on the selflessness of phenomena. Immediately following such individual investigative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), there arises that which follows upon non-referential great compassion, which is completely liberated from subject and object, naturally luminous, and transcends the nature of parts.

One should cultivate the wisdom of the emptiness of the utterly pure dharmadhātu. Then, because one is devoid of performing the welfare of sentient beings, the yogin should arise through the power of the mental continuum cultivated by previous aspirations and manifest the wisdom of diligent application (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) by means of non-referential great compassion.

Because it is precisely the pure mundane gnosis obtained subsequent to non-conceptual gnosis, it completely fulfills all the welfare of sentient beings through that very [gnosis]. Furthermore, this should be understood as the bodhicitta characterized by engagement, which is the bodhicitta of purification consisting of the nature of the conventional and the ultimate.

Then, the yogi should contemplate the nature of mind itself as an illusory form abiding in the direction of space, naturally luminous and resembling the appearance of a star, [visualizing] the syllable ĀḤ.

From that, one should meditate upon the great syllable HŪṂ, which is the nature of supreme joy and Samantabhadra under another name; it is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of light rays of many colors, entwined with garlands of blazing wrathful deities, and blue in color. From that syllable HŪṂ, various forms of light are emitted, and from the tips of those light rays, all the Tathāgatas are emanated.
All those Tathāgatas went to all the buddhafields, leaving none out.

Having thoroughly purified all realms of sentient beings within all non-existent world-systems, and having performed the generation of the bodhicitta and so forth, one should visualize that even after displaying the miraculous manifestations of all the Buddhas, one returns once more and enters that syllable *HŪṂ*.

One should meditate on the five-pronged wisdom-vajra at the six gates, which is difficult for all Māras to overcome due to its blazing majesty that pervades the six Buddha-fields, such as Abhirati, with the six colors—blue and so forth—arising from it. Within its bulb, one should visualize a white syllable *BHRŪṂ*.

One should visualize a celestial mansion, which is the nature of the four kinds of jewels produced from that [mandala], as the great trichiliocosm world-system. What is it like? It has a square shape, the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). Above that, from the syllable *āḥ*, arises a double vajra (*viśvavajra*), which consecrates the ground as a vajra-realm, white in color.

Then, one should visualize the celestial mansion of the multi-storied palace with a vajra pinnacle and a precious jewel, marked by the syllable *bhrūṃ*. What is it like? It is square with four doors, adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*). It is hung with bells, silks, and streamers, as well as flower garlands and yak-tail fans. At all its corners and junctions...

At the junctions of the porticoes as well, it is perfectly adorned with vajras, jewels, and half-moons; it is inlaid with various forms within the arrangement of lattices and half-lattices. One should also draw the outer mandala using five-colored powders. Having entered that state of the mandala, [one proceeds to] the inner celestial palace.

Then, one should depict the second [mandala] called the Vajradhātu; it is completely surrounded by a vajra-fence, adorned with eight pillars, and features lattices and half-lattices formed by the five colored powders. Furthermore, on the exterior of the mandala, all the characteristics as they have been described should be included, summarized particularly in brief.

Everything should be performed within that [mandala]; however, at the junctions of the gates and the *tvaranas*, one should not act as a single unit. Therefore, the gates of that [mandala] and the *tvaranas* should not be examined [as separate]. One should arrange the seats of the deities from the outside according to their respective order, just as the deities are [arrayed].

37b1. In sequence. Then, that which is arranged in the center is the seat of the Principal One. In all directions, beginning with the east, the seats of Akṣobhya and the others are to be examined according to the sequence of application as being produced from their respective seed-syllables. Regarding the examination of those seats: in the center is a lion throne; in the east, an elephant throne; and in the south, a horse throne.

In the west is the peacock seat, and in the north is the garuḍa seat. One should clearly visualize moon mandalas generated from the syllable Ā, beginning with Vajrasattva and ending with Vajrāveśa. Then, upon the central seat, there is the Great Vairocana, completely generated from the syllable Ā.

Because the very mind, being free from grasping and so forth, is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. That itself is the four-faced one, which are the four liberations such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because it is the cause for the arising of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) precisely by taking the *dharmadhātu* as its object, its body color is white.

Because his nature is that of the *dharmadhātu*, he possesses a crown of matted locks. Because his mind is peaceful, his body is without ornaments. Because he is the embodiment of skillful means and wisdom, he bears the mudrā of supreme enlightenment. One should cultivate devotion to such a being as the Great Vairocana himself.

This is through the application of the seats of the four Buddhas. At his heart, upon a moon mandala, from the syllable *dhīḥ* is fully generated the Blessed One, the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*), who has five faces and possesses five topknots (*śikhā*). For this very reason, it is said: "He has five faces and five topknots."

He possesses five colors and has five topknots (*śikhā*) connected to those very [colors]. The east is blue, the south yellow, the west red, and the north green. Above his head, there is a white face, peaceful and adorned with the ornaments of a child, which abides like the face of the supreme horse (*hayagrīva*). He is endowed with grace and wears garments of various kinds.

His eight hands have the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* divided into four parts, which he perfectly holds at his heart with four hands; with the other four hands, he holds a sword of wisdom in the manner of striking. He is seated upon the seats of the four Buddhas.

38a1 || One should meditate on the abiding through the basis. Here, it is connected with the statement: "The verses consisting of the essence of words indicate the twelve stages of the Tathāgata. How is this so? It is said: "Possessing the six kings of mantra," which refers to possessing the six mantras that will appear later. What is its nature? It is "arising as non-dual."

Regarding this: "duality" refers to the grasped and the grasper. That which is the absence of these two is "non-duality. To arise from that is "origination. To originate as non-dual is "non-dual origination. A verse in which this exists is a "verse endowed with non-dual origination. Furthermore, what other specific qualities does it possess?

Regarding the statement, "This which has the nature of non-arising was taught," it means the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and the nature of emptiness. "This was taught" refers to the meaning that has been explained. In the *Śrīvajramaṇḍālaṃkāra-tantra*, this is taught as the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) of the Tathāgata, the great stage of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*). It is like the orb of the sun.

The second is Amṛtaprabha (Nectar Light), which is like the moon of supreme radiance; the third is Gaganaprabha (Space Light), which is firmly established like the foundation of space; the fourth is Vajraprabha (Vajra Light), for that ground is the light of joy. Through the application of a firm superior intention, it is designated as "Vajra"; the fifth is called Ratnaprabha (Jewel Light), which is firmly established in empowerment.

The sixth is called "Lotus Light," for it arises perfectly like a lotus; because its nature is the purity of *dharmatā*, it is stainless and without grasping. The seventh is called "Karma Light," which is held to perform the enlightened activities of a Buddha. The eighth is called "Incomparable," for there is no comparison for it. The ninth is called "Possessing Comparisons," for it understands all things through their respective analogies.

"The tenth is called the Light of Wisdom (Prajñābhāsa); it is the unsurpassed Buddha-ground. The eleventh is Omniscience (Sarvajñatā), the great ground that is intensely radiant. The twelfth is Individual Self-Cognition (Pratyavekṣaṇā), in which yogic wisdom is perfectly fulfilled. Thus it is said. These should be understood as the twelve grounds of the Tathāgata, which are the complete perfection of the twelve syllables beginning with the letter *A*.

"Of the Buddhas residing in the three times" refers to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. "Abiding in the heart" means that they reside in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas. "The body of primordial wisdom" (jñānakāya) means that its very nature is the body of primordial wisdom.

"Buddha" is so called because of the realization of the meaning of reality as it abides. Now, one should meditate on the wheel of wisdom at the heart of that primordial Buddha. If one asks what kind [of wheel] it is, it is said to be that which reveals the meaning of dependent origination. As it has been explained: "It perfectly holds the hub of the spokes."

"The spokes also rest upon the hub; this wheel, which joins dependent origination, is set in motion. Thus it is said. One should visualize the syllable *āḥ* at the center of that well-arranged hub, which possesses six spokes and four rims, and is endowed with the six colors generated from the syllable *a*.

O Bhagavān, regarding the root mantra of the Jñānasattva and the other mantras on the four rims, one should meditate on them as being exclusively white in color. Among those, for the first rim: oṃ sarvadharmā abhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavajrā ā āṃ āḥ.

Therefore, on the second rim on the outside, one should meditate upon the twelve syllables of the sound that expresses the twelve stages of the Tathāgata. Then, beginning from the first tongue, one should arrange the colors of the families according to the sequence of the six mantras as follows: for the first, oṃ vajratīkṣṇāya te namaḥ; for the second, oṃ duḥkhacchedāya te namaḥ.

On the third [petal]: oṃ prajñājñānamūrtaye namaḥ | On the fourth: oṃ jñānakāyāya te namaḥ | On the fifth: oṃ vāgīśvarāya te namaḥ | On the sixth: oṃ ārapacanāya te namaḥ | On the rim outside the wheel, arrange the mantra of the garland of the wisdom-body of all the Blessed Tathāgatas.

*Ā Āḥ Oṃ Sarvatathāgatahr̥daya Hara Hara Oṃ Hrūṃ Hrīḥ Bhagavān Jñānamūrti Vāgīśvara Mahāvaca Sarvadharmāgaganāmala Supariśuddhadharmadhātujñānagarbha Āḥ.* On the second outer rim, one should arrange the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*.
That is the sequence for arranging the mantras of the wheel. From the syllable *āḥ* situated in the center of that wheel, [the deity] is generated.

The Blessed One Jñānasattva, with six faces, having the color of the autumn moon, his crown-tuft (*uṣṇīṣa*) like the supreme *aindranīla* gem, surrounded by a halo of light like the orb of the rising sun, absorbed in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the natural ornaments of all the Tathāgatas, seated upon a variegated lotus throne.
Visualize oneself as having a peaceful nature, holding two volumes of the Prajñāpāramitā resting upon a red utpala and a blue utpala with both hands; then, meditate on a moon mandala at one’s heart.

Upon that, he arranged the syllable ĀḤ, which is the nature of the Perfection of Wisdom, the creative cause for the arising of the omniscient gnosis (*sarvajñājñāna*), the source from which all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born, the embodiment of the accumulations of merit and wisdom of all great Bodhisattvas, and the creative cause of all ultimate gnoses.

Then, one should meditate on the mantra syllables residing upon the wheel as possessing the colors as they were described, beautifully arranged, and endowed with light capable of shattering mountains that are otherwise unknowable; one should meditate on those lights illuminating one's own body. Immediately upon being illuminated by the light, [the mantras] are emitted from the four faces.

Having illuminated the Sahā world-system, six-colored rays of light were then emitted from the six vajra-gates; pervading the entire expanse of space, they proceeded to various buddha-fields and accomplished the welfare of the realms of sentient beings without exception or remainder, [reaching] all the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas.

The mandalas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were also illuminated; [the light] entered through their mouths, circled the vajras at their hearts, drew forth their wisdom-knowledge (jñāna), and through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, entered back out through one's own mouth.

One should meditate on [the mantra] abiding as having become one with the syllables of the mantra upon the moon situated at one's own heart. Thus, the bodhisattva who practices the conduct through the gateway of mantra, abiding in the meditation of the stream-enterer, [is empowered] by the Blessed One...

"O Bhagavān, one perceives the form of Mañjuśrī Jñānasattva by way of his wisdom-body (jñānakāya)," it is said; "one should contemplate his form by way of the shape of a lunar mandala," it is said; and "one should meditate upon his form by way of the form of the syllable *āḥ*," it is said.
By meditating in this manner through these three modes, one will, in no long time, behold the nirmāṇakāya of that very [reality], having taken into account the capacity of those to be trained.

"One will see all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abiding in the expanse of space, endowed with their emanated form-bodies (nirmāṇakāya). This means that through the power of that very meditation, one attains Buddhahood itself and the state of Vajrasattva in this very life.

Thus, by this sequence, the stage of manifestly perfect awakening according to the *Māyājāla* has been explained. Now, the other six wheels of wisdom will also be explained through their classification by family. In that regard, first, having performed all the preliminary yogas, one should visualize the Blessed One, the Great Vairocana, residing in the center of the maṇḍala.

At that location, one should visualize the red-colored Amitābha generated from the syllable *hrīḥ*, endowed with the mudrā of meditative concentration, abiding in a state of samādhi; then, one should likewise meditate upon the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*) at his heart.

Furthermore, one should visualize in his heart an eight-spoked wheel with four rims, completely encircled by the root mantra and so forth. Then, one should arrange the seed-syllables upon the eight spokes as follows: OṂ VAJRA TĪKṢṆAYA TE NAḤ.

One should meditate on the center of the hub of the wheel as the body of the one called Refined Vajra (Tīkṣṇavajra), arisen from the syllable *Hrīḥ*, red in color, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, his head decorated with five topknots, wearing garments of various silks, holding a lotus in his left hand and a sword of wisdom (*prajñā-khaḍga*) in his right.

In his heart, as before, one should meditate on a *hrīḥ* atop a moon mandala; then, having performed the sequential emanation and reabsorption as described above, one should meditate. Likewise, according to reality, in the center of the mandala, from the syllable *hūṃ*, there arises Akṣobhya, blue in color, in the posture of treading down (*ākramaṇa-mudrā*).

Having meditated, one should likewise meditate upon the Primordial Buddha in his heart and an eight-spoked wheel; the mantra should be placed as before. Having arranged the eight seed-syllables—*oṃ duḥ khāṃ tshe dā yate namaḥ*—upon the spokes, [one should proceed].

At the navel, one should meditate on the Blessed One Mañjuśrī-duḥkhaccheda, generated from the syllable *hūṃ*. He is blue in color, has the form of a youth, and is adorned with all the ornaments of a child. He has five topknots and wears Chinese silk robes. He holds a vajra in his left hand and a sword in his right. Having visualized him thus:

Visualize the syllable *hūṃ* upon a moon mandala in his heart, and likewise perform the emanation and so forth. Furthermore, in the very same manner, visualize Vairocana in the center of the maṇḍala, generated from the syllable *āḥ*, white in color and bearing the mudrā of supreme enlightenment; in his heart is the Primordial Buddha.

In that same manner, having arranged the seed-syllables *oṃ prajñājñānamūrtaye maḥ* upon the ten spokes of a ten-spoked wheel, one should visualize the Blessed One arising from the letter *āḥ* at the hub of the wheel—white in color, with five topknots, adorned with the ornaments of a youth, and decorated with variegated garments.

Having visualized [himself] holding a wheel with the left hand and the sword of wisdom (*prajñā-khaḍga*) with the right, one should meditate on the syllable *āḥ* upon a moon disc at his heart, and perform the emanation and so forth in that very same manner. Likewise, one should visualize Amoghasiddhi arising from the seed-syllable *āḥ* in the center of the maṇḍala, green in color and endowed with the mudrā of fearlessness.

Having meditated on the primordial Buddha at his heart, and having visualized the eight-spoked wheel at that [Buddha’s] heart with the root mantra and so forth arranged as before, one then places the eight seed-syllables—*oṃ jñānakāyaya te namaḥ*—upon the eight spokes.

On the hub of the wheel (40a7), one should meditate on the Blessed One, the body of primordial wisdom, arisen from the syllable *āḥ*, green in color, adorned with the ornaments of a youth and his head graced by five topknots; he holds a crossed vajra in his left hand and a sword of wisdom in his right. Having meditated on the syllable *āḥ* upon a moon disc at his heart, [one should visualize] it exactly as it is.

Having performed the expansion and withdrawal, one should meditate. Furthermore, just as before, one should meditate on the center of the maṇḍala as the yellow-colored Ratnasambhava, arisen from the syllable OṂ and endowed with the mudrā of supreme generosity (varada).

One should meditate on that very Primordial Buddha at his heart as being endowed with the eight-spoked wheel and the root mantra and so forth; having placed the seed-syllables *oṃ āḥ vāgīśvara yate namaḥ* upon its eight spokes, one visualizes the Blessed Lord Vāgīśvara, yellow in color, generated from the seed-syllable *oṃ* at the hub of the wheel.

Visualize [the deity] adorned with all ornaments, having five protruding humps, and wearing various garments; holding a jewel in the left hand and the sword of wisdom in the right. Having visualized the syllable *Oṃ* upon a moon mandala at his heart, one should likewise perform the emanation and reabsorption [of light rays], and so forth.

In that same manner, one should meditate upon the Bodhicittavajra, white in color, arising from the syllable ĀḤ at the center of the maṇḍala; possessing a graceful and charming demeanor, adorned with the crown of the five families, seated with vajra-pride, arrayed in all ornaments, and holding a vajra and bell.

Having visualized the Bhagavān and the Primordial Buddha at his heart, one should arrange the nine seed-syllables—beginning with "oṃ āra-pacana-aya-te namaḥ"—upon the spokes of a nine-spoked wheel that has been placed at his heart.

On the hub of the wheel, one should meditate on the Blessed One known as Ārapacana, generated from the syllable *ā*. He is the Jñānasattva, white in color, adorned with the ornaments of a child, possessing five topknots, and clad in variegated garments; he holds a book and a sword in his hands.

Having visualized the syllable ĀḤ upon a moon disc at his heart, one should meditate after performing the emanation, withdrawal, entry, and abiding as described above, until stability and so forth are achieved; this should be applied to all [deities]. Furthermore, here too, the six stages of manifest awakening according to the *Śrī-māyājāla* should be understood through the distinctions of the [five] families.

For that very reason, in the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti*, there are seven wheels and seven families; these are to be understood from the oral instructions of the Guru. That which possesses these is the stage of manifest enlightenment through the *Māyājāla*.

From the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā* entitled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, this is the third verse concerning the stage of manifestly perfect awakening through the Net of Magical Illusion; it is the fourth [chapter].

Next, the emission of the vajra-bodhicitta and so forth through the gateway of the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu is taught in the passage beginning with, "In this way, the Buddha, the Bhagavān... The meaning of "the Buddha, the Bhagavān" has already been explained. Regarding the phrase, "The Perfectly Awakened One arose from Ā," it means:

The meaning of the *saṃbuddha* has already been explained. "Arisen from *ā*" means generated from the syllable *ā*, because it is the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body, which is the utterly pure wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) of the Bhagavān. Now, the specific characteristics of that syllable *ā*, which is situated upon the moon mandala at his heart, are described:

"Now, regarding the phrase *'the supreme of all syllables'*: 'supreme' (*praṇīta*) means excellent; the state of being excellent itself is 'supremacy' (*praṇītatva*). 'All syllables' (*sarvākṣara*) refers to every single letter. The 'supreme' among them is the most excellent, because it serves as the gateway for them all. Regarding the term *'great purpose'* (*mahārtha*): it is both a 'purpose' (*artha*) and 'great' (*maha*), and thus it is a 'great purpose'."

It is because it is the very cause for benefiting all living beings. Regarding the phrase "the supreme syllable" (*akṣara-parama*): it is because it does not change through various other enumerations, since it is immovable by its very nature as the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). It is both a syllable (*akṣara*) and supreme (*parama*), and thus it is called the "supreme syllable."

By this sequence as well, the nature of the syllables of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) and so forth is expressed. Each of these is to be individually examined as being the very essence of all the deities of the mandala arising from the yogin’s own mind, which is the nature of turning back every discordant factor without exception.
Thus, it demonstrates that one's own meditative absorptions and their distortions are non-referential.

Because it is precisely that [emptiness], it has the characteristic of being the door to liberation of emptiness, which serves as the antidote to discordant objects of observation. Thus, for those possessed of signs (*nimitta*), perverse aspirations (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and distorted formative activities (*viparyāsa-saṃskāra*), the nature of the side of the antidotes is, respectively, signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

One should perform the liberations that are the nature of the doors of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Regarding those, they are taught with reference to the nature of the consorts belonging to the families, such as Vajrasattvī and so forth, respectively. "Arising from within is unborn" refers to the nature of Vajracittā; therein, "arising from within" is the syllable *ā*.

That too is of the nature of non-arising, because it is the very essence of the *dharmadhātu* and because it is the cause of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). "Free from verbal expression" refers to the perspective of Ratnavajrī: "verbal expression" means the utterance of words; the absence of that is "free [from them]."

This is because there is no exertion of words within the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Regarding the phrase "the supreme cause of all expressions," this is stated from the perspective of Dharmavajrī. "Expression" (*abhilāpa*) means verbal designation; "all expressions" refers to the verbal designations of all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. The "cause" of these is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), which is the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

For that very reason, it is supreme; this is the meaning of "the principal. Regarding the phrase "it makes all words perfectly clear": it is by way of the nature of Karmavajrī. "All words" refers to both the words themselves and all meanings, such as the language of the gods, the language of the nāgas, the language of the yakṣas, and so forth.

For that very reason, it is called "that which makes clearly manifest," because individual appearances arise within the mental continuums of all fortunate sentient beings. Furthermore, the teaching of the Dharma through various doors is due to the very nature of the gnosis of applied effort (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Therefore, these four pāramitās, beginning with Vajrasattvī and the others, are as follows:

One should generate [the deity] from the four syllables: *ā āḥ āṃ āḥ*. Then, that very mind, which is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, being free from the ordinary aspects of grasping and so forth, is itself the adventitious stain.

Because it is devoid of self and is luminosity itself, and because it is the very sign for the arising of other primordial wisdoms, it has the nature of mirror-like primordial wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Because it does not grasp at excellence in transforming other mental continuums through the nature of compassion and so forth that take phenomena as their object, it is the primordial wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

The wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) consists in being unerring with respect to all objects of knowledge. The wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) has the nature of the very cause for benefiting the entire world. These, moreover, are respectively the permanent [nature], the principal, the essence, and the suchness. This is stated as follows: "Great worship, great passion," and so forth.

Furthermore, first of all, being "appropriated by Amitābha" means that it is apprehended primarily through passion; this very point is stated as: "Passion, hatred, and delusion... At the time when the teaching on the offering that pervades the entire space of all Tathāgatas is presented, it is called the "Great Offering."

The word *maha* (great) is used in the sense of "worship. It is the great nature of passion, that is, "great passion" (*mahārāga*). Since it is both worship and great passion, it is called "great worship, great passion. In this context, "great passion" is characterized by the maturation and liberation of sentient beings.

Furthermore, this is the characteristic of the Blessed One, Śrī Vajrasattva, because it is said: "The Blessed One of great passion, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva. As for the phrase "causing all sentient beings to rejoice," it means that he brings joy, satisfaction, and the nature of great bliss to those sentient beings who engage in passion.

It brings joy to all sentient beings and is the nature of Amitābha. With reference to those who act out of hatred, it is said: "Great worship is great hatred; it is the great enemy of all afflictions. The meaning of "great worship" has already been explained. "Great hatred" refers to Akṣobhya.

Furthermore, it is the great enemy of all afflictions; that is to say, it is the great adversary of the primary and secondary afflictions. This is by virtue of one who acts under the influence of delusion.

Having done so, it was said: "The great offering is great ignorance; it is the mind of ignorance that removes ignorance. Here, "the great offering" is as explained above. "Great ignorance" is Vairocana. Regarding "the mind of ignorance," it is the mind that is ignorant; since it is both ignorance and the mind, it is called "the mind of ignorance. "That which removes it" means that which destroys it.

This was spoken with reference to those who engage in anger: "The great offering is great wrath; the great wrath is the great enemy. Here, "the great offering" is as explained above. "Great wrath" refers to Amoghasiddhi. "The great wrath is the great enemy" means that it is a great wrath because its objects are both sentient beings and non-sentient entities.

Thus it is called "the great enemy of that very [reality]. With reference to that which causes attachment, it is said: "The great offering is the great attachment; it removes all attachments. The meaning of "great offering" is explained as above. "Great attachment" is Ratnasambhava.
It removes all attachments because its very purpose is to completely purify all mundane and supramundane excellences. [It also possesses] the four doors of liberation, such as emptiness and so forth.

Because it is the very cause of all meditative absorptions by way of the sense-field of the dharmadhātu, that [emptiness] itself is, internally, the aspect of internal emptiness as the antidote contrary to error, and externally, it has the nature of external emptiness because it is free from objective referents.

The nature of emptiness of the internal and external, by virtue of the fact that their support and body are unobservable and are like pus; and the characteristic of the emptiness of the great, by virtue of being free from excessive attachment to the world of the vessel.

It is said that these very [deities] are based upon the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and consist of the four meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of Vajrasattva and the others: "Great desire is great bliss; great joy is great delight. In this context, "great desire" (*mahārāga*) is Vajrasattva. That which causes one to desire is "desire" (*rāga*), meaning aspiration (*chanda*).
Great bliss is Vajrarāja; great joy is Vajrarāga; great delight is Vajrasādhu. By that very [bliss], the latencies of the eye, forms, and so forth abide.

It is established from the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which is the nature of transformation, because it is itself the blessing (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the non-apprehension of an internal self and so forth. Just as each [wisdom] reverses its own respective discordant factors of error, so too do they give rise to, summon, and take hold of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Furthermore, their sequence is established because they constitute a continuum of excellent qualities. Thus, because that very wisdom of emptiness is itself without signs, there is the emptiness of emptiness; and because one does not grasp even at the signs of the ultimate as being supreme, there is the emptiness of the ultimate.

Because one does not grasp at the signs of the accumulation of merit that is conditioned, there is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); and because one does not grasp at the signs as supreme even regarding the unconditioned accumulation for awakening, there is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). For this very reason it was said: "The body is great, and form is also great."

"Great in color (43a4), great in physical stature, great in name, and vast; it is the expansive great maṇḍala. In this context, "great in form and great in body" refers to the Vajraratna. It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is suitable to be formed, meaning that it is impermanent. That which possesses great form is "one with great form" (*mahārūpin*).

He is "majestic" because, in the form of a wish-fulfilling jewel, he possesses the nature of being consecrated as the Dharma King over the triple world of all Tathāgatas. For that very reason, he is said to have a "vast body," because he manifests throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields. He has a great complexion and a vast physical stature.

"Thus" refers to Vajrasūrya; since he is both the color and the great one, he is the "Great Color," because he possesses six faces. That which possesses a large physical stature is the "Large Stature."

This is because the very mandala of the light of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) is the reality of hearing, reflection, and meditation that are utterly pure. Furthermore, "Great Name" refers to the Vajraketu; one who possesses such a great name is "of Great Name," which means having great renown. From what [does this renown arise]?
It is because it has reached the ultimate perfection of the perfection of generosity. Therefore, as for its vastness: it is both "vast" and "great."

It is vast because it bestows everything. The "vast great maṇḍala" is the vajra-laughter. It is a "maṇḍala" (*maṇḍa*) because it serves as an ornament and an adornment; it is a "la" (*la*) because it takes up that ornament—thus, it is a "maṇḍala. It is "vast" (*visāla*) because it is expansive, for it pervades all world-systems.

That which is the essence of the great mandala described as vast is indeed the great and vast mandala, because it illuminates the three realms. Furthermore, those [mandalas] consist of the nature of the four, such as Vajraratna and so forth, which are the retinue of the wisdom of equality.

Because the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), having undergone transformation, is the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), it possesses the characteristic of signlessness as taught through the purification of subject and object and so forth; and because it has abandoned its own discordant factors, it is characterized by empowerment, the increase of light, and application to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

The sequence of those four, beginning with Vajraratna, is for the sake of accomplishing supreme joy. Furthermore, because there is no attachment to the aspirations of sentient beings who possess limits, there is the emptiness that transcends limits.

Because one does not grasp at the vow, "I shall not abandon cyclic existence which is without beginning or end," there is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end; and because one does not have attachment to the thought, "I shall not intentionally forsake virtue within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder," there is the emptiness of non-abandonment.

Because they are devoid of the desire to purify [phenomena] through the characteristics of intrinsic nature or through a lord of the family (*gotra*), they are the emptinesses of intrinsic nature. For this very reason, it is said: “Wielding the great weapon of wisdom, The supreme great hook for the afflictions; Of great renown and great fame, Great illumination and great clarity.”

Regarding "holding the great weapon of wisdom," this refers to Vajradharma. Here, "wisdom" (prajñā) is the *sōsor kun tu rtog pa’i ye shes* (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna, the wisdom of individual discernment); that itself is the "weapon" (*mtshan*), meaning the instrument of piercing. Because he holds that, he is "one who holds the great weapon of wisdom," for it is the very nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, because he is both the one who holds the great weapon of wisdom and is himself the "great" one, he is the "Great Weapon of Wisdom."

44a1 || It is the Great Holder. The supreme great hook for the afflictions is the Sharp Vajra. "Afflictions" refers to desire and so forth. Because it serves as the hook for those [afflictions], it is the "hook of afflictions. It is a "hook" because it is like a hook, since it attains mastery over the afflictions. 44a2 ||

Since that very thing is both the hook of the afflictions and the great one, it is the "Great Hook of Afflictions. For that very reason, it is also supreme; this is the meaning of the term "Excellent" (*pra*). It is the "Great Renown" (*mahāyaśas*), which means great fame; it is the "Vajra Cause" (*vajrahetu*).

Regarding all mandalas taught in the tantras as means for bringing sentient beings to full maturity, he who possesses great renown because of his very nature as a universal monarch (cakravartin) is "the one of great renown" (Mahāyaśas).

For that very reason, he who possesses renown that pervades the world-systems without exception or remainder is called "the one of great renown. He who possesses great illumination and great clarity is the "Vajra Speaker" (Vajrabhāṣa). He who possesses great rays of light that illuminate the three realms is "the one of great illumination."

Then again, having completely abandoned the verbal faults of haste, hesitation, and indistinctness, during the time of recitation, one should maintain a nature of silence; because [the mantra] appears extensively within the mental continuums of all sentient beings, it is "greatly luminous" (*mahāprabhāsa*).

These also have the nature of Vajradharma and others, who rely upon the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) characterized by the transformation of the conceptualizing mind; for, through the purification of the distortions as taught regarding the discerning wisdom, they discern the suchness of all phenomena, and thus, by way of that, [they are] the naturally pure dharmatā.

Because it is the very continuum of those such as Vajradharma, who possess wisdom and gnosis, are irreversible, and have fully realized the entire intended meaning, this itself constitutes their sequence. Furthermore, because it brings about the form body (*rūpakāya*) whose nature consists of the major marks and minor signs, it is the emptiness of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*).

Because the dharmakāya, which is the nature of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, is not something to be accumulated, all phenomena are emptiness; and because there is no accumulation through the superimposition of a person or phenomena, it is the emptiness of non-entities.
