Because they deprecate the very nature of things and the characteristics of emptiness as they have been taught, and because they do not engage in formative activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), there are the emptinesses of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Regarding this, it is said: "The wise one who holds the great illusion, Who has accomplished the purpose of the great illusion, Rejoices with joy in the great illusion."

"Possessing the magical illusions of the Great Illusion" means that the "Vajra-holder who is skilled in the Great Illusion" arises from the Vajra. In this context, "illusion" refers to the emanations of the manifold and extensive offerings of all the Tathāgatas. Because he holds these, he is called the "Holder of Illusion."

Since that which is great is also that very same illusion, he is the "Holder of the Great Illusion" (Mahāmāyādharin). For that very reason, he is the wise Paṇḍita, because through the act of worship he accumulates the collection of merit. The accomplishment of the purpose of the Great Illusion is the Vajra Protection. In this context, the meaning of "illusion" (māyā) is the meaning of "emanation" (nirmāṇa).

Because he brings about great inspiration in sentient beings who are lazy, he is Māyājālasiddhi; since he is both "Great" (mahat) and "Māyājālasiddhi," he is Mahāmāyāsiddhi. Mahāmāyānandānanda is Vajrayakṣa. One who delights in *māyā* is "Delighting in *Māyā*" (*māyānanda*).

This means "delighting in the emanations of the offerings to the Tathāgatas. Attachment to the delight of *māyā* is "delight"; one delights through the delight of *māyā*. It is both "great" and that very same delight of the *māyā*, thus it is "delighting in the great delight of *māyā*. The "great *māyā* with magical eyes" is the Vajramuṣṭi.

The "magician" (māyākāra) is the collection of emanations; it is the unification of the vajras of body, speech, and mind. One who knows that is the "magician. Since he is both the "great illusion" (mahāmāyā) and the "magician," he is the "Great Illusion Magician. In this context, because these are words of the sublime Dharma, they should be understood as being without long vowels [i.e., *māyākāra*].

These, moreover, are based upon the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and consist of the fourfold nature of the vajra and so forth; they abide as the wisdom of accomplishment, which is the nature of the transformation of the sense-consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness.

By way of abandoning the aforementioned perversions, one performs worship to all the Sugatas, provides them with protection, and pacifies obstacles; because the body and so forth are emptiness and because they constitute gnosis, for that very reason, the sequence of the activities of those [deities] such as Vajra and the rest is called the "sequence of activities."

Likewise, by way of being the very antidotes to stinginess, immoral conduct, intolerance, and laziness, he is the embodiment of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence. Therefore it is said: "The great lord of donors, the supreme upholder of great ethical discipline."

"He is the steadfast one who maintains great patience, and he is the one committed to great diligence. Regarding that: "The great donor, the sovereign" refers to Vajralāsyā. She is called a "donor" (dānapati) because she bestows the desired gifts of worship and favor. She is the "master" (pati) of that gift, and thus a "donor"; since she is both that donor and "great," she is the "great donor" (mahādānapati).

This is because she bestows the nature of material wealth, refuge, the Dharma, and empowerment. Therefore, she is the "Principal One" (Pradhānī), for she is the most excellent among all worlds. She who upholds the great morality is the supreme Vajramālā.

Because body, speech, and mind are placed in equipoise, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is "equipoised"; this is the meaning of the verbal root [*sam-ā-dhā*]. It is characterized by the abandonment of the ten non-virtuous actions and has the nature of the *prātimokṣa*; because one upholds these, one "maintains ethical discipline."

Since he is both great and one who maintains ethical discipline, he is "one who maintains great ethical discipline. For that very reason, he is supreme, because he goes before [all others]. The steadfast one who maintains great patience is Vajravāṇī. Because she acts with firm resolve, she is "patience" (kṣānti); because she upholds that, she is "one who maintains patience" (kṣāntidhara).
Since that very greatness is itself patience, he is "the bearer of great patience. That very [patience] is also steadfast, because it is firm and enduring even amidst great suffering. Diligence...

Great diligence (*vīrya*) is the *vajranṛtyā* [mudrā]. Great diligence is enthusiasm for what is virtuous; enthusiasm for evil and the like is merely indolence and not diligence, because it is base. Its "undertaking" (*vrata*) is the complete fulfillment of all mundane and supramundane roots of virtue.

Therefore, because the nature of the four secret offerings is established respectively from the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the others, they are rendered as the excellence of the manifest Joyful Realm (*Abhirati*), spontaneously accomplished through the power of the purity of one's own doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). That very [state] is [the remedy for] impaired wisdom and distraction.

It was spoken out of a delight in being without authentic aspirations, in [sympathy with] those who are weak, and in overcoming discordant factors: "Abiding in the great meditative concentration of samādhi, bearing the body of great wisdom, possessing great power and great skillful means, he is a great ocean of aspiration and primordial wisdom."

In this verse, one should understand that *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom) are interchanged. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the bearer of the body of great wisdom is Vajradhūpā. Great wisdom is *prajñā*; because she bears that very body, she is the bearer of the body of great wisdom.

The Great Dhyāna, the abode of samādhi, is Vajrapuṣpā. Samādhi is characterized by one-pointedness of mind. Because it is based upon that, it is the "abode of samādhi"; since it is both great and dhyāna itself, it is the "Great Dhyāna. It is "great" because its nature consists of the four dhyānas.

One abides in the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of those four dhyānas. The *praṇidhāna* is the Vajra Lamp. It is called *praṇidhāna* because one makes a vow; for bodhisattvas are born through the power of their vows. The "Great Skillful Means" (*mahopāya*) is the Vajra Perfume Water. It is both great and a skillful means, and thus it is the "Great Skillful Means."

This is because, through the power of skillful means itself, it completely fulfills the hopes and intentions of all world systems without exception or remainder. That very [skillful means] is wisdom and...

The fourfold nature of external offerings consists of the characteristics of the perfections of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and skillful means (*upāya*). Because they have the nature of entering the *dharmadhātu* through the two—power (*bala*) and gnosis (*jñāna*)—by means of the entities that cause delight in the path together with its enjoyments, there is the thorough differentiation of those powers and gnoses.

Regarding those, the powers are the five beginning with faith. Wisdom consists of the path of seeing and the path of meditation. Among these, the path of seeing comprises the seven factors of enlightenment, while the path of meditation comprises the eightfold noble path. Furthermore, these have the nature of the four gatekeepers, which are the essential identities of faith, diligence, mindfulness, and meditative concentration.

This is because it involves manifest conviction in the Mahāyāna, entering it, maintaining that continuity without interruption, and bringing about complete satisfaction. That very [nature] consists of the sixteen meditative absorptions (samādhi) such as loving-kindness (maitrī) and so forth, by way of the distinctions of emptiness (śūnyatā) as taught, which depend solely upon the complete purity of wisdom (prajñā). Therefore, it was said:

"Of the nature of immeasurable great love, supreme intellect through great compassion, possessing great wisdom and a vast mind, a great sage with great skillful means. Regarding this, "of the nature of immeasurable great love" refers to loving-kindness (*maitrī*). One who possesses affection is "affectionate," and the suffix indicates one who is endowed with that condition.

That is the nature endowed with love for all sentient beings; since it is both greatness and the very nature of loving-kindness, it is the "nature of great loving-kindness. For that very reason, it is immeasurable, because its loving-kindness extends toward all world-systems as if toward an only son. Mañjuśrī is the supreme intellect of great compassion.

Great compassion has the nature of non-apprehension. One who possesses that is "one endowed with great compassion. The supreme intellect is the primordial wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*. By this, it is stated: "The Blessed One is of a profound and vast nature."
One who possesses great wisdom and a vast intellect is the "Scent Elephant" (*gandhahastin*);

he is one of great wisdom, whose very nature is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). One who possesses this is "wise"; since he is both "great" and "wise," he is "one of great wisdom and vast intellect. One who is highly skilled and possesses great skillful means is the "Wisdom Banner" (*jñānaketu*). One who has great skillful means is "one of great skillful means."

In this regard, the "greatly wise" one possesses the great perfection of intellect, because he teaches the sublime Dharma through his knowledge of the intentions and latent tendencies of all sentient beings. He possesses great miraculous power, strength, and great speed; he is renowned for his great miraculous power, the great strength that overcomes adversaries, and great vigor.

Thus, regarding that [verse], "possessing the power of great miraculous feats" refers to Bhadrapāla. "Power of miraculous feats" means the power of *ṛddhi*; one who possesses that is "possessing the power of miraculous feats. Since he is both "great" and "possessing the power of miraculous feats," he is "one possessing the power of great miraculous feats."

He is of great power and great speed, the Ocean of Intelligence. He is of great power because he possesses the strength to travel through many worlds for the sake of making offerings and rendering service to all the Tathāgatas; it is for this very reason that he is called "of great speed. He is of great miraculous power and renowned far and wide, the Inexhaustible Intelligence.

Because he possesses the accumulations of merit and wisdom of the world, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas, he is of great miraculous power (*mahārddhi*). Because he has perfected the accumulations of merit and wisdom of all the Tathāgatas, he is widely renowned (*mahāyaśas*). He who overcomes great adversaries with his powers is the one whose eloquence is a mass of peaks (*pratibhānakūṭa*).

Since that which is great is also power itself, the ten powers of the Tathāgata—beginning with the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible—are to be understood as those that arise hereafter. As for their "overpowering," whoever possesses the initiation of diligence toward them is the one who overpowers through great power. He shatters the great mountain of existence.

"Holder of the great, firm, great vajra; the great fierce one of great violence; the great terrifier who causes fear"—this refers to his great power in crushing the great mountain of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

[This is] the attainment of the state [of a Buddha]. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*). That itself is a mountain, because it is a sheer cliff of ignorance. One who possesses the manner of destroying those [aggregates] by attaining perfectly non-erroneous primordial wisdom (*aviparīta-jñāna*) is a destroyer. Since that is both "great" and the destroyer of the mountain of existence, it is the Great Destroyer of the Mountain of Existence.

"He destroys the great mountain of existence. Thus it is said. "The bearer of the great, firm vajra" refers to the deliverer from all lower realms. The "great vajra" is the primordial wisdom (jñāna) of Samantabhadra; because he holds that, he is the "bearer of the great vajra. He is "firm" because of his solidity and because he possesses a body.

47a3. "The Great Fierce One of Great Ferocity" refers to the intellect that utterly destroys the darkness of sorrow. Because he is both great and fierce, he is the "Great Fierce One," for he manifests in the form of a great wrathful deity (*krodha*) for the sake of those sentient beings who are difficult to discipline.

"Great ferocity" means that although the Blessed One Mañjuśrī is peaceful, he manifests as one who possesses ferocity for the sake of taming sentient beings. "The terrifier of great terror" refers to Jālinīprabha. He is "great terror" because he assumes the form of Mahābhairava; furthermore, because he terrifies even that [Mahābhairava], he is "the terrifier of great terror."

"The Protector, the Great Supreme Family, the Guru, the Supreme among the Great Secret Mantra, abiding in the way of the Mahāyāna, the supreme among the ways of the Mahāyāna. Regarding this: "The Protector, the Great Supreme Family" refers to the Youthful Candraprabha. He is both great and belongs to that very family; thus, he is the "Great Supreme Family," which refers to the four dhāraṇīs. Furthermore, it says: [and so forth].

These are the essences of the meaning, the mantras, and the mudrās. He is the Protector, because he perfectly purifies all sins of body, speech, and mind committed by all sentient beings without exception. The supreme great secret mantra of the Guru is Amitābha.

Since it is both the Great (Mahā) and the Secret Mantra (Guhyamantra), it is the "Great Secret Mantra" (Mahāguhyamantra); its nature is that of Mahāmudrā. Its "supreme" (uttama) means its preeminence. It is the Guru itself, for having understood the intentions and latent dispositions of all sentient beings exactly as they are, it reveals the proximate realization.

Because of that. Abiding in the system of the Mahāyāna is the "Treasury of Space. The Mahāyāna is what is taught below; its "system" (naya) is the path. To "abide" in it means to mount it. The supreme system of the Mahāyāna is the "Removal of Obscurations."

The non-conceptual primordial wisdom that realizes both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as the ineffable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called the Mahāyāna. Alternatively, it is said that the Mahāyāna is subsumed by three unsurpassed aspects: the mode of abiding of saṃsāra, its objective sphere, and the nature of its support.

If that is so, one might ask: how is it "great" (mahat)? It is great because of the Blessed Buddhas who act for the benefit of the entire world; for them, this vehicle is established as the ultimate goal for the sake of definitive emergence. Therefore, because it is a vehicle together with that greatness, it is the Mahāyāna, or the Great Vehicle.

It is the Great Vehicle because it is the vehicle of greatness itself. Alternatively, it is the Great Vehicle because of the seven aspects of greatness: due to its greatness of objective referent (*ālambana*), practice (*pratipatti*), gnosis (*jñāna*), diligence (*vīrya*), skillful means (*upāya*), perfect accomplishment (*samyak-samudāgama*), and activity (*karman*). Since it is both great and a vehicle, it is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Because those [qualities] do not exist in other vehicles. Therefore, in brief, the Mahāyāna should be understood as having three aspects—the nature of the cause, the object, and the support—for the purpose of manifesting them. This is either in view of the mere means, or...

Because he is the nature of the entire world and that which transcends the world, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*), is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of the Tathāgata. Thus: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, has arisen from the letter A."

One should regard Mañjuśrī, the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) who dwells in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas—distinguished by the specific characteristics of the syllables of the name-mantra, such as "Thus" (iti) and so forth, which consist of verses and prose without connecting particles—as "Mañjuśrī, the supreme and glorious wisdom-being."

Those deities of the maṇḍala, such as Cittavajrī and the others, are also emanated through union with the mahāmudrā, possessing their respective body colors and hand implements. Having been emanated, they perform the buddha-activities for the sentient beings of all world systems; then, returning once more, they transform themselves into the colors of their respective families according to the syllables of the name-mantras.

Having meditated on oneself as residing within the moon mandalas arranged in the five great Vajradhātu maṇḍalas according to the sequence of the objects [of practice], one should resolve with conviction that one's own self is the wisdom-body of all the Tathāgatas, the form of Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, as described above, abiding at the hub of that wheel.

Blessed One, if any son of noble family or daughter of noble family—any bodhisattva practicing the conduct through the gateway of mantra—recites this *Mañjuśrī-nāma-saṃgīti*, the crown jewel of names which is the non-dual, authentic ultimate reality of that very Body of Wisdom (*jñānakāya*), three times a day, or reads and recites it from a manuscript;

Whether pure or impure, by reciting the syllables of the name-mantra in verse in such a way that one says nothing at all and no one hears it as it truly is, before long one will indeed attain the collection of qualities described as qualities, and furthermore, other accomplishments will be achieved.

Any person who correctly upholds the *Mañjuśrī-nāmasamgīti* of the ultimate truth will have thoroughly accumulated the collections of merit and wisdom; having swiftly perfected all the qualities of the Buddhas, they will manifest complete awakening in unsurpassed, perfect, and full enlightenment.

For many eons, they will become those whose nature is not to pass into parinirvāṇa; they will teach the unsurpassed Dharma to all sentient beings and become Dharma Kings who resound the drum of the sublime Dharma throughout the ten directions.

Having condensed the syllables and phrases of the mantras that constitute the names of that great Vajradhātu maṇḍala into a single set, there are eighty-six names; these, moreover, should be applied by being distributed among the deities of the great maṇḍala. Among those, four are the *jñāna*...

The letter *a* belongs to Vajrasattva and the lunar mandala; it is the third [vowel]. There are eleven [syllables] belonging to Vajrasattvī and the others, as well as Nityā and the rest, beginning first with Vajrasattva.

Up until the ultimate point where all obscurations are completely cleared away, one should apply [the names] in their proper sequence according to the specific and distinctive nature of each syllable, mantra, and phrase of the names without exception. There are fourteen verses, and the syllables, mantras, and phrases of the names number eighty-six; this is the oral instruction.

From the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā-vistara*, titled *The Secret Mantra Meaning of Names: A Detailed Exposition*, this is the fifth chapter, concerning the sequence of the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Expanse of the Bodhicitta.

[306] Now, the second wheel of Vairocana is described. Having thus manifested the majesty of Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva—the gnosis-body of all Tathāgatas—through the sequence of the arrangement of the deities of the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, he now, desiring to demonstrate the pervasion of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena by means of the Suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna through the gateway of Mahāvairocana, spoke on the arrangement of his own wheel for the sake of disciplining sentient beings who act out of delusion, by means of his own door of liberation.

In that regard, it is not known what the distinction is between Vairocana and Mahāvairocana; therefore, it is said: [Vairocana] is characterized by the natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the flow-on body (*naiṣyandikakāya*), and the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and he resides in the world of the king of gods in Akaniṣṭha.

Therein, for the sake of experiencing the enjoyment of the Dharma by those Bodhisattvas reborn in that divine assembly, the Lord Vairocana—who is characterized by the manifestation of perfectly pure gnosis and is the outflowing body (*naiṣyandika-kāya*) produced by turning back the ripening body (*vaipākika-kāya*) through the sequence of the samādhi of perfect awakening—manifests himself right there in that celestial abode, surrounded by a host of great Bodhisattvas.

As it is said in the *Śrīguhyendutilakatantra*: "In the delightful realm of Akaniṣṭha, situated above the Pure Abodes, there the Perfect Buddhas awaken; but here, it is the emanation who awakens"—thus is the verse.

Mahāvairocana, however, is the body consisting of gnosis, utterly liberated from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, and capable of manifesting the appearance of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

How is it that this Blessed One is capable of manifesting all phenomena precisely through the very nature of reality? Thus it is said in the *Śrīvairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*: "The Blessed Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, having attained the knowledge of omniscience, distribute that knowledge of omniscience among all sentient beings and teach the Dharma through various methods, various intentions, and various skillful means."

To some they taught the method of the Śrāvaka vehicle; to some, the method of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; to some, the method of the Mahāyāna; to some, the method of the knowledge of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); to some for rebirth as a god; and to some for rebirth as a human. They taught the Dharma even for the sake of rebirth as a *mahoraga*, *yakṣa*, *rākṣasa*, *asura*, *gandharva*, *garuḍa*, *kiṃnara*, and so forth. Among them, some beings who were to be disciplined by a Buddha saw him in the form of a Buddha; others saw him in the form of a Śrāvaka.

Some saw him in the form of a Pratyekabuddha; some in the form of a Bodhisattva; some in the form of Maheśvara; some in the form of Brahmā; some in the form of Nārāyaṇa; some in the form of Vaiśravaṇa; and others saw him in the forms of Mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. He was established in various modes of conduct through their respective ways of speech and illustration; yet that omniscient wisdom is of a single flavor—that is, the flavor of being inseparable from suchness.

Therefore, he says "Mahāvairocana. He is called Vairocana because he shines (*virocyate*) or blazes; Vairocana is simply Virocana, with the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) applied for the sake of the word itself. He is Mahāvairocana because he is both great (*mahān*) and Vairocana. He is a Buddha because of his awakening to all phenomena exactly as they exist. He is Mauna because of his union with the silence of body, speech, and mind. It is Great Silence (*mahāmauna*) because it is both great and silence. Why is it Great Silence? Because he is perpetually in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). And so it has been said:

Because of the statement that "the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are indeed always in a state of meditative equipoise," and because of the absence of any coarseness (dauṣṭhulya) pertaining to the body and so forth, he possesses this [state]; thus, he is the Great Sage (mahāmaunī). Furthermore, those who are both great and sages are the Great Sages (mahāmunayaḥ), such as Vyāsa, Vaśiṣṭha, Vālmīka, and others. He is called the Great Sage because he appears in such a form to those to be trained by him.

"Arising from the Great Mantra Method" (*mahāmantranayodbhūta*) means that the Mantra Method is the Vajra Mahāyāna; because he arises from that Mantra Method, he is "arisen from the Mantra Method. He is both great and arisen from the Mantra Method, thus "Great and Arisen from the Mantra Method," because he is accomplished from that very source. For this reason, he is "of the nature of the Great Mantra Method," which means his essence is the Vajra Mahāyāna. And for that reason, he is "Mahāvairocana. Thus, through these and other such titles, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is to be called "the Best among the Glorious Ones."

"Attainer of the ten perfections, basis of the ten perfections, purity of the ten perfections, and the method of the ten perfections. (MNS 6.2) In this regard, showing the path of the attainment, basis, and purity of the perfections, he says: "attainer of the ten perfections. Therein, regarding the "ten perfections," it is stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*: "Giving, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge—these are the ten perfections."

In this regard, generosity is threefold: the gift of the Dharma, the gift of material things, and the gift of loving-kindness. Ethical discipline is threefold: the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings. Patience is threefold: patience in reflecting on the Dharma, patience in enduring suffering, and patience in forbearing the harm inflicted by others. Diligence is threefold: the diligence of armor, the diligence of application, and the diligence of final accomplishment. Meditative concentration is threefold.

The removal of faults is threefold: pertaining to the forest-dwelling life (*vaihārika*), and pertaining to supernatural power (*vaibhūtika*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) is threefold: consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*), consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*), and consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). Skillful means (*upāya*) is threefold: that which removes one's own faults, that which introduces sentient beings [to the path], and that which brings about swift awakening (*kṣiprābhisambodhaka*). The vow (*praṇidhi*) is threefold: that which ensures the continuity of one's own accumulations (*svasambhāra-prābandhika*), that which follows after the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha-anubandhika*), and that which purifies the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra-pariśodhana*). Power (*bala*) is threefold.

It turns back karma, removes afflictions, and wards off Māra and adversaries. Knowledge is threefold: non-conceptual, that which awakens to the equality of conceptualization, and that which is direct regarding all means. These [practices] beginning with generosity, when they fulfill the mind of complete enlightenment and are permeated by a foundation of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, receive the name "perfections" (pāramitās). Furthermore, these are both mundane and supramundane. Among them, those perfections in which there is an unobstructed apprehension of a self and so forth are mundane.

The supramundane aggregates and so forth are those that proceed from the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in selflessness and the like regarding the aggregates, and are further manifested through the realization of reality (*tattva*). For this very reason, Candrakīrti says in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*: "Supramundane perfection is the gift that is empty of the recipient, the object given, and the giver; therein, that which is born of attachment is designated as mundane perfection."

The term *pāramitā* is derived as follows: having analyzed [the compound] as "one who goes to the limit (*paryanta*) of the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through the sequence of the arising of knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation," the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule "there is occasional non-elision of an augment" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*), the augment *tuK* is not added. Next, by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix, the case-ending is frequently not elided," the accusative case-ending is retained. Thus, from *pārami*, the abstract state is formed as *pāramitā*. The perfection of giving is *dānapāramitā*; the same should be applied to morality and the other perfections as well.

Therefore, the giving of Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*), which is characterized by the purity of the three spheres (*trikoṭipariśuddhi*), is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). However, the giving of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) is merely giving and not the perfection of giving, because it lacks the knowledge of the purity of the three spheres. Consequently, among the perfections such as giving, it should be understood that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) alone is the eye. For this very reason, Candrakīrti says in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*:

Just as an entire multitude of blind people is easily led to whatever destination they desire by a single man who possesses eyes, so too does wisdom proceed here, taking along those devoid of sight; thus it attains the qualities [of the path] and Buddhahood. Therefore, the Blessed One who has reached and realized the ten perfections in such a manner is described as "Thus-Gone" (Tathāgata).

[Regarding the phrase "the basis for the ten perfections": In this context, "basis" (*āśraya*) means support (*ādhāra*). This is because these very ten perfections function as the support and because they are that which is supported by it. What is intended by this is that the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is indicated through the relationship of mutual support and supported.
Regarding "the purity of the ten perfections": because they are purified of the three spheres, there is the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient in these perfections.

"The method of the ten perfections" means that which has the ten perfections as its method, path, and means; it is so described. Furthermore, these are to be applied to the stages (*bhūmi*). For example: on the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā*), the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) becomes preeminent; on the Stainless (*vimalā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); on the Luminous (*prabhākārī*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); on the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); on the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); on the Facing (*abhimukhī*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); and on the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*), the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
On the Immovable stage is the perfection of aspiration; on the Good Intelligence stage is the perfection of power; and on the Cloud of Dharma stage is the perfection of primordial wisdom.

In this regard, although there is no distinction in the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) across these stages, they receive their specific designations based on the purification of the perfections (*pāramitā*), such as generosity (*dāna*). Furthermore, by the power of their vows, their magnificence (*audārya*) is infinite and not shared with any of the śrāvakas or others. In this context, "stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to a state of knowledge (*jñāna*); that is to say, it is a sphere of activity (*gocara*).

In this context, they are called "grounds" (*bhūmi*) because, through the attainment of awakening, they involve the establishment of ever-higher knowledge and the acquisition of the qualities of each respective knowledge. Since the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) possesses a common characteristic everywhere—because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is excluded from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—they realize the equality of self (*ātmasamatā*) due to the non-distinction of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Furthermore, although that knowledge is one, it is said to be tenfold due to the distinction of its states. Therefore, he says:

"The Lord who is the master of the ten stages, established upon the ten stages" (MNS 44ab). This means he is the master (*īśvara*) or sovereign (*adhipati*) of the ten stages, beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*). He is called the "Lord" (*nātha*) because, on each respective stage, he has attained mastery over the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity and the rest. He is said to be "established" because he is firmly grounded in those very ten stages.

The ten knowledges are: knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), knowledge of destruction (kṣaya-jñāna), and knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).

What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? It is the untainted knowledge regarding the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) associated with the realm of desire; it is the untainted knowledge regarding the cause of the conditioned factors associated with the realm of desire; it is the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of the conditioned factors associated with the realm of desire; and it is the untainted knowledge regarding the path for the abandonment of the conditioned factors associated with the realm of desire.

Furthermore, that untainted knowledge regarding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the stage of the knowledge of phenomena is called the knowledge of phenomena. What is subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)? It is the untainted knowledge regarding the conditioned factors (saṃskāra) associated with the realms of form and formlessness; the untainted knowledge regarding the cause of the conditioned factors associated with the realms of form and formlessness; and the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of the conditioned factors associated with the realms of form and formlessness.

It is the untainted knowledge regarding the path for the abandonment of the conditioned phenomena associated with the realms of form and formlessness. Furthermore, it is the untainted knowledge within subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and on the stage of subsequent knowledge; this is called subsequent knowledge. What is the knowledge of others' minds? It is that knowledge consisting of cultivation, which is the fruit of cultivation, attained through the path of cultivation and not lost.

That knowledge by which one knows the mental states and mental factors—whether belonging to the desire realm or the form realm—that are present and manifest in others, as well as certain untainted (anāsrava) dharmas; this is called the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna). What is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)? It is tainted wisdom (prajñā). What is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?

The untainted knowledge that arises for one who attends to the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—this is called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*). What is the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*)? It is the untainted knowledge that arises for one who attends to tainted causes as cause, origin, production, and condition; that is the knowledge of origin. What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)?

The untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of one who attends to cessation as cessation, as peaceful, as sublime, and as a state of escape, is called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). What is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)? It is the untainted knowledge of one who attends to the path as the path, as the correct method, as practice, and as leading to liberation; this is called the knowledge of the path. What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)? It is knowing: "Suffering has been fully understood by me," and "The origin has been abandoned by me."

He knows: "Cessation has been realized; the path has been cultivated. Based on that, there is knowledge, vision, science, awakening, the light of wisdom, and clear realization. This is called the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*). What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)? He knows: "Suffering has been fully understood by me; it is not to be understood again. "The origin has been abandoned; it is not to be abandoned again. "Cessation has been realized; it is not to be realized again."

He knows: "The path has been cultivated by me; it is not to be cultivated again. Based on that, there is knowledge, vision, science, awakening, the light of wisdom, and clear realization; this is called the knowledge of non-arising. Therefore it is said: "His self is purified by the ten knowledges; he possesses the purity of the ten knowledges. (MNS 44cd = 6.3cd)

And thus, the Blessed One—whose self-nature (ātmasvabhāva) is purified by these ten knowledges—is one whose self is purified by the ten knowledges (*daśajñānaviśuddhātmā*). Because he maintains that very purity of the ten knowledges, which is knowledge naturally luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*), he is "the upholder of the purity of the ten knowledges" (*daśajñānaviśuddhadhṛk*). This is due to the departure of all signs (*nimitta*).

And so it is said in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*: "Regarding [the views of] being a single entity, being a cause, being an enjoyer, being an agent, being independent, having sovereignty, being permanent, being the basis for affliction and purity, being a yogi, and being unliberated or liberated—verily, the view of a self operates with respect to these [aggregates and so forth]. This tenfold grasping at a self proceeds with respect to the aggregates and so on; namely: the grasping at unity, the grasping at causality, the grasping at being an enjoyer, the grasping at being an agent, the grasping at independence, the grasping at sovereignty, and the grasping at permanence."
The grasping at [the self as] being defiled or purified; the grasping at [the self as] being a practitioner of yoga; and the grasping at [the self as] being liberated.

Therefore, he says: "of ten aspects" (*daśākāra*). They are called "aspects" (*ākāra*) because by means of them the mind is directed toward or distracted from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) onto the aggregates and so forth; these are the ten forms of grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*). For this very reason, the venerable Dignāga stated in the *Saṅgraha*: "The mind is distracted elsewhere by the ten distractions of the mind; thus it becomes unfit for the attainment of non-dual knowledge by the foolish. Therefore, the Blessed One is described as such because he has [overcome] those who possess these ten aspects of grasping at a self. If one asks why, it is because he appears even in the form of all that is to be countered (*vipakṣa*).

The ten meanings that serve as the antidotes to those [ten views] are recited in that very same [text]: "The reality of the fundamental characteristic, the characteristic of non-perversion, the reality consisting of fruit and cause, and likewise the subtle and the gross; the well-established, the object of purification, the summarized, the characteristic of differentiation, and the reality of skillfulness—these are the tenfold [realities] as the antidote to the view of self. Thus, reality is of ten kinds.

Namely: the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), the reality of non-perversion (*aviparyāsatattva*), the reality of cause and fruit (*phalahetutattva*), the reality of the coarse and the subtle (*audārikasūkṣmatattva*), the well-established reality (*prasiddhatattva*), the reality of the sphere of purification (*viśuddhigocaratattva*), the reality of inclusion (*saṃgrāhakatattva*), the reality of differentiation (*bhedatattva*), and the reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*). Furthermore, these ten types should be understood as being the antidotes to the ten kinds of grasping at a self. Therefore, it is said: "the meaning of the ten objects."

In this regard, the reality of these ten objects of skill (*kauśalyārtha*), which serve as the arising of their respective antidotes, is as follows: "object" (*artha*) is so called because it is sought after (*arthyate*). Since they possess the nature of the ultimate object (*paramārtha*), the meaning of those ten objects should be understood as the reality of the ten skills (*kauśalyatattva*), by way of being the antidote to the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). This has been explained in detail in that very [text], but it is not intended to be discussed here for fear of excessive prolixity. Consequently, what is stated is this: that Blessed One alone should be understood as having the nature of the antidote to all opposing factors (*vipakṣa*).

In this regard, because he taught the non-erroneous dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), [the Buddha] is the unsurpassed Teacher, enriched with the sovereign power of the complete accumulations of merit and wisdom; since the status of a Lord of Munis (*munīndra*)—which is exceedingly difficult to attain even for the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and other sages—is his alone, it is said: "The Lord of Munis. For this very reason, the venerable master Nāgārjuna stated: "Homage to that Lord of Munis, who proclaims dependent origination," and so forth.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are as follows: the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible; the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma; the power of knowledge regarding the various elements; the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations; the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties; the power of knowledge regarding the various meditative concentrations and attainments; the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere; the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth; the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of former abodes; and the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows.

And this power of the ten knowledges (*daśajñānabala*) is so called because it is characterized by the specific power of the Blessed One’s own nature; because he abides in non-conceptual equality and has realized the proliferation of states and so forth, he says: "The One Endowed with the Ten Powers" (*daśabala*). He is described thus because those ten powers of a Tathāgata exist within him.
For this very reason, he is "the All-pervading One" (*vibhu*), for his majesty consists in being the intrinsic nature of all things, both stable and moving.

Regarding the phrase *aśeṣaviśvārtha*: it means the purpose (*artha*) of the entire, complete, and exhaustive universe (*viśva*). He whose nature is to effect that purpose for the entire universe is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), the one who effects the welfare of the entire universe (*aśeṣaviśvārthakara*).

"Master of the ten forms, the Great One. In this context, the "ten forms" are the ten masteries (*vaśitā*). They are as follows: mastery over life, mastery over karma, mastery over requisites, mastery over liberation, mastery over aspiration, mastery over supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), mastery over rebirth, mastery over phenomena (*dharma*), mastery over mind, and mastery over knowledge. He whose nature it is to exercise control over those phenomena characterized by these ten forms of mastery is "master of the ten forms. And because he has attained all the qualities of mastery, he is therefore called "the Great One."

"Beginningless" (*anādi*) means that which has no beginning, that is, no origination; because there is an absence of arising, it follows by implication that there is no destruction. Because of the attainment of non-abiding gnosis, the meaning is that neither a beginning nor an end exists.

"Of a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcātman*). Conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are those phenomena characterized by the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the grasped and the grasper; their "nature" (*ātman*) is their own-form (*svarūpa*). Since that [reality] is devoid of such a nature of proliferation, it is "of a nature free from conceptual proliferation. For this very reason, it is "of a pure nature" (*śuddhātman*), because adventitious stains have been removed. Yet, there is no alteration of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for this very reason, it is "consisting of suchness" (*tathatātmaka*). In this context, "suchness" (*tathatā*) means being thus (*tathā*) without change, in the sense that it is eternally just so. That which has suchness as its self, its intrinsic nature, is "consisting of suchness"; the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"One who speaks of reality" (*bhūtavādī*): therein, "realities" (*bhūtāni*) are the four noble truths, namely those called suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He whose nature it is to speak—that is, to utter—those [truths] is such [a person]. Alternatively, the meaning of profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the "reality" (*yathārtha*). To speak of that is as explained before. For this very reason, the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna said: "There is nothing to be removed from this, nor anything at all to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; he who sees reality is liberated."

"One who acts as he speaks" means that just as he declares all phenomena to be empty, selfless, and like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or the moon reflected in water, he likewise attends to them in that very way; thus he is called "one who acts as he speaks. For this very reason, he is "one whose speech is not otherwise," because his speech is truthful and he turns the wheel of Dharma without error according to the spiritual lineage of all sentient beings.

"Non-dual" (*advaya*) means the absence of duality, that is, the absence of the grasped and the grasper. The existence of that absence is called "non-dual. Although the Blessed One is non-dual from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he speaks of duality according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). "Established in the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭivyavasthita*) means that, in the sense of being non-erroneous, the limit of reality is the non-substantiality of error; he is established in that limit of reality because he is not distinct from its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the term *nairātmyasiṃhanirnādī*: therein, selflessness (*nairātmya*) is threefold—selflessness of lack of characteristics (*alakṣaṇanairātmya*), selflessness of distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇanairātmya*), and selflessness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇanairātmya*). This very triad of selflessnesses is the lion; because it is entirely undaunted in every respect, it is like a lion, thus a "lion of selflessness" (*nairātmyasiṃha*). That which possesses the roar (*nirṇāda*) of this lion of selflessness is called *nairātmyasiṃhanirnādī*.

"Terrifying the deer-like heretics": A *tīrtha* is a path for the purpose of entering the lake of *nirvāṇa*. Those who act by means of that are called *tīrthyas* (heretics). They are both contemptible (*kutsita*) and *tīrthyas*, hence "bad heretics" (*kutīrthyas*). For this very reason, they are like "deer," because they are by nature prone to fear due to the lion's roar of selflessness (*nairātmya*); thus, he is "terrifying" (*bhīkara*). He is the one who terrifies the deer-like bad heretics. And so it has been said: "All proponents of doctrines have been terrified by the lion’s roar of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); wherever these [heretics] enter, there indeed is emptiness."

Regarding the term "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*): it is like the knowledge of reality that arises based on that [foundation]. The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is designated as "pervasive" in that same way. Alternatively, regarding "pervasive": there are five pervasive factors. Because they have a great ground (*mahābhūmi*), they are called "great-grounded" (*mahābhūmika*); they exist in every state of mind. These are the factors consisting of contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). That which possesses these is "pervasive."

"Amoghagati" means one whose gati—meaning movement or course—is amogha, that is, unfailing or not in vain; thus he is Amoghagati. "Tathāgatamanojava" means because he traverses immeasurable world-systems in a single moment. "Jina" means he is called Jina because he has conquered (jita) unwholesome states (akuśala-dharma). "Jitāri" means his enemies (ari), which are the afflictions (kleśa), have been conquered by him; thus he is Jitāri. And consequently, he is "Vijayī," meaning he possesses victory (vijaya); thus he is Vijayī.

Regarding the term *cakravartin*: four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) are taught in the Abhidharma. Concerning their appearance—when they arise, what they possess as wheels, whether they appear simultaneously, and how many continents they traverse—Vasubandhu says: "The appearance of a wheel-turning king does not occur when the human lifespan is below eighty thousand years. They are the ones possessing wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron, respectively, according to descending order. They rule over one, two, three, or four continents; however, two do not appear together, just like Buddhas.
They conquer by being met with welcome, by going themselves, by quarrel, or by weapons; yet they are non-violent. He is called a *cakravartin* because he appears in the form of a wheel."
Alternatively, he is a *cakravartin* because, as stated in the *Śrīsaṃvara*, he possesses the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

For this very reason, he is called "of great power" (*mahābala*). These powers are both "great" and "powers," thus they are "great powers. He who possesses these fourfold limbs is called "of great power."
"The leader of the hosts, the teacher of the hosts, the lord of the hosts, the master of the hosts, the self-controlled one" (MNS 6.8ab).

In this context, "leader of the hosts" (*gaṇamukhya*) means that the "hosts" (*gaṇa*) are the assemblies of *śrāvakas*, and he is their "leader," meaning their preeminent chief. "Teacher of the hosts" (*gaṇācārya*): the "hosts" are the assemblies of *pratyekabuddhas*; Mañjuśrī himself is their teacher because he provides them with unerring instruction. "Lord of the hosts" (*gaṇeśa*): the "hosts" are the assemblies of *bodhisattvas*; he is their lord (*īśa*), the "lord of the hosts. "Master of the hosts" (*gaṇapati*): the "hosts" are the multitudes of *tathāgatas*; he is their master (*pati*) and sovereign because his essential nature is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). For this very reason, he is "self-controlled" (*vaśī*).
Because it manifests all forms by way of revealing their respective intrinsic natures.
He is of great majesty, a leader, not led by others, and the Great Way. (MNS 6.8cd)

In this context, "of great majesty" (*mahānubhāva*): majesty (*anubhāva*) means greatness; that which is both great and majesty is "of great majesty. "A leader" (*dhaureya*): one who is capable in the yoke of the Dharma; thus, a leader. "Not to be led by others" (*ananyaneya*): not to be led by others is "not to be led by others," because of being oriented toward the profound Dharma. Furthermore, since one's own established tenet—primarily through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—cannot be taken away by proponents of other doctrines, he is "not to be led by others. "Great method" (*mahānaya*): that which is both great and a method is a "great method"; the meaning is "great skillful means. || 0 ||

"Lord of Speech, Master of Speech, Eloquent, Lord of Words, of Infinite Voice" (MNS 6.9ab). Regarding these: "Lord of Speech" (*vāgīśa*) means the lord (*īśa*) of words (*vāc*), because of the attainment of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*). "Master of Speech" (*vākpati*) means the master (*pati*) or owner of words; this is the sense, because of the attainment of the analytical knowledge of etymology (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). "Lord of Words" (*vācaspati*) [is so called] because of the attainment of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). Because one attains the four analytical knowledges on the stage of "Good Intelligence" (*sādhumatī bhūmi*), one is called a "Dharma-preacher. For this very reason, he says: "of infinite voice."
He whose speech and voice are infinite is "Anantagīḥ," because he turns the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings through all languages according to their respective capacities.

"One whose speech is truth, a speaker of truth, and the teacher of the four truths" (MNS 6.9cd). Regarding that, "one whose speech is truth": there are two truths, namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Among these, the conventional is threefold: the convention of designation (*prajñaptisaṃvṛti*), the convention of practice (*pratipattisaṃvṛti*), and the convention of manifestation (*udbhāvanāsaṃvṛti*); by means of these, there is conventional truth. Ultimate truth, however, is to be understood from the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*). Furthermore, that ultimate is threefold: the ultimate as object (*arthaparamārtha*), the ultimate as attainment (*prāptiparamārtha*), and the ultimate as practice (*pratipattiparamārtha*).

In this context, the ultimate reality as object (*arthaparamārtha*) is suchness (*tathatā*), because it is the object of the supreme gnosis. The ultimate reality as attainment (*prāptiparamārtha*) is nirvāṇa, because it is the supreme goal. The ultimate reality as practice (*pratipattiparamārtha*) is the path, because the supreme goal belongs to it. One whose speech proceeds by relying upon these two truths is called a speaker of truth (*satyavāg*).

And so it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Mūlamadhyamaka*: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths: the conventional truth of the world and the truth that is ultimate. Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the Dharma; [this applies] to the profound teaching of the Buddha."

And thus, "one who speaks the truth": he whose nature it is to speak in this way—that which is true, real, and has emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its very essence—is so described. "Teacher of the Four Truths": the four truths are characterized by the summary of all that is to be known (*jñeya*). The truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) consists in the nature of perversion regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, because it is contrary to the noble ones (*ārya*). The truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is, in brief, suffering itself as previously described, because ignorance (*avidyā*), by being the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so on, is the cause of the sufferings of birth and so forth.

The truth of cessation is the [cessation] of all phenomena because they possess the characteristic of being conceptually constructed; thus, the Blessed One is the antidote to delusion. And the truth of the path, through the fulfillment of perfect awakening, is the source of loving-kindness and renunciation and so forth, and he is the teacher of these, the teacher of the four truths.
"For he is irreversible, a non-returner, a rhinoceros-like solitary leader" (MNS 6.10ab).

Regarding that, "irreversible" (*avaivartika*) means one who is not turned back from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; such a person is called irreversible. Just as in the lineage of the *śrāvaka*s, one who does not turn back is "non-turning" (*avivartaka*); he shines because of this, being irreversible due to having obtained the prophecy on the Immovable stage (*acalā bhūmi*). "Non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) refers to those who have attained through faith or through vision. Because he has abandoned nine categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm, he is called a non-returner.

And so it has been said: "In the realm of desire, by the elimination of the sixth category and by the elimination of the ninth in number, the person becomes a once-returner and a non-returner respectively."

[296: There are two kinds of *pratyekabuddhas*: the rhinoceros-like (*khaḍgacārī*) and the group-dwelling (*vargacārī*). With reference to the rhinoceros-like one, it is said: "The rhinoceros" (*khaḍga*). Like a rhinoceros, he is a rhinoceros. A rhinoceros is a wild ox (*gaṇḍaka*); in its mouth there is only a single horn. Because of his similarity to that, the solitary *pratyekabuddha* is called a "rhinoceros. The "leader of a group" (*pratyekanāyaka*) refers to the group-dweller; he is a leader for each individual, hence "leader of a group," because of his practice of dwelling in groups.]

[298: “He has emerged through various means of deliverance; he has the great elements as his sole cause” (MNS 6.10cd). Regarding this, “he has emerged through various means of deliverance” (*nānāniryāṇaniryāta*) means that he has gone forth (*yāta*), having emerged (*niryāta*), by means of the various deliverances—the nirvāṇas of the Śrāvakas and others—because he appears in whatever form is necessary within the mental continuums of those beings who are to be trained. “He has the great elements as his sole cause” (*mahābhūtaikakāraṇa*): therein, the elements (*bhūta*) are the four, beginning with earth.]

But surely, since space (*ākāśa*) is also a great element (*mahābhūta*), how can there be four great elements instead of five? It is said in reply: they are called "great elements" because they are both "great" (*mahat*) and "elements" (*bhūta*). They are "great" because they occupy vast regions of space; and these [other] elements, such as the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and so forth, possess the quality of being "elements" because they are produced from specific common and uncommon karmas. Therefore, while this space possesses greatness by providing the opportunity for the arising of all forms, it does not possess the quality of being an "element," because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for the root *bhū* is used in the sense of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, space is not a great element (*mahābhūta*). Consequently, there are only four great elements. That which is the singular, non-dual cause and reason for those four great elements is described as such. [294:
"An Arhat, a monk whose outflows are exhausted, free from passion, and with senses conquered" (MNS 6.11ab)].

Regarding the term "monk" (*bhikṣu*): likewise, in the Abhidharma, four types of monks are taught. Namely, the monk by designation (*saṃjñā-bhikṣu*), the monk by habit of begging (*bhikṣaṇa-śīla-bhikṣu*), the monk by formal ritual (*jñapti-bhikṣu*), and the monk in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-bhikṣu*). Among these four, this [latter] is the monk in the ultimate sense, because his afflictions have been shattered and he cannot be broken by any Māras.

[294: Regarding "the Arhat" (*arhan*): the *arayaḥ* are the afflictions (*kleśa*). He is an *arhat* because he has slain those enemies. Alternatively, in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he is so called because of his state as an Arhat, or because his purpose is entirely fulfilled. Or, he is so called because he is worthy (*arhati*) or capable of providing instruction to others. Or, he is so called because he is worthy of the Three Jewels—the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Or, he is so called because he is worthy of the manifold kinds of worship performed by the foremost beings within the three realms. Or, he is so called because he honors and worships the unsurpassed Tathāgata through the worship of practice. Thus, the Blessed One is called the Arhat.]

[296] Regarding the phrase "one whose outflows are exhausted" (*kṣīṇāsrava*): therein, four factors are the roots of unwholesomeness that flow forth, or rather, they give rise [to them]. Or, they are called "outflows of affliction" (*kleśāsrava*) because they flow as the *yakṣas* of affliction. From the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci hell, they afflict and oppress sentient beings through the six wounds of the sense bases (*āyatana*). These are the outflows of form and so forth. They consist of the three realms of existence (*bhava*), innate ignorance (*avidyā*) and conceptually constructed ignorance, and the sixty-two views.

The outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*), and the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭyāsrava*) are so called. By means of the aggregate of ethical discipline and concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the outflow of sensual desire is exhausted. By means of the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, the outflow of views is exhausted. By means of the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, the outflow of existence is exhausted. By means of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training, the outflow of ignorance is exhausted. Alternatively, on the stage of the perfection of ethical discipline, the outflow of views is exhausted by means of right view on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

On the stage of the fulfillment of concentration (*samādhiparipūribhūmi*), the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) is exhausted through right concentration on the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimārga*). On the stage of the fulfillment of wisdom (*prajñāparipūribhūmi*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*) is exhausted through right liberation on the path of the arhat (*arhanmārga*). [... Alternatively, on the path of the arhat, the outflow of sensual desire is exhausted through the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the basis of sensual desire; the outflow of ignorance is exhausted through the full comprehension of the basis of conditioned formations (*saṃskāropadhi*). For all views have as their objective support the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

Through the abandonment of the truth of all suffering and the truth of its origin, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) is exhausted. Through the realization of the truth of cessation, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is exhausted. Through the cultivation of the truth of the path, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*) is exhausted. By abandoning the outflow of sensual desire, the Māra who is a son of the gods (*devaputramāra*) is defeated. By abandoning the outflow of existence, the Māra of death (*maraṇamāra*) is defeated. By abandoning the outflow of ignorance, the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) is defeated. By abandoning the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭyāsrava*), the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) is defeated.
Thus, because of his victory over the four Māras, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī has exhausted the outflows (āsrava). Therefore, he is "Tathā" because those outflows have been exhausted by him.

By the very term "one free from passion" (*vītarāga*), he is called "free from passion" because, through the paths of seeing and cultivation, he has abandoned the ninety-eight afflictions within the three realms by means of the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths. For this very reason, he is "one who has conquered the senses," because he cannot be overcome by any sense objects.

"Having attained security, having attained fearlessness, he has become cooled and is indeed undisturbed. (MNS 6.11cd) In this context, "having attained security" means that bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is secure; one who has attained that is "one who has attained security. Fear (*bhīti*) is dread (*bhaya*); that which has no dread is "fearless" (*abhaya*), referring to vocal action (*vākkarman*) because of the absence of all defects of speech in vocal action. One who has attained that is "one who has attained fearlessness."

By the term *śītībhūta* ("become cooled"), it is meant that the mental activity is "cool" because of its tranquility due to the absence of all disturbances of the mind; it is "not cool" (*aśīta*) because it was previously overwhelmed by passion and so forth, but later, through the disappearance of those [afflictions], it becomes cooled—thus it is called *śītībhūta*. For this very reason, as indicated by the word *hi* (which has the sense of "because"), it is said to be "undisturbed" (*anāvila*) due to the absence of defects in body, speech, and mind.
"Endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the supreme one.

(MNS 6.12ab) In this context, by the phrase "endowed with knowledge and conduct," he demonstrates the cause for the attainment of the perfection of the Teacher by that Knowledge-Being (*jñānasattva*). "Knowledge and conduct" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path: right view is "knowledge," while the remaining limbs are "conduct. This is because one who does not see [the truth] or lacks conduct is incapable of proceeding. Alternatively, the three trainings constitute "knowledge and conduct": the training in higher wisdom, the training in higher ethics, and the training in higher mind.

In this context, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the first two [trainings], while "conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), because the former acts as its preliminary preparation; for "conduct" is indeed called *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary practice). The mention of "knowledge" first is because, through its purification, there is the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, seeing with the eye of wisdom itself and proceeding by means of those two—ethical discipline and meditative concentration—as if by feet, one reaches the destination; it is in this sense that the three trainings are indicated by the compound term "knowledge-and-conduct" (*vidyācaraṇa*).
Therefore, one who is endowed with the threefold knowledge is called "endowed with knowledge and conduct."

By the term *sugata*, he shows how he has gone: he has gone well (*suṣṭhu gataḥ*), meaning he has not returned, like one whose fever has been completely cured. He has gone without remainder (*niḥśeṣaṃ gataḥ*), meaning he has gone to the end of all that is to be known, like a jar that is perfectly full. These two meanings are intended to distinguish [the Buddha] from outsiders, Śrāvakas, and others. For outsiders have not gone well, because they return again. Although Śrāvakas and others have gone well, because they lack the capacity to return to the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatā*), they have not gone without remainder, because their knowledge is obstructed regarding all objects of knowledge.

Thus, by means of these two terms—"knower of the world" (*lokavit*) and "supreme" (*para*)—he demonstrates the activity of that Teacher, the Blessed One, the Jñānasattva, who has perfectly and completely attained the perfection of knowledge and conduct and has achieved the perfection of a Teacher. Furthermore, that activity of a Teacher is twofold: the illumination of the world of those who are capable and incapable [of liberation], and the disciplining of those who are capable. Therein, by the term "knower of the world," the observation of those who are capable and incapable is indicated. He is called a "knower of the world" because he knows the world; that is, through his thorough knowledge of the world of those who are capable and incapable, he is termed a "knower of the world."

For thus the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, three times during the night and three times during the day, surveys the world with the eye of wisdom: "Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into distress? Who is headed for the lower realms? Whom shall I lift up from evil and establish in heaven and liberation? In whom shall I plant roots of merit that have not yet been planted? Whose already planted roots shall I bring to full maturity? Whose immature [roots] shall I bring to fruition? It is for this very reason that the Blessed One is supreme among others.

"Free from 'mine,' free from 'I,' abiding in the system of the two truths" (MNS 6.12cd). Therein, by the term "free from mine," the apprehended aspect is negated; by the term "free from I," the apprehending aspect is negated, because both of these are false appearances. Thus it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Ratnāvalī*: "‘I exist’ and ‘mine exists’—this is false from the perspective of ultimate reality, because through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, neither of these two arises. The phrase "abiding in the system of the two truths" has already been explained.
Standing at the far shore of saṃsāra, having accomplished what was to be done, he stands on firm ground. (MNS 6.13ab)

In this context, by the phrase "standing at the far limit of saṃsāra," the following is shown: saṃsāra is indeed of the nature of existence (*bhāva*), because it consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). For these very five aggregates of clinging, when impelled by afflictions and karma, moving from one state of existence (*gati*) to another state of existence, are called "saṃsāra. Its "far shore" (*pāra*) is nirvāṇa, and that is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*). "Saṃsāra and the far shore" are *saṃsārapārau*; their "limit" (*koṭi*) is the *saṃsārapārakoṭi*. One who stands upon that is "standing at the far limit of saṃsāra" (*saṃsārapārakoṭistha*).

This is what is meant: that Blessed One Mañjuśrī exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) within the natures of existence and non-existence, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Why? Because not even the subtlest phenomenon (*dharma*) of those two is perceived. And so it has been said: "The limit (*koṭi*) of nirvāṇa and the limit of saṃsāra—between these two, not even the slightest difference is found."

"Having done what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*) means that which must necessarily be performed has been performed. In this context, because he has fulfilled morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), and because he has completed the primary task of liberation from all suffering, he is said to have "done what was to be done. Furthermore, he is called one who has "done what was to be done" because he has fulfilled these specific modes of conduct (*vṛtti*)—such as the conduct of few desires, the conduct of contentment, the conduct of the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), and the conduct that inspires affection—which were to be accomplished by him. "Standing on firm ground" (*sthale sthita*): "firm ground" (*sthala*) refers to *nirvāṇa*, because it is a place of security.
He is always established therein because he abides in the *dharmakāya*; that is, because he dwells in non-dual reality (*advayadharmatā*).
"Established in the knowledge of isolation (*kaivalyajñāna*), he is the shatterer with the weapon of wisdom" (MNS 6.13cd).

That which is born therein, being absolute and pure, is *kaivalya*; that which is *kaivalya* and is knowledge is "the knowledge of isolation. He is so described because he is born from, or established in, that [knowledge]. Regarding "the shatterer with the weapon of wisdom": wisdom (*prajñā*) has the characteristic of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); it is itself a weapon because it cuts through all afflictions (*kleśa*). He is so described because, by means of that weapon of wisdom, there is the awakening to the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted regarding all phenomena.
"The True Dharma is the King of Dharma, radiant, the supreme illuminator of the world" (MNS 6.14ab).

In this context, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is twofold: secondary and primary. Therein, the Dharma of the virtuous is the True Dharma; for the virtuous are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and their Dharma consists of the twelve branches of the scriptures (*pravacana*). Therein, the twelve branches are: *sūtra*, *geya*, *gāthā*, *vyākaraṇa*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *jātaka*, *itivṛttaka*, *avadāna*, *vaipulya*, *nirukti*, and *adbhuta*—these are the branches.

Those [teachings] established in books through perceptible syllables are called the secondary *saddharma*; the primary, however, is the King of Dharma (*dharmarāj*), whose nature is the *dharmadhātu*, because it is devoid of both the signified and the signifier.

[326: He is unknowable. Thus it is said in the *Triśatikā*: "The Buddhas are to be seen through their nature (*dharmata*); for the Guides are the Dharma-body. And that nature is unknowable; it cannot be known. Therefore he says: "Radiant" (*bhāsvān*). Both types of phenomena—external and internal—destroy the darkness of ignorance. He is the "Illuminator of the World" because he reveals the phenomena exactly as they are to the world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; thus he is the Illuminator of the World. And for this reason, the Blessed One is supreme and preeminent.]

[328] "Lord of Dharma, King of Dharma, instructor of the path to excellence" (MNS 6.14cd). Regarding that, "Lord of Dharma" (*dharmeśvara*): he is the lord (*īśvara*) of the dharmas, namely the ten paths of wholesome action; thus it is said: "Abstention from all unwholesome [deeds], and constant engagement in the wholesome through mind, action, and speech—this dharma is remembered as being threefold. Regarding "King of Dharma" (*dharmarāja*): he is the king of the dharma, which is divided into the external, the secret, and the three vehicles.

"Teacher of the path to the supreme good" (*śreyomārgopadeśaka*): the path to the supreme good is the "path to the supreme good" (*śreyomārga*); the Dharma that establishes it is called the "path to the supreme good. The Blessed One is the teacher of that, hence he is the "Teacher of the Path to the Supreme Good. Thus it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Furthermore, the Dharma leading to the supreme good is subtle and its vision is profound; when taught to the ignorant who have not heard [the Dharma], it causes them to tremble, so the Jinas have said."

[323] "Siddhārtha" means one whose resolve is accomplished and who is free from all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*). In this context, "object" (*artha*) is that which is sought after; its domain consists of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and it is extremely well-known in the world by way of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. That which is both accomplished (*siddha*) and an object (*artha*) is "accomplished-object" (*siddhārtha*). For instance, the adherence to the reality of external objects—such as the entities of form and so forth as they are conceptually constructed, or the characteristics of the self such as genus, quality, and action—is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

And so it has been said by the venerable Master Vasubandhu: "By whichever conceptualization whatever object is conceptualized, that is merely the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva); it does not exist. Regarding the term *siddhasaṃkalpa*: it is called *saṃkalpa* because it is conceptualized (*saṃkalpyate*). That which is both accomplished (*siddha*) and a conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) is *siddhasaṃkalpa*, namely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). It is called *paratantra* because it is produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

For instance, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is that conceptualization characterized by mind and mental factors—which, although in reality non-dual, appears as dual due to delusion—arising moment by moment from its own collection of causal factors accompanied by various latencies (*vāsanā*) such as wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral formations; it is the conceptualization of this [nature] as being permanent, as a cause, or as an object. And so it has been said: "The dependent nature, however, is conceptualization arising from conditions. It is "devoid of all conceptual constructions" (*sarvasaṃkalpavarjita*).

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This very dependent nature (*paratantra*), through its intrinsic nature or through the purification of the path, becomes stainless non-dual emptiness due to the removal of all obscurations; this is the perfected nature. And so it has been said: "The perfected is its constant absence of the former. Therefore, the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Being (*jñānasattva*) of all Tathāgatas, possesses the three natures.
"The non-conceptual, inexhaustible realm, the supreme, undecaying *dharmadhātu*.

(MNS 6.15cd) Regarding that, "non-conceptual" means because there is an absence of conceptualization regarding perfected knowledge (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). And so it is said: "Apart from conceptualization, nothing called 'saṃsāra' exists; therefore, for one who is free from conceptualization, there is always the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirvṛti*). "Inexhaustible" means because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is equal to space. "Realm" (*dhātu*) means because it is the causal nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which possess origination; for here the meaning of "realm" is the meaning of "cause. "Dharmadhātu" means...

Because it is manifested by having the noble dharmas as its object. "Supreme" means because it is distinguished from outsiders, such as the śrāvakas and others. "Inexhaustible" means because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

"Virtuous, possessing the accumulation of merit, wisdom, and the great mine of wisdom. (MNS 6.16ab) In this context, "merit" (*puṇya*) means that which purifies; one who possesses this is "virtuous" (*puṇyavān*). Regarding "accumulation of merit" (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*): "accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*) means perfect gathering. Thus, an "accumulation of merit" is the gathering of merit. Consequently, by these two terms, the following is expressed: the meaning is that he is never separated from the mundane and supramundane accumulations of merit. Regarding "wisdom" (*jñāna*): this refers to the wisdom of outsiders, śrāvakas, and so forth. Regarding "another wisdom": [this refers to...]

Knowledge other than the knowledge of external Śrāvakas and others is "other knowledge" (*jñānāntara*), which is the knowledge of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* and that mind which has reached such knowledge. This is because external objects are non-existent, as they are contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because such contradiction has been demonstrated in detail. It is "mind-only," O Sons of the Conqueror, namely the triple world; this is established by scripture (*āgama*) and because the manifestation of all entities is contradicted by all means of valid cognition. It is "other knowledge" precisely for this reason, and it is "great" because its intention is to protect the realm of sentient beings without exception or remainder.
