[332] “One who possesses knowledge, one who knows the existent and the non-existent, and one who has accumulated the two provisions” (MNS 6.16cd). “One who possesses knowledge” (*jñānavān*) means that he possesses such knowledge; thus, he is one who possesses knowledge. “One who knows the existent and the non-existent” (*sadasajjñānī*): that which is existent (*sat*) and that which is non-existent (*asat*) are the "existent and non-existent" (*sadasat*); he who possesses the knowledge of those two is one who knows the existent and the non-existent. And so it was said by the venerable Āryadeva: “For one to whom no position (*pakṣa*) is attributed—neither ‘existent,’ nor ‘both existent and non-existent,’ nor ‘non-existent’—criticism cannot be leveled against him even after a long time.”
The meaning is that he is "endowed" (*sambhṛta*), that is, fully perfected, by the two accumulations just mentioned.

[335] "The eternal, the sovereign of the universe, the yogin, the object of meditation, and the master of intellects" (MNS 6.17ab). In this context, "eternal" (*śāśvata*) refers to his permanence as a continuum (*prabandha-nityatā*), because he remains present as long as *saṃsāra* lasts; the intention is that the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is never subject to loss. "The universe" (*viśva*) is the entire world. He is the "sovereign" (*rāṭ*) because he shines (*rājate*) or plays (*divyate*). He is the "sovereign of the universe" (*viśvarāṭ*) because he is the essence of all things, both stable and moving. Regarding "the yogin":

Because of the statement, "Yoga is defined as the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in mere gnosis (*jñāna*)," yoga is non-dual gnosis; one who possesses that is a *yogin*. It is called "meditation" (*dhyāna*) because its nature consists of the four meditations. It is called "the object of meditation" (*dhyeya*) because it is the objective domain to be meditated upon. It is called "the lord of intellects" (*dhīpati*); he is the lord or master of the intellects—that is, of the Buddhas—because his essential nature is the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of all the Tathāgatas.

"[339: For it is to be personally realized, immovable, primordial, and the bearer of the three bodies (trikāyadhṛk). (MNS 6.17cd) Regarding that, "to be personally realized" (*pratyātmavedya*) means: it is to be realized by oneself through one's own realization; it is "personally realized" because the gnosis of the *dharmadhātu* is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). It cannot be manifested to others, like the pleasure of a maiden’s sexual union. And so it has been said:

I pay homage to that incomparable Dharmakāya of the Victors, which is neither one nor many; which is the foundation for the great perfection of the welfare of self and others; which is neither non-existence nor existence, like space, of equal flavor, and of an inscrutable nature; which is untainted, changeless, auspicious, unequaled yet equal to all, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation, and to be realized within oneself.

[343: Therefore, he is "Immovable" (acala). For "hi" has the sense of "because. And for this reason, that Blessed One Mañjuśrī is immovable, because he is beyond the range of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Regarding "Supreme Primeval" (*paramādya*): "Primeval" (*ādya*) means existing from the beginning; he is both supreme (*parama*) and primeval (*ādya*), thus "Supreme Primeval. And he is the Blessed One Śrī Vajrasattva. Regarding "Bearer of the Three Bodies" (*trikāyadhṛk*): there are three bodies, characterized as the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body. He who sustains these is the "Bearer of the Three Bodies."]

“The Buddha consists of the five bodies; the all-pervading one consists of the five gnoses; he has the five Buddhas as his crown; he possesses the five eyes and holds them without attachment” (MNS 6.18). In this context, “consisting of the five bodies” means that he consists of the five bodies—the *svābhāvika*, *sāmbhogika*, *vaipākika*, *nairmāṇika*, and *dharmakāya*. He whose very self (*ātman*) or nature (*svabhāva*) is these is “one consisting of the five bodies. “Buddha” has already been explained. “Consisting of the five gnoses” means:

The perfectly pure knowledge of the dharmadhātu consists in the performance of the task of discerning the tenfold equality; these are the five knowledges. That which has these as its self or intrinsic nature is "consisting of the five knowledges" (*pañcajñānātmaka*). The term "pervasive" (*vibhu*) has already been explained. Regarding "having a crown consisting of the five Buddhas": the five Buddhas are Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vairocana. He whose crown has that as its essence—that is, whose crown has that as its intrinsic nature—is "one who has a crown consisting of the five Buddhas. Regarding "the five eyes":

There are five eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. He who possesses these is "one with the five eyes. For this very reason, he is called "one with unimpeded vision" (*asaṅgadṛk*). His vision (*dṛk*), his seeing, is unimpeded (*asaṅga*) and unattached (*asaṃsakta*) toward all objects of knowledge; thus he is one with unimpeded vision. As it is said in the *Abhidharma*: "The vision of the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha (*khaḍga*), and the Teacher [the Buddha] extends over two, three, and incalculable [thousandfold world systems, respectively]."

"Janaka, the supreme and excellent son of all Buddhas" (MNS 6.19ab). Regarding "janakaḥ sarvabuddhānām": therein, *janaka* means the progenitor of all Buddhas because he has the nature of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrī-tattvasaṃgraha*: "The Tathāgatas who have arisen and those who will arise do so by relying upon you. Regarding "buddhaputra" (son of the Buddha):

The Buddha is the specific non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*) that is liberated from all obscurations of habitual tendencies (*vāsanāvaraṇa*), which brings about the awakening to all phenomena in every aspect, and which serves as the basis for all minds. His son is a "son of the Buddha. A son is called one who is born from oneself (*ātmaja*). And his "self" is, in the ultimate sense, suchness (*tathatā*), because [the gnosis] is manifested by it; or, because he is born as the counterpart to that non-conceptual gnosis, he is called a "son of the Buddha. In this sense, a bodhisattva is called a "son of the Buddha."

"Para" means because of being supreme (*utkṛṣṭatvāt*). "Vara" means because of being the most excellent among those who are to be approached (*abhigamanīyānām*). Regarding the passage: "The source of the arising of wisdom, the womb of the Dharma, the ender of existence" (MNS 6.19cd): therein, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and that is the supramundane discrimination between phenomena and persons (*dharmapudgalayor vivekaḥ*). Wisdom itself is "existence" (*bhava*); thus, it is "the arising of wisdom-existence" (*prajñābhava*). These consist of the five pure aggregates (*pañca śuddhaskandhāḥ*), which have the nature of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of knowledge (*vijñānadarśana*). Because he arises from these, the Blessed One is called "the source of the arising of wisdom-existence."

"Yoni" means a cause (*kāraṇa*), because it is the source from which all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that possess origination arise. "Dharmayoni" means the womb (*yoni*) of phenomena; that is, the source of phenomena. Phenomena here refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*); the meaning is that it is their source or cause. "Bhavāntakṛt" means one who brings about the end of existence (*bhava*). Existence is *saṃsāra*; its end is its final limit. One who effects that [end] is called "Bhavāntakṛt."

"Solid, of single essence, diamond-natured, born-afresh, the Lord of the World. Regarding this, "solid, of single essence" (*ghanaikasāra*): he is both solid (*ghana*) and of single essence (*ekasāra*), thus "solid, of single essence. Solid means dense, because there is no interior [to it]. Of single essence means due to the absence of the stains of affliction (*kleśamala*). For this very reason, he is "diamond-natured" (*vajrātmā*); diamond refers to gnosis (*jñāna*) because of its indestructibility. That which has this as its nature or intrinsic being is "diamond-natured," because he is the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas. "Born-afresh" (*sadyojāta*)...

Wherever he perceives the welfare of sentient beings, there, at that very moment and instantly, by assuming birth, he is called "Sadyojāta" (the Newly Born), because he has attained mastery over arising. He is called "Jagatpati" (Lord of the World); "jagatpatiḥ" means the lord of the worlds, which signifies the master of the world, since he is the basis for all their prosperity.

"Arising from space, self-existent, the great fire of the wisdom of insight" (MNS 6.20ab). Regarding that, "arising from space": space is the gnosis of emptiness; because he arises from that, he is "arising from space. "Self-existent": he exists by himself, thus he is "self-existent," because his nature is the vajra of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). "The fire of the wisdom of insight": the wisdom of insight is the knowledge of insight, which has the characteristic of non-duality and is non-conceptual in nature.

That very [Self] is "Anala" (Fire) because it is capable of burning the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). It is "Great" (*mahān*) because it possesses eight forms—earth, water, wind, fire, the sacrificer, ether, moon, and sun—and because it is endowed with the sixfold attributes of knowledge, strength, valor, splendor, power, and sovereignty.

“Vairocana, the great radiance, the light of gnosis, Virocana” (MNS 6.21ab). In this context, “Vairocana” has already been explained. Regarding “great radiance” (*mahādīpti*): great radiance is *mahādīpti*. It is radiance by way of the gateway of perfectly pure gnosis, through its similarity to the illumination of the objects of knowledge. Regarding “light of gnosis” (*jñānajyotis*): because it is devoid of subject and object, gnosis is non-dual. Its light is the “light of gnosis,” because its intrinsic nature is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*). He is “Virocana” because he shines and sports, since he performs the welfare of the entire world by means of the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*).

"Lamp of the world, torch of wisdom, of great splendor, and luminous" (MNS 6.21cd). "Lamp of the world" means he is the lamp of the worlds because his essential nature is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "Torch of wisdom" means he whose brilliance is like that of a torch of wisdom; thus he is the "torch of wisdom," by virtue of having the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) as his intrinsic nature. "Of great splendor" means he whose splendor—that is, radiance—is great; thus he is "of great splendor," by way of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). "Luminous" means...
The Lord Mañjuśrī is "resplendent" (prabhāsvara) because he shines intensely, consisting of the nature of the five wisdoms; he is the Blessed One whose nature is to illuminate in every direction.

"The King of Vidyās, the Lord of Supreme Mantras, the King of Mantras who accomplishes the Great Purpose" (MNS 6.22ab). Regarding that, "King of Vidyās" means the king of vidyās; he is the King of Vidyās because he is born from all vidyās belonging to the dhāraṇī-maṇḍala. "Lord of Supreme Mantras" means that which is both supreme and a mantra is a supreme mantra (*agramantra*); its lord is the master. And here, the syllable *hūṃ* should be understood as the supreme mantra.

Because it consists of Mahāmudrā, it is called the "King of Mantras" (*mantrarāja*); that is, among the mantras recited in the Dharma-maṇḍala, it is the king, hence "King of Mantras. Regarding the term "performer of great purpose" (*mahārthakṛd*): it is both "great" (*mahān*) and "purpose" (*artha*), thus "great purpose" (*mahārtha*). It performs that, and so it is the "performer of great purpose. This is because it accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings by performing worship to all Tathāgatas through the worldly and supramundane offerings described in the Karma-maṇḍala—namely, the three types of external, secret, and mental offerings—and by serving as the cause for the accumulation of immeasurable merit and gnosis.

“Mahoṣṇīṣa, Adbhutoṣṇīṣa, Viśvadarśin, and Viyatpati” (MNS 6.22cd). Regarding that, “Mahoṣṇīṣa”: he is both great (*mahān*) and a crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), thus Mahoṣṇīṣa; because he is established as having become a mass in the form of the *uṣṇīṣas* of all the Tathāgatas, and because he is upon the heads of all the Tathāgatas, he is therefore called Mahoṣṇīṣa. [Regarding] “Adbhutoṣṇīṣa”:

That Blessed One, the Wisdom Being of all Tathāgatas (*sarvatathāgatajñānasattva*), who emerged from the *uṣṇīṣas* of all Tathāgatas by way of the mass of radiance (*tejorāśi*) and is established upon the head of Vajradhara—he is called the "Marvelous *Uṣṇīṣa*" (*adbhutōṣṇīṣa*). Regarding "the All-Seeing" (*viśvadarśin*): he is the All-Seeing because it is his nature to display the manifold aspects of meditative absorption (*samādhimukha*)—that is, the entire universe—in its various forms, through the essence of all mundane and supramundane meditative absorptions. Regarding "Lord of the Sky" (*viyatpati*): the sky (*viyat*) is space (*ākāśa*); its lord is the Lord of the Sky.

The meaning is "the Lord of emptiness. And so it has been said: "The abiding of the mind that is without support has the characteristic of space; this very cultivation of space is considered the cultivation of emptiness."

"The foremost embodiment of all Buddhas, the eye that brings joy to the world" (MNS 6.23ab). Regarding that, "the foremost embodiment of all Buddhas": all those who are Buddhas are "all Buddhas," such as the Eternal One (*śāśvata*) and so forth. Their self (*ātman*) is the "self of all Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhātman*); the existence (*bhāva*), the being (*sattā*), of the nature (*svabhāva*) of that self of all Buddhas is the "embodiment of the self of all Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhātmabhāva*), which is the *dharmadhātu*. Its state of being supreme is "foremost" (*agra*).

By virtue of being the embodiment of all Buddhas and having the single flavor of suchness (*tathatā*), the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is supreme, because he is the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas. Regarding the phrase "the eye of joy for the world": the joy of the world is "world-joy"; the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is the eye of that world-joy. For, by means of the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*), which consists of the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, [he perceives].

"He is the one of universal form (*viśvarūpī*), the creator (*vidhātā*), worthy of worship (*pūjya*), and venerable (*mānya*) by the great seers (*maharṣi*). (MNS 6.23cd) Regarding that, "of universal form" means that he manifests various forms because he possesses the intrinsic nature of all things, both stable and moving. "The creator" means that he brings forth all mantras, mudrās, samayas, and maṇḍalas for all sentient beings according to their respective capacities. He is "worthy of worship" (*pūjya*) because he is deserving of all mundane and supramundane offerings; for this very reason, he is "venerable" (*mānya*), meaning he is to be honored by all sentient beings. "By the great seers" refers to...
He is both great and a seer, thus he is a "great seer" (maharṣi); the Buddha, the Blessed One, is called a great seer.

"The mantra-practitioner who upholds the three families and maintains the mantra of the great pledge" (MNS 6.24ab). In this context, "upholding the three families" means that he maintains those [families] through their division into body, speech, and mind. Regarding "mantra-practitioner": *mantra* refers to all mundane and supramundane [mantras]; he in whom these exist is a *mantrī*. This is because the Blessed One, the Knowledge-Being (*jñānasattva*), possesses the forms of all mantras. Regarding "maintaining the mantra of the great pledge": [it refers to one who holds the essence-mantra of the Great Pledge].

It is both great and a pledge (samaya), thus it is the Great Pledge (mahāsamaya). That is the Blessed One, the Vajra of Bodhicitta; his mantra is that which is called "mantra" because it protects through being composed of wisdom and compassion. He who upholds that is the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Body of all Tathāgatas, the Upholder of the Mantra of the Great Pledge.

"The bearer of the Three Jewels, the most excellent, the teacher of the supreme three vehicles" (MNS 6.24cd). Regarding "bearer of the Three Jewels": the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*) are so called because they are like jewels (*ratna*)—due to their rarity, their great value, and their illuminating nature—and these three, known as the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, he bears; thus, he is the "bearer of the Three Jewels. He who is worthy of being approached before all others who are to be approached is called "the most excellent" (*śreṣṭha*).

And that Blessed One Mañjuśrī is the "Teacher of the Supreme among the Three Vehicles. This means he is the teacher of the supreme [truth] regarding the three—namely, the vehicles of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Mahāyāna—because he knows the spiritual lineages (gotra), faculties (indriya), dispositions (āśaya), and latent tendencies (anuśaya) of all sentient beings.

"Amoghapāśa, the Victorious One, Vajrapāśa, the Great Seizer; Vajrāṅkuśa, the Great Noose. (MNS 6.25abc) In this context, "Amoghapāśa" means one whose noose (*pāśa*) is like a noose that is "unfailing" (*amogha*), that is, not fruitless (*abandhya*); for he appears in such a manner to those beings who are to be disciplined by the *bodhicitta-vajra*. "Victorious" (*vijayī*) refers to his mastery through the primary gateway of the *trailokya-samāpatti* samādhi. "Vajrapāśa" refers to him by way of the gateway of Ratnasambhava. "Great Seizer" (*mahāgraha*)— [refers to him as]...

"Seizing" (*grahaṇa*) means "grasping" (*graha*); and that which is both great and a grasping is the "Great Grasping" (*mahāgraha*), the adamantine shackle (*vajranigaḍa*), and that is by way of the nature of Amitābha. "Adamantine Hook" (*vajrāṅkuśa*) is by way of the form of Akṣobhya. "Great Noose" (*mahāpāśa*)—the term "noose-stupor" (*pāśastobha*) is a synonym for "possession" (*āveśa*)—and that which is both great and a noose is the "Great Noose," the adamantine possession (*vajrāveśa*), and that is by way of the form of Amoghasiddhi.

Therefore, that Blessed One is to be understood as the signified (*abhidheya*) by these collections of words, the name-mantras and syllables beginning with Mahāvairocana and so forth, which serve as designators (*abhidhāyaka*), produced with the nominative case ending.

Then, as before, Mahāvairocana and the others emerge from this [mandala] having become white in color and holding a wheel and a sword in their hands; having emerged and gone to all buddha-fields, they purify sentient beings through their own gates of liberation, and returning once more, one should visualize them becoming the syllables of the name-mantra and remaining as wheels within one's own wheel.

Then, as before, the bodhisattva who practices the conduct of mantra-revelation (mantramukhacaryā) attains those very same multitudes of qualities while reciting the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. Regarding the second great Vairocana-circle, the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) is that one should divide its name-mantra syllables and words into twenty-six groups according to the sequence of the divisions beginning with Śāśvata, and apply everything [the ritual] as previously described.
And there are twenty-four and a quarter verses; the number of syllables in the name-mantras is one hundred and eighty-one, even by calculation.

In the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti-ṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the sixth chapter, the section on the praise of the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*), is concluded.

From here on, the third [chapter], which has the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as its essential nature, describes the praise of the Blessed One’s wisdom of all the Tathāgatas in the form of the *Trailokyavijaya* wrathful wheel. Regarding the phrase "Vajrabhairava, the Terrifier" (*vajrabhairavabhīkara*), it is an indication by means of a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Consequently, the meaning is as follows: Vajrabhairava and Bhīkara [constitute] Vajrabhairavabhīkara. In that regard, these two are recited together in the *Vajrabhairava-tantra*.

That is to say, he whose nature (*svabhāva*) is to manifest as Vajrabhairava and Vajrabhīkara is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, Vajrabhairavabhīkara. Why is this? To this he says: because gentleness is of no use for those beings who are to be disciplined through hatred (*dveṣa*). Thus it is said in the *Śrīsaṃvaratantra*: "Gentleness is of no use toward those who are extremely wicked and fierce; all the Tathāgatas have manifested wrath consisting of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*)."

"The King of Wrath, six-faced, fearsome, six-eyed, six-armed, and powerful" (MNS 7.1ab). In this regard, "King of Wrath" (*krodharāj*) is recited in the *Śrī-krodhavijaya*: "He reigns with wrath, thus he is the King of Wrath (*krodharāj*). And so it has been said: "Then, upon seeing this Yamāntaka—the wrathful one of Mañjughoṣa's name—all other wrathful deities dropped their weapons. For this very reason, he is called the "King of Wrath."

Regarding the term "Ṣaṇmukha" (Six-faced) in the *Śrīmāyājālatantra*: he who possesses six faces is Ṣaṇmukha; by implication, it should be understood that there are also six [limbs] for his hands and feet. And that Blessed One is "Bhīma" (Terrible), as stated in the *Vajrapāṇyabhiṣekatantra*: "Bhīma means terrifying."

And likewise, having emanated mandalas such as Vajratejas from all his limbs and all his pores, and having expanded within those mandalas wrathful kings of various appearances, equipped with various weapons, with furrowed brows and wrinkled foreheads, and with faces and eyes made terrifying by great beards, he is called "Terrible" because he displays fear.

"Six-eyed" (*ṣaṇnetra*) means one who has six eyes; this is a praise by means of a part [of the whole], through the metaphorical application of a component to the aggregate, just as Bhīmasena is called Bhīma, or Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā. "Six-armed" (*ṣaḍbhuja*) is stated in the *Śrīvajramaṇḍālaṅkāra-tantra*: he who possesses six arms is "six-armed. Regarding "the powerful" (*balī*): physical capacity is "strength," and he who possesses that is "powerful. He is renowned as "Great Power" (*mahābala*) in the *ŚrīMahāvidyottama-tantra*.

"Daṃṣṭrākarālakaṅkālo halāhalaśatānanaḥ" (MNS 7.1cd). Regarding that, "Daṃṣṭrākarāla" is [explained] in the *Śrīvajraghanoccaya*: he whose fangs have terrifying tips and are fearsome is Daṃṣṭrākarāla. "Kaṅkāla" is [explained] in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*. "Halāhalaśatānana": this also is a dual compound as before. "Halāhala" is [explained] in the *Śrīamoghapāśatantra*. "Śatānana" is [explained] in the *Śrīvajraśekharatantra*: he who has hundreds of faces or mouths is Śatānana.

"Yamāntaka, Vighnarāja, Vajravega, and Bhayaṅkara" (MNS 7.2ab). Regarding this, "Yamāntaka" is explained in the *Śrī-Samāja*: Yamāntaka is the one who brings an end to, that is, the destroyer of Yama. "Vighnarāja" means he who rules (*rāṭ*); he is the king (*rāṭ*) of the obstacles (*vighna*), such as Gaṇapati and others; thus he is Vighnarāja. [He is] Amṛtakuṇḍalin, who is well-known from the *Māyājāla* and other tantras. "Vajravega" is explained in the *Śrī-Mahāsamayatantro*.

*Vajravega*: the speed of a *vajra* is *vajravega*; he whose speed is like that is *Vajravega*. Regarding "terrifying" (*bhayaṅkara*): in the *Śrī-Guhyendutilaka*, it says he is "terrifying" because he causes fear through the intimidation of all the wicked.

"Vighuṣṭavajra, Hṛdvajra, Māyāvajra, and Mahodara" (MNS 7.2cd). Regarding that, "Vighuṣṭavajra": in the *Śrī-Advayasamatāvijaya*, "vighuṣṭa" means proclaimed with distinctions; that is to say, a great sound. He for whom that very [sound] is a vajra because of its indivisibility is Vighuṣṭavajra. "Hṛdvajra": in the *Śrī-Guhyendutilaka* itself, he for whom there is a vajra in the heart is Hṛdvajra. "Māyāvajra": this is recited in this very [text], the *Ṣoḍaśasāhasrikā*.

*Māyānirmāṇa* is that very emanation; because it is of an indivisible nature (*abhedyarūpatva*), he is *Māyāvajra*. Regarding *Mahodara*: in that same context, he whose belly (*udara*) is great (*mahat*) is *Mahodara*.

"The Lord of the Thunderbolt, the Vajra-source, the Vajra-essence, like the sky" (MNS 7.3ab). Regarding that, "Lord of the Thunderbolt" (*kuliśeśa*) means the lord or master of the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), which is the vajra. And he is [described] in the *Śrī-Vajrapātāla-tantra*. "The Vajra-source" (*vajrayoni*): in the *Śrī-Bhūtaḍāmara-tantra*, "vajra-source" means he whose source or cause is the vajra. "The Vajra-essence" (*vajramaṇḍa*): in the *Śrī-Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra*, "vajra-essence" means he whose essence is the vajra; the meaning is "the core. "Like the sky" (*nabhopama*): [as follows].

In the *Śrī-Guhyakośa*: "It does not exist" refers to the sky or space (*ākāśa*), because it provides room for those things that possess origination and because it is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). "It does not exist" is its meaning. That which has emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its essential nature is what is described by that [term]; the meaning is "resembling emptiness."

"Immovable, with a single mass of matted hair, wearing a moist elephant-hide garment" (MNS 7.3cd). In this context, "immovable, with a single mass of matted hair" (*acalaikajaṭāṭopa*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the immovable (*acala*) and the single mass of matted hair (*ekajaṭāṭopa*). Therein, the immovable is [found] in the *Śrī Māyājāla* and other tantras; the single mass of matted hair is [found] in the *Śrī Vajrakirīṭi Tantra*. It is called "immovable" (*acala*) because it is not moved and cannot be conceptualized by any of the Māras.

"Ekajaṭāṭopa" means one who possesses a majestic elegance (*sauṣṭhava*) by means of that single matted lock (*ekajaṭā*). Regarding the phrase "wearing a fresh elephant-hide garment" (*gajacarmapaṭārdradhṛk*): in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*, an elephant’s hide is "elephant-hide" (*gajacarma*); it is both a garment (*paṭa*) and fresh (*ārdrā*), thus "fresh garment" (*paṭārdrā*). That which is an elephant-hide and is a fresh garment is "the fresh elephant-hide garment" (*gajacarmapaṭārdrā*). One who wears that is "the wearer of the fresh elephant-hide garment" (*gajacarmapaṭārdradhṛk*).

"The great and terrible *hāhākāra*, the fearsome *hīhīkāra*" (MNS 7.4ab). Regarding that, "the *hāhākāra*" refers to the mandala named *Hāhābhūta* in the *Śrī-Krodhavijaya*; it is called *hāhākāra* because one remains there having uttered "hā hā. "The great and terrible" (*mahāghora*) means that very same [mandala] is both great and terrible, hence *mahāghora*. "The *hīhīkāra*" refers to the *Śrī-Krodhendutilaka*, so called because of arising by imitating that sound. "The fearsome" (*bhayānaka*) refers to the *Śrī-Sarvatantrasamuccaya*.

"Aṭṭahāsa, Mahāhāsa, Vajrahāsa, and Mahārava" (MNS 7.4cd). Regarding these: in the *Śrī-Asādhāraṇa-guhyālaṅkāra-vyūha-tantra*, "laughter" (*hāsa*) means laughing. "Aṭṭahāsa" is laughter that is loud (*aṭṭaiḥ*), meaning high-pitched laughter. "Mahāhāsa" is according to its etymological derivation (*nairuktayena*). "Vajrahāsa" is the laughter of gnosis (*jñāna-hāsa*), and it is mental. "Mahārava" is because it fills the three worlds; it is a great roar (*mahān* and *ravaḥ*), thus "Mahārava.
All four of these are recited in that very same [tantra].

"Vajrasattva, the Great Being; Vajrarāja, the Great Bliss" (MNS 7.5ab). Regarding these: "Vajrasattva" is [stated] in the *Paramādya*; "Great Being" refers to Mahāvajradhara in the *Śrī-Samāja*; "Vajrarāja" is [stated] in the *Guhyakośa*; and "Great Bliss" is [stated] in the *Śrī-Saṃvara*. In that context, "Great Bliss" refers to that untainted (*anāsrava*) bliss of the Tathāgatas, which is called "Great Bliss. It is stated in that very same [text]: "Bliss is renowned as peace; this is the Great Bliss of all Buddhas."

"Vajracaṇḍa, Mahāmada, Vajrahūṃkāra, and Hūṃkṛti" (MNS 7.5cd). Regarding that: "Vajracaṇḍa" is [explained] in the *Śrī-Vajraguhyālaṅkāra-tantra*: "The fierce one of the vajra is Vajracaṇḍa; 'caṇḍa' is said to mean 'impulse' (*vega*) because of its swift movement. "Mahāmada" is [explained] in the *Śrī-Guhyamaṇitilaka*: "That which is both great (*mahān*) and joy (*mada*) is Mahāmada. "Vajrahūṃkārahūṃkṛti" is [explained] in the *Śrī-Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"He who possesses the four *hūṃ*-syllables, which are the utterances (*hūṃkṛti*) of the maker of the *vajra-hūṃkāra*, is Vajrahūṃkārahūṃkṛti."

"Holder of the weapon of the vajra-arrow, wielder of the vajra-sword, the cutter" (MNS 7.6ab). Regarding that, "holder of the weapon of the vajra-arrow": in the *Śrī-Mahāsamaya-tantra*, he is called the "holder of the weapon of the vajra-arrow" because he holds that very weapon, which is an arrow marked with a vajra and a bow. "Vajra-sword": here in the *Māyājāla*, a vajra and a sword are a "vajra-sword"; he whose weapons are those two is the "vajra-sword. "The cutter" refers to that same [text].

"The Holder of the Universal Vajra, the Vajrin, the Single Vajrin, the Vanquisher of Battle" (MNS 7.6cd). Regarding that, "Holder of the Universal Vajra": in the *Śrī Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, the universal vajra is four-faced; he who holds that is the Holder of the Universal Vajra (*viśvavajradhara*). "The Vajrin" is explained in that same [text]: like a vajra is a vajra—namely, gnosis—because it is indivisible. "The Single Vajrin" is explained in the *Śrī Advayasamatāvijaya*: he is both single and a vajrin, thus "Single Vajrin," because his essential nature is non-dual gnosis.
Regarding the term *raṇañjaha*: in the *Śrī Trailokyavijaya*, "battle" (*raṇa*) refers to combat with the afflictions (*kleśa*); he who abandons that is *raṇañjaha*.

"Vajra-flame-fierce-eyed, with vajra-flames for hair" (MNS 7.7ab). Regarding "vajra-flame-fierce-eyed": in the *Śrī-Vajrabhairava*, "vajra-flame" (*vajrajvālā*) refers to the flame of a vajra; he whose eyes are as fierce as that is "vajra-flame-fierce-eyed. Regarding "with vajra-flames for hair": those which grow on the head are "hair" (*śiroruha*), meaning locks of hair. He whose hair is like vajra-flames is "vajra-flame-haired."

"Vajrāveśa, Mahāveśa, Śatākṣa, and Vajralocana" (MNS 7.7cd). In the *Śrīvajrapāṇyabhiṣeka-tantra*, these four wrathful deities (*krodha*) are recited. Regarding them: "Vajrāveśa" means the descent (*āveśa*) of the vajra; the meaning is the empowerment of gnosis (*jñānādhiṣṭhāna*). He who possesses that is Vajrāveśa. "Mahāveśa" is so called because he has the nature of the essence of all phenomena (*sarvabhāvasvabhāvātmakatva*). "Śatākṣa" means one who has hundreds of eyes; thus he is Śatākṣa. "Vajralocana" means one whose two eyes (*locane*) are like a vajra; thus he is Vajralocana.

"His body has hair-tips like vajras; he has a single form consisting of vajra-hair. (MNS 7.8ab) These two [epithets] are recited in the *Śrī-Vajramaṇḍālaṅkāra*: "He whose body is sprouted—that is, thrilled with horripilation—by hairs made of vajras, is 'vajraromāṅkuratanuḥ'. Regarding "vajromaikavigrahī": it is both one (*eka*) and a form (*vigraha*), thus a "single form" (*ekavigraha*). He whose single form consists of vajra-hairs—that is, hairs of gnosis—is "vajraromaikavigrahaḥ."

"His onset is with claws having diamond-points; his skin is dense with the essence of diamond. (MNS 7.8cd) These two [phrases] are recited in the *Śrīvajraśekhara-tantra*. In that context, the "point of the diamond" (*vajrakoṭi*) is the tip of the diamond; the claws are like that point, thus they are "diamond-pointed claws" (*vajrakoṭinakhāḥ*). That which has its onset (*ārambha*) by means of these is "one whose onset is with diamond-pointed claws" (*vajrakoṭinakhārambhaḥ*). Regarding "his skin is dense with the essence of diamond": he whose skin (*chavi*) is dense (*ghana*), meaning thick (*nibiḍa*), like the essence of diamond (*vajrasāra*), is "one whose skin is dense with the essence of diamond" (*vajrasāraghanacchaviḥ*).

"The glorious one who wears a vajra-garland, adorned with vajra-ornaments" (MNS 7.9ab). These two [epithets] are recited in the *helācakra* of the illustrious Krodhavijaya. In that context, he is called "vajramālādharaḥ" because he wears a vajra-garland (*vajramālām dhārayati*). "Śrīmān" is an epithet of him alone, because he is endowed with good fortune (*bhāgyasaṃpannatvāt*). Regarding "vajrābharaṇabhūṣitaḥ": a vajra itself is the ornament; thus, a vajra-ornament (*vajrābharaṇa*). He is "adorned" (*bhūṣita*), meaning decorated, by that; therefore, he is called "vajrābharaṇabhūṣitaḥ."

"Hāhāṭṭahāsa, Nirghoṣa, Vajraghoṣa, and Ṣaḍakṣara" (MNS 7.9cd). Regarding these, in the *Śrī-Subāhuparipṛcchā-tantra*, "Hāhāṭṭahāsa" is recited. As for "Aṭṭahāsa": it is a loud laugh; having uttered "Hāhā," the laughter is "Hāhāṭṭahāsa. "Nirghoṣa" is [explained] in the *Śrī-Saśuddhikara-tantra*: "The sound has gone forth, thus it is Nirghoṣa"; the meaning is that the sound is directed inwardly. "Vajraghoṣa" is [explained] in the *Śrī-Satsāhasrikā-Tattvasaṃgraha*.

He whose voice is like the roar at the striking of a vajra is Vajraghoṣa. Regarding "the six-syllabled one," it is stated in the *Śrīṣaṭprajñānayasamvaratantra*: he who possesses six syllables is the "six-syllabled one."

"Mañjughoṣa, the great roar, the single sound of the three worlds, the great. (MNS 7.10ab) Regarding "the single sound of the three worlds": in the *Second Trailokyavijaya Tantra*, "in the three worlds"—namely the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar—"single" means having no second; he whose sound or resonance is such is "the single sound of the three worlds. For this very reason, he is called "great. "The resonance reaching to the limits of the realm of space" is stated in the *Āryamañjuśrī Tantra* itself.

When the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave permission to Yamāntaka for the invitation to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system in order to hear the Mañjuśrī-tantra, then that Blessed One Yamāntaka, remaining right here upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, uttered a single great roar, by which a sound was produced reaching to the limits of the realm of space. Therefore, it is said: "the voice reaching to the limits of the realm of space."

Therefore, he is the Blessed One, the best among those who possess sound (*ghoṣavatām vara*). In this context, "those who possess sound" refers to those in whom sound exists; thus, he is the best among them, meaning the most excellent and the foremost.

Now, he describes the procedure for the emanation of the third wrathful wheel: that very Blessed One Mañjuśrī, for the sake of favoring beings who act out of hatred, takes on the forms of wrathful deities as taught in the *Yogacaryā-kriyā-tantra* in order to subdue the three worlds; then, from his own body, [emanate] those whose interiors are filled with universal flames, possessing furrowed brows, knitted foreheads, and mouths made terrifying by fierce fangs.

One should visualize that wrathful forms, with hands busily occupied by weapons such as the vajra-hook, the noose, and the blazing vajra-flame fire, wearing various colorful ornaments and diverse raiment, emerge and subdue all malevolent beings in all world-systems; then, returning, they settle in due order upon the third wheel outside the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, having become the seventy-one syllables of their respective name-mantras, possessing the colors and forms of their own families.

Having divided those [syllables] into five groups and formed fourteen name-mantra syllables and phrases for each of the families beginning with Buddha and Hūṃ, and having performed the emanation, reabsorption, and so forth, one should recite the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti* while identifying oneself with each single name-mantra syllable and phrase according to the previously mentioned sequence. It is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) that by doing so, one attains those very same infinite varieties of qualities.
And including one quarter-verse, there are seventy-one syllables of the mantra of the ten names, even when calculated by numerical figures. || 71 ||
The seventh chapter, the Praise of the Nature of Mirror-like Wisdom, from the *Nāmamantrāvalokinī*, a commentary on the *Āryanāmasaṅgīti*.

Now, by way of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), he utters a hymn of praise to the Wisdom-Being Mañjuśrī, the Gnosis-Body of the Blessed One: “Suchness, true selflessness, the limit of reality, and the syllableless. (MNS 8.1ab) “Suchness” (*tathatā*) means that by its very nature there is no distinction between the subject [of cognition] and so forth, because it possesses an identical form in both states of knowledge and ignorance. This is the supreme limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because it is in accord with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because conceptual constructions such as a “self” (*ātman*) are sublated by what is commonly experienced.

For this very reason, Mañjuśrī, the Knowledge-Being of all Tathāgatas, has taught that the supreme means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the non-apprehension of the aggregates and so forth as a self and so on. It is called "real" (*bhūta*) because it is the truth of reality (*bhūtyasatya*), since suchness consists solely in the absence of conceptual construction. Nor should one entertain the doubt: "If there is no self and so forth, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, or what is the fruit?"

Since this very [reality], characterized solely by the discernment of phenomena, persons, and so forth, is the element (*dhātu*) of all phenomena whose nature consists of the conceptualization of appearances—being the ultimate, immovable essence—and since it is the cause of the qualities of the fruit characterized by the powers (*bala*) and so forth, as well as the cause of the qualities of the path, it is therefore called the "dharma-element" (*dharmadhātu*), which is selflessness.

Because these [factors], such as suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth, are the causal gateways for the phenomena consisting of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others—since one enters into the intrinsic nature of all phenomena by way of suchness as their cause—the mirror-like wisdom, which is empowered by those [causes], is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is due to the excellence of its realization.

Therefore, because he possesses these four—characterized by the wisdoms of the mirror, equality, discernment, and the performance of duties—that Blessed One Mañjuśrī is called "Suchness," "the Reality of Selflessness," and "the Ultimate Limit. Regarding the term "without syllables" (*anakṣara*): in another sense, he is "without syllables" because he does not perish (*na kṣarati*), owing to his having the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

"The bull among proponents of emptiness, with a deep and vast roar" (MNS 8.1cd). Regarding that, "the bull among proponents of emptiness": emptiness is threefold—emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of not being that [nature] (*atadbhāva-śūnyatā*), and natural emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Among these, emptiness of non-existence is the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); it is emptiness of non-existence because it does not exist in any form whatsoever. Emptiness of not being that [nature] is the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); it does not exist in the manner in which it is imagined.

But it is not that [the thing] does not exist in every respect; rather, its emptiness consists in its being devoid of that [imagined nature]. The perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpannalakṣaṇa*) has emptiness as its very intrinsic nature (*śūnyatāsvabhāva*); thus, that very nature is emptiness. And because he has the habit of teaching this threefold emptiness, he is a "proponent of emptiness" (*śūnyatāvādī*). "Bull" (*vṛṣabha*) means preeminent or chief, because he is the foremost of all. He is both a proponent of emptiness and a bull, hence "the bull among proponents of emptiness" (*śūnyatāvādivṛṣabha*).

Regarding the term "Deep and Vast Thunder": "Deep" refers to the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings through the Buddha-body whose nature is Samantabhadra, which possesses a pervasive radiance accompanied by various emanations; furthermore, it is deep because it is free from the conceptualization of subject and object and has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its nature. "Vast" refers to skillful means (*upāya*), which, though characterized solely by one's own mind, is established as distinct according to its different modes of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Since the "thundering" by means of these two—the deep and the vast—is the overcoming of all non-Buddhist teachers and others, he is called by that name.

"The Dharma-conch of great sound, the Dharma-gong of great resonance" (MNS 8.2ab). Regarding that, "the Dharma-conch": when [the Blessed One] desired to descend from the Tuṣita host of gods to Jambudvīpa, then the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Being of all Tathāgatas, descended after filling the Dharma-conch; therefore, he is the Blessed One known as the Dharma-conch. Furthermore, what are its specific qualities? It says: "of great sound."

Because it is heard throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, it is called the "Gong of the Dharma. Having defeated the four Māras and realized the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, and having subsequently understood the difficulty of comprehending the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Blessed One said: "The Dharma I have realized is difficult to master; it is not to be proclaimed to all beings because it is difficult for them to master. Thus, he dwelt in fewness of desires.

Then Mahābrahmā, having approached, made this request: "O Blessed One, there are beings who possess sharp faculties, who have accumulated roots of merit, who understand through a mere hint, and who are endowed with faith; therefore, may the Blessed One teach the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, having approached the *dharmacakra*, struck the gong for the purpose of hearing the Dharma; hence it is called the "Dharma-gong" (*dharmagaṇḍī*). Furthermore, its specific qualification is stated as "the great battle" (*mahāraṇa*); that which is both great and a battle is the "great battle."
And thus, this is what is meant: that very Blessed One is to be seen as having the nature of the Dharma-conch.

"Non-abiding nirvāṇa, the Dharma drum in the ten directions" (MNS 8.2cd). Regarding that, "non-abiding nirvāṇa" means: *bhava* is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), while *nirvāṇa* is the total severance of the continuum, as in the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas. One does not abide in either of these two; for one does not abide in existence because of being untainted by the defects of existence, nor does one abide in nirvāṇa because, being dependent on compassion, one remains until the end of cyclic existence. Thus it has been said:

"Because they see the faults of existence, they do not remain in existence; because they possess compassion, they do not remain in nirvāṇa. Having been consecrated for the arising of the welfare of others, they remain in existence. By this, non-abiding nirvāṇa is expressed; and that is because there is no conceptualization of a distinction between existence and nirvāṇa, since both are perceived as non-different, having emptiness as their single flavor. Thus it has been said: "When knowledge arises correctly regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, then for him, saṃsāra itself becomes nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One Mañjuśrī, being thus, is called "one whose nirvāṇa is non-abiding. Regarding the phrase "the drum of Dharma in the ten directions": the drums of the dharmas are the "drums of Dharma"; he is so called because he possesses the drums of Dharma in the ten directions.

"Formless, yet possessing form, foremost, manifold in form, and mind-made" (MNS 8.3ab). Regarding that: "formless" because his intrinsic nature is the *dharmakāya*; "possessing form" because his intrinsic nature is the *sāmbhogikakāya*; "foremost" because he is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmadhātu*; "manifold in form" because his essence is the *nirmāṇakāya*; and "mind-made" because these three bodies are mind-made by virtue of having gnosis as their essence. Therefore, these phenomena, beginning with form, should be understood as belonging to the Blessed One, the Gnosis-Body of all Tathāgatas; for they have the same intrinsic nature as the Blessed One Mañjuśrī.

"Glory of the manifestation of all forms, bearing all reflections" (MNS 8.3cd). Regarding that, "glory of the manifestation of all forms": the manifestation of all forms by way of the nature of the world to be converted is the "manifestation of all forms. He whose glory consists of the manifestation of all forms is thus described. "Bearing all reflections": the reflection of all things without exception is "all reflections"; he who holds that is the "bearer of all reflections."

Therefore, he is invincible, the Great Lord (*maheśākhya*), the Great Sovereign (*maheśvara*) of the triple world (*traidhātuka*). [... The triple world: in that triple world, he is the Great Sovereign; he is both great and a sovereign, thus a "Great Sovereign" (*maheśvara*). "Standing upon the uplifted Noble Path, the Banner of Dharma, of great success": regarding this, "standing upon the uplifted Noble Path" means—

"Samucchritāryamārgasthaḥ" means one who stands upon that which is the "samucchrita-āryamārga"—that is, the Noble Eightfold Path which is perfectly raised up and manifested. "Dharmaketu" means the banner (*ketu*) of the dharmas; the meaning is the standard (*dhvaja*) of the dharmas. "Mahodaya" means that from which [greatness] arises (*udeti*); it is both great (*mahān*) and an arising (*udaya*), thus "mahodaya," meaning great increase (*mahāvṛddhi*).

"His body is the sole youth of the three worlds; he is the elder, the ancient, the Lord of Creatures. (MNS 8.5ab = 81ab) In this context, "his body is the sole youth of the three worlds" means that within the three worlds characterized by the previously mentioned attributes, he is the one and only, without a second. He is "one whose body is like the body of a youth," thus "trailokyaikakumārāṅgaḥ. "He is the elder" (*sthavira*) because he demonstrates those teachings to the Śrāvakas and others, and he is "ancient" (*vṛddha*) because he is the foremost among the Pratyekabuddhas as the teacher of their dharma. "He is the Lord of Creatures" (*prajāpati*)... [text continues].
"Each one reciting [the mantra]" refers to the beings, who are bodhisattvas; their lord is Prajāpati, the master, who is Mañjuśrī himself.

"Endowed with the thirty-two marks, he is lovely, the beauty of the three worlds. (MNS 8.5cd = 81cd) In this context, "endowed with the thirty-two marks" refers to: feet that stand firmly; soles of the feet marked with wheels; long heels; high-arched feet; long fingers and toes; hands and feet joined by a web; a body that is well-proportioned and full; antelope-like calves; the private organ withdrawn into a sheath; the upper part of the body like that of a lion; a broad space between the shoulders; and well-rounded shoulders.

The arms are long and hang down without bending; the neck is shaped like a conch shell; the jaw is like that of a lion; there are forty teeth, even in number; the teeth are white; the tongue is broad and long; there is a supreme sense of taste; the voice is like that of Brahmā and like the song of the kalaviṅka bird; the eyes are intensely blue-black; the eyelashes are like those of a cow; the skin is smooth; the skin is golden-colored; each hair grows individually; the body hairs curl upward and turn to the right; the hair of the head is as dark as sapphire; between the eyebrows and on the forehead is a very fine *ūrṇā* (tuft of hair); the head is crowned with a protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*); and the body is well-proportioned like the banyan tree.

These are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*). They are not shared by universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), disciples (*śrāvaka*), and others; for the marks of a Great Man, which constitute the sprouting of the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bīja*), do not arise in the coarse fields of the bodies of other men. Thus it is said in the *Abhidharma*: "The excellence of the Sage’s marks [is due to their] being well-placed, prominent, and complete. Regarding the term "lovely" (*kānta*): it means desirable, because he is longed for by all sentient beings. Regarding the term "beautiful in the three worlds" (*trailokya-sundara*): [it means...]

The three worlds are as described previously. Within them is the Beautiful One (Sundara), who is lovely to behold because his form is never-tiring to look upon (*asecanaka*). In this context, the excellence of the physical basis (*āśraya*) is to be understood through the quality of his form being never-tiring. For that Blessed One, even when gazed upon for a long time in every limb and member, appears as if he were seen for the first time; because he provides an inexhaustible flood of joy (*prīti-āsecanāt*) to those who behold him, he is said to possess a "never-tiring form" (*asecanakārūpa*).

"The Teacher of the qualities of worldly knowledge, the Teacher of the world, the Fearless One" (MNS 8.6ab). Regarding that, "the Teacher of the qualities of worldly knowledge": knowledge (*jñāna*) and qualities (*guṇa*) are "knowledge-qualities"; the knowledge-qualities of the worlds are the "worldly knowledge-qualities," and the Blessed One is the teacher (*ācārya*) therein. "The Teacher of the world" (*lokācārya*): because he teaches the true path to the world—consisting of gods, humans, and so forth—according to their respective capacities, he is called the Teacher of the world. "The Fearless One" (*viśārada*): because he accomplishes the welfare of the entire world by means of manifesting various emanations; "fearless" (*viśārada*) means being without fear.

"The Lord, the Protector, the Friend of the three worlds, the Refuge, the Savior, the Unsurpassed" (MNS 8.6cd). In this regard, "Lord" (*nātha*) means that he has become the protector of those beings who are without a protector and are submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra*. "Protector" (*trātā*) means a guardian, because he is the very embodiment of protection for those seeking refuge. "Friend of the three worlds" (*trilokāpta*) means one who is attained by the three worlds; he is the friend of the three worlds because, by manifesting the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) in all its aspects, he eradicates the dense thicket of all false views. "Refuge" (*śaraṇa*) means...

Because he is a refuge for those seeking refuge; because he is a protector (*tāyin*) due to ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is not interrupted; and because he is unsurpassed (*niruttara*) due to attaining the unsurpassed wisdom of all Tathāgatas.

"The enjoyment of the expanse of space, the ocean of omniscient wisdom" (MNS 8.7ab). Regarding that, "expanse of space" (*gaganābhoga*) refers to the enjoyment (*ābhoga*) of the equality-wisdom (*samatājñāna*) of space; it is the capacity for excellence-wisdom, the perfect enjoyment, which is "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*). It is the enjoyment of the expanse of space, hence "the enjoyment of the expanse of space. This is because it bestows the consecration of the sovereignty over the Dharma of the three realms. "The ocean of omniscient wisdom" (*sarvajñajñānasāgara*) means:

One who knows everything is "omniscient" (*sarvajña*); his knowledge is "omniscient knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*). The ocean of that [knowledge] is the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*), because of its extreme vastness.

"The shatterer of the eggshell of ignorance, the breaker of the cage of existence" (MNS 8.7cd). In this context, "ignorance" refers to delusion regarding karma, its fruits, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels; this is the "egg. It is called the "eggshell" because it is the primary basis of dependent origination and the cause for the arising of the world. One who "shatters" it is one whose nature is to break it, because its very essence is to rend it asunder. For this very reason, it is said to be "the breaker of the cage of existence. "Existence" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); that itself is the "cage."
Because it is not subject to departure; it is the shatterer of that [obscuration], due to reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of the cultivation of the true meaning.

"One who has pacified all afflictions and has gone to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra" (MNS 8.8ab). Regarding that, "one who has pacified all afflictions": there are three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*): the affliction of defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the affliction of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the affliction of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*). Among these, the affliction of defilements consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*). The affliction of karma consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*). The affliction of birth consists of the remaining links [of dependent origination]. Furthermore, affliction is also twofold: the affliction of cause (*hetu-saṃkleśa*) and the affliction of fruit (*phala-saṃkleśa*).

In this context, the defilement of cause consists of those members whose intrinsic nature is affliction and karma; the defilement of result consists of the remaining members. Furthermore, there are seven types of defilement, which correspond to a sevenfold cause: ignorance is the cause of perversion (*viparyāsa*); formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are the cause of projection (*ākṣepa*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the cause of bringing [the result] near (*upanayana*); name-and-form and the six sense bases (*nāmarūpa-ṣaḍāyatana*) are the cause of appropriation (*parigraha*); contact and feeling (*sparśa-vedanā*) are the cause of enjoyment (*upabhoga*); craving, grasping, and becoming (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna-bhava*) are the cause of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); and birth, along with old age and death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*), are the cause of agitation (*udvega*).

And all this affliction proceeds from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*). It is "entirely stilled" (*sarvaśamita*), meaning that in which every single affliction has been pacified without remainder; because it is thus, he is called one who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.

"Jñānābhiṣekamakuṭaḥ samyaksambuddhabhūṣaṇaḥ" (The crown of the consecration of gnosis, adorned by the perfectly awakened ones). Regarding that, "jñānābhiṣekamakuṭaḥ": a crown for the purpose of consecration is an *abhiṣekamakuṭa*; one who possesses the crown of the consecration of the gnosis of Samantabhadra is "jñānābhiṣekamakuṭaḥ. And consequently, he is "samyaksambuddhabhūṣaṇaḥ" because he is adorned by them.

"The pacifier of the three types of suffering, the triple-extinction, the infinite, and the one possessing the three liberations" (MNS 8.9ab). Regarding that, "the pacifier of the three types of suffering": this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). "The three sufferings" are: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of appropriation (*upādānaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*lakṣaṇaduḥkhatā*). In the sense of the feeling and the cause of feeling within the truth of suffering—taking the principle that "whatever is felt here is suffering"—the "cause of feeling" should be understood as those phenomena that serve as the basis for feeling. And so it has been said:

"The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering. [The term] "suffering" refers to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), because it is the engagement with its causes. The practice for the sake of the signless nature of the truth of suffering is [the truth of cessation]. "Tranquility" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) by virtue of the meaning of the pacification of those two. Therefore, it is said: "The Blessed Mañjuśrī is the pacifier of the three types of suffering. "The end of the three" means that the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) is the end of the [first] three truths.

Furthermore, because it is stated that the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), there is the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma through the arising of remedies for the eighty-four thousand types of mental conduct (*cittacarita*) of sentient beings. For this very reason, he says: "Infinite" (*ananta*) and "Going to the three liberations" (*trimuktiga*). The Blessed One Mañjuśrī is "going to the three liberations" (*trimuktiga*) because he goes to those three liberations according to the distinctions of the Śrāvaka and other vehicles.

"Completely liberated from all obscurations, he has attained equality with space" (MNS 8.9cd). Regarding that, "completely liberated from all obscurations" (*sarvāvaraṇanirmukta*) means: "all" (*sarva*) and "obscurations" (*āvaraṇa*) together constitute "all obscurations. These are said to be fivefold, based on the divisions of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, maturation (*vipāka*), the knowable (*jñeya*), and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). The Blessed One, the gnosis-body of all Tathāgatas, is liberated from these. For this very reason it is said: "he has attained equality with space," because of his liberation from all obscurations.

"Transcending the stains of all afflictions, he has gone to the state that is beyond the paths of the three times" (MNS 8.10ab). Regarding this, "transcending the stains of all afflictions" means: all afflictions (*kleśa*) have the characteristics already described; they themselves are the stains (*mala*). He has transcended (*atīta*), meaning he has emerged from them, because he is free from the stains of all primary and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding "the three times" (*tryadhva*): it is called the three times because its nature consists of the past, future, and present; thus, by way of having the form of the three periods of time, it is the three times. Regarding "gone to the state that is beyond the paths" (*anadhvagatiṃ gata*): that which is not a path is "beyond the path" (*anadhva*). He has gone to that state.

Furthermore, because the past is past, the future has not yet arrived, and the present exists as both [past and future], there is no abiding; and since the three times are thus not established, the movement of that path is "movement on a non-path. He has gone to that movement on a non-path throughout the three times.

"Great elephant among all beings, the crest-jewel of crests of qualities" (MNS 8.10cd). Regarding that, "great elephant among all beings": because he has attained the dharma of distinguished realization, he is a great elephant; he is the great elephant among all beings. "Great elephant among all beings" means the preeminent one. For this very reason, he is called "the crest-jewel of crests of qualities."

He is called Guṇaśekhara because he is the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*) and the pinnacle of all mundane and supramundane qualities that lead to higher attainment, even among those who are themselves the crowns of excellence. Just as in the world there is the designation "crest" (*śekhara*) for flowers placed upon the head, so too, because he stands above the entire multitude of virtues, he is the "Crest of the Crests of All Virtues."

"Completely liberated from all substrata, well-established on the path of space" (MNS 8.11ab). Regarding that, "completely liberated from all substrata": there are four substrata, characterized by dharma, artha, kāma, and nīti. Because he is liberated from even these four factors, he is said to be "completely liberated from all substrata," due to being unshakable by all phenomena and free from transformation. "Well-established on the path of space" means because he is firmly established in the path of space, which is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
And so it is said in the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā*: "Subhūti, this cultivation of space is what is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."

“Bearing the great wish-fulfilling gem, the supreme of all jewels, the pervasive one” (MNS 8.11cd). It is a "great wish-fulfilling gem" (*mahācintāmaṇi*) because it is both great and a wish-fulfilling gem. He is "bearing the great wish-fulfilling gem" (*mahācintāmaṇidhara*) because he wears that which accomplishes the attainment of whatever desired object is wished for. For this very reason, he is "the supreme of all jewels," because he is the most excellent among all jewels. The term "pervasive one" (*vibhu*) has its meaning already explained.

"The great wish-fulfilling tree (*mahākalpataru*) and the supreme great auspicious vase (*mahābhadraghaṭottama*). (MNS 8.12ab) Regarding that, "the great wish-fulfilling tree" (*mahākalpataru*): it is both great and a wish-fulfilling tree, hence "the great wish-fulfilling tree. Because it bestows the accomplishment of desired objects, it is for that very reason "expanded" (*sphīta*), owing to its complete prosperity. Regarding "the supreme great auspicious vase" (*mahābhadraghaṭottama*): it is both an auspicious vase and supreme, hence "the auspicious vase supreme"; and it is both great and the auspicious vase supreme, hence "the great auspicious vase supreme."

"One who acts for the benefit of all beings, a doer, a seeker of welfare, and one who is affectionate toward sentient beings" (MNS 8.12cd). Regarding that, "one who acts for the benefit of all beings": because he performs the welfare of all beings by means of these [objects] such as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and so forth, Mañjuśrī is "one who acts for the benefit of all beings. For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Candragomin in the *Jambhalastotra*: "The auspicious vase, the wish-granting tree, and the wish-fulfilling gems—even though they are insentient—they bring happiness to sentient beings; how much more so the Blessed One, who has taken them up out of compassion?"

Because he appears even in the form of stationary beings (*sthāvara-nāmarūpa*) for the sake of disciplining sentient beings; because he acts as a "teacher" by providing instruction in the Dharma according to their respective capacities; because he is a "seeker of welfare," meaning that which is beneficial and conducive to the future—that is his nature, hence he is a seeker of welfare; and because he is "affectionate toward sentient beings" due to his love for the world as if it were his only son.

"Knowing the auspicious and the inauspicious, knowing the time, knowing the occasion, the pervasive master who observes the commitments" (MNS 8.13ab). Regarding that, "knowing the auspicious and the inauspicious": *śubha* and *aśubha* together are *śubhāśubha*; the meaning is "the wholesome and the unwholesome. He knows that, thus the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is "one who knows the auspicious and the inauspicious. In some cases, he even understands what is inauspicious for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. As it has been said: "For one possessed of compassion, there is no such thing as the inauspicious. "Knowing the time": he knows the time, thus he is "one who knows the time" (*kālajña*).

"This is the time for descent; this is the time for teaching the Dharma; this is the time for acting for the benefit of sentient beings; this is the time for equanimity; this is the time for final nirvāṇa"—such are the [distinctions]. "One who knows the *samaya*" (*samayajña*) means one who knows and understands the essential nature of the heart-seals (*hṛnmudrā*), mantras, and vidyās; for that very reason, he is a *samayin*. "The pervasive lord" (*vibhu*) has already been explained.

"Knowing the faculties of beings, knowing the right time, and skilled in the three liberations" (MNS 8.13cd). Regarding that, "knowing the faculties of beings" (*sattvendriyajña*) means: the faculties of beings are the "faculties of beings" (*sattvendriyāṇi*); these are the faculties associated with sentient beings, such as those of dull faculty and so forth. He knows them, thus he is "one who knows the faculties of beings. "Knowing the right time" (*velajña*) means: he knows the time, thus he is "one who knows the time. This is because giving and other such acts, when bestowed at the proper time after having understood the intentions of the beings who are supplicants, become inexhaustible. "Skilled in the three liberations" (*vimuktitrayakovida*) means:
He is called "skilled" because of his proficiency in the three types of liberation of the śrāvakas and others, which are characterized by conceptual differentiation.

"Endowed with qualities, a knower of qualities, a knower of the Dharma, praised, and the source of auspiciousness" (MNS 8.14ab). In this context, "endowed with qualities" means he himself possesses them. "A knower of qualities" means he knows the qualities of external disciples and others; thus, he is a knower of qualities. "A knower of the Dharma" means he knows the mundane and supramundane Dharma; thus, he is a knower of the Dharma. "Praised" means he is endowed with the uncommon marks of a Great Being and so forth. "The source of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalodaya*): that from which something arises is its "source" (*udaya*).
Since the arising of mundane and other forms of auspiciousness occurs from him, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is the source of auspiciousness.

"The most auspicious of all that is auspicious; fame, fortune, glory, and virtue" (MNS 8.14cd). Regarding this, "the most auspicious of all that is auspicious" (*sarvamāṅgalyamāṅgalya*) means: that which is suitable for what is auspicious (*maṅgala*) is "auspicious" (*māṅgalya*); thus, he is the most auspicious among all things that are auspicious and most purifying. "Fame" (*kīrti*) refers to his fame remaining undiminished even today due to his performance of many marvelous deeds for the benefit of sentient beings in [previous] births such as those of Viśvantara and Śaśa; this is because the Blessed One has taken on a physical form [as those beings]. "Fortune" (*lakṣmī*) refers to...

Because he is the source of all prosperity for sons of noble family and others who are devoted to cultivation with one-pointed minds, the Blessed Mañjuśrī is *lakṣmī*. He is called *yaśas* because he has reached the ultimate limit of excellence in generosity and the other perfections, and because he is a mass of stainless fame due to the absence of all defects and impurities. He is called *śubha* because his nature consists of the ten paths of wholesome action.

"The great festival, the great breath, the great bliss, and the great delight" (MNS 8.15ab). Regarding that, "the great festival" (*mahotsava*): it is a great festival (*mahān* and *utsavaḥ*) which is a "great festival. One is called a *yāyāvara*. He who performs the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) every year according to the rule, and who is constantly engaged in sacrifice—he is called a *yāyāvara*. Others know one who has entered the path of liberation as being constantly a *yāyāvara*.

In both respects, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī alone is a traveler (*yāyāvara*), because he constantly engages in giving and because he is perpetually established on the path to liberation due to his exclusive inclination toward the side of virtue. He is called "the Great Consolation" (*mahāśvāsa*): consolation is *āśvāsa*; that which is both great and a consolation is "Great Consolation," so named because he thoroughly consoles those beings who are inclined toward passion and the like through meditative absorptions such as Śrīvajrasattva. He is called "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*): that which is both great and bliss is "Great Bliss."

Because he produces joy by teaching the unsurpassed Dharma according to the spiritual capacity of all worlds; thus, "Mahāratih" means great delight (*mahatī ratiḥ*). He whose delight is characterized by being untainted (*anāsrava*) is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, Mahāratih.

"Honor, veneration, prosperity, joy, the lord of glory and fame" (MNS 8.15cd). Regarding that, "honor" (*satkāra*) means being worthy of respect and worship within the three realms. "Veneration" (*satkṛti*) means the act (*kṛti*) of honoring; it is the practice of the virtuous (*santaḥ*). For the "virtuous" are the disciples (*śrāvaka*s) and others, and their practice is in accordance with reality. As it has been said: "He who teaches the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs according to the rule, and explains the meaning of the mantras, is designated as one who practices veneration (*satkṛti*)."

The Blessed One and Mañjuśrī are said to be "honored" because they have taught the twelvefold word of the Buddha, which is the realization of the ultimate truth, and because they have correctly explained all mantras. He is "prosperity" because he is the form that serves as the basis for all manifestations. He is "delight" because his nature is that of universal joy. He is the "Lord of Fortune and Fame": Fortune refers to the goddesses, and their fame consists of happiness and mental well-being; the Blessed One is their Lord and Master.

"Vareṇya, Varada, Śreṣṭha, Śaraṇya, Śaraṇottama" (MNS 8.16ab). Regarding these: "Vareṇya" means because he is the foremost among all those who are to be approached for refuge. "Varada" means a giver of boons (*vara*), because he fulfills [the wishes] according to one's intentions. "Śreṣṭha" means because he is the most excellent among outsiders, the *śrāvakas*, and so forth. "Śaraṇya" means because he is worthy of being a refuge for the wretched, the suffering, and those without protection. For this very reason, he is called "Śaraṇottama" (the supreme refuge).

"The supreme enemy of great fears, the destroyer of all fears without exception" (MNS 9.16cd). Regarding that, "the enemy of great fears" means he is the adversary of the eight great divine fears: disease, death, famine, fire, water, demons, locusts, and mice; he is their enemy because he destroys calamities by means of his power to strike down disease and the rest. For this very reason, he is called "supreme. As for "the destroyer of all fears without exception":

The eight fears without remainder are the great fears beginning with lions, elephants, fire, and so forth. Because he is the destroyer of all those fears without exception, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī is the "Destroyer of All Fears. This is because all fears are destroyed by the mere recollection of him.

Now, by virtue of his nature as the discipliner of the world for all sentient beings, he appears even in various forms to those who are devoted to each of them. Thus it is said: “He has a crest, he has a topknot, he has matted locks, he has braided hair, he is shaven-headed, and he wears a crown” (MNS 9.17ab). Regarding that, “he has a crest” (*śikhī*): he is one who possesses a crest (*śikhā*), meaning he appears in some places in the form of a child. “He has a topknot” (*śikhaṇḍī*): in the form of Kārttikeya. “He has matted locks” (*jaṭila*): he is one in whom matted locks (*jaṭā*) exist; thus, he appears in the form of one who bears matted locks.

"Jaṭī" means in the form of one with matted locks. "Mauṇḍī" means in the form of one who bears a shaven head. "Kirīṭimān" means one who possesses a *kirīṭi*, that is, a crown; he exists in the form of Āditya and others. This is because these [forms] arise as appearances within the mental continuums of those beings who are to be trained, appearing in whatever form is appropriate for them. And so it has been said:

"Five-faced, five-crested, with a crest of five locks. (MNS 8.17cd) This half-verse in the *anuṣṭubh* meter is to be understood as pertaining to Ādibuddha within the *ādiyoga* according to the guru’s instruction; since it has already been explained in that very context, it is not stated here again.

"One who upholds the great vow, wears the girdle of muñja grass, is a celibate student, and possesses the supreme vow" (MNS 8.18ab). Regarding this, "one who upholds the great vow" is so called because he sometimes appears in the form of being adorned with the five mudrās. "Wears the girdle of muñja grass" refers to his practice of the vow of wearing a belt made of muñja grass. "A celibate student" (*brahmacārī*) is so called because he has practiced celibacy for infinite eons; he is that very Blessed One Mañjuśrī, whose mind is not disturbed even when faced with causes of transformation. Thus, he sometimes appears in the form of a celibate student.

Regarding the term *vratottama*: it is sufficient and complete to say that one who, having practiced celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years for each Veda, has spent his entire life in the state of a mendicant or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) without even entering the householder stage (*gṛhāśrama*), is called one who has "sufficiently dwelt in celibacy" and is a "supreme observer of vows" (*vratottama*). For this very reason, because he is the most excellent among all observances, Mañjuśrī alone is appropriate [for this title], owing to his practice of the conduct of gnosis throughout immeasurable eons.

"Mahātapas, devoted to austerity, a *snātaka*, Gautama, the leader" (MNS 8.18cd). Regarding this, "mahātapas": he whose austerity (*tapas*) is great is "mahātapas," because he remained engaged in difficult practices for six years, subsisting on only half a sesame seed. His demonstration of this was for the purpose of winning over those to be trained by him (*tadvineyānām āvarjanārtham*). Consequently, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī is called "mahātapas. As for "devoted to austerity" (*taponiṣṭha*):

The culmination (*niṣṭhā*) or finality of the austerity (*tapaḥ*) of the entire world, which is characterized by the pacification of the senses, is found in him; thus he is "one who has reached the culmination of austerity" (*taponiṣṭha*), and that one is Mañjuśrī. Regarding the term *snātaka*: one who has studied the Vedas and completed his vows is a *snātaka*. Because he has reached the ultimate limit of all vows and all branches of knowledge, the noble Mañjuśrī alone is called the *snātaka*. *Gautama* is a name of his lineage (*gotra*); by means of that, the Blessed One is designated. For this very reason, he is called the "Leader" (*agraṇī*):
because of his attainment of the knowledge of the Omniscient One, he holds the position of seniority among those of his own lineage.

"The knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa, [becomes] Brahmā, having attained the nirvāṇa of Brahman" (MNS 8.19ab). Regarding the term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*): by the word *brahma*, the Veda is meant. One who knows or understands these is a "knower of Brahman," which refers to a learned reciter (*anūcāna*). Indeed, Brahmā and the others were such learned reciters. For it is so recorded in tradition: Viṣṇu and Maheśvara first followed the Veda as it resided in space and proclaimed it to Prajāpati; Prajāpati [taught] it to Indra; and Indra [taught] it to Vasiṣṭha.

Vasiṣṭha [taught] Pārāśara; Pārāśara [taught] Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana [taught] Jaimini, and so forth. The Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī, possessing such characteristics, is indeed the one who has correctly studied and is appropriately endowed [with this lineage], because the Blessed One, having followed the entirety of the sacred teachings (pravacana) comprised within the three vehicles, spoke them for those to be trained. Therefore, that Mañjuśrī appears even in the form of a knower of Brahman (brāhmaṇa) to his devotees. Thus, he is called "the Brāhmaṇa."

"Austerity, sacred learning, and birth—these are the causes of a Brahmin. Since the Blessed One is endowed with austerity produced over infinite time and with infinite, boundless sacred learning, and because he is the source for the arising of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), he is endowed with these three qualities; thus, the Blessed One is the supreme Brahmin. Alternatively, the Veda is twofold by way of the division between Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. Therein, that Veda which consists of the Brāhmaṇa is the Blessed Mañjuśrī.

Because the effect to be accomplished by that [path] is accomplished by the Blessed One alone; therefore, he also appears in that form in some instances. Regarding "Brahmā": here, Brahmā is understood as one who has attained the first dhyāna in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), because the Blessed One also appears in that form. Regarding "the nirvāṇa of Brahmā" (brahmanirvāṇa): the nirvāṇa of Brahmā is "brahmanirvāṇa," and that is bliss (ānanda). Thus it has been said: "Bliss is the nature of Brahmā; it is called consciousness. The Blessed One himself is also [present] in that form. He is "one who has attained" because he has attained the state of being a source of the Lokasāra (lokasāratva) for the world. He is "one who has attained" because he has attained the state of being a source of the Lokāgra (lokāgratva) for the world. He is "one

One who is non-deceptive is an *āpta* (reliable authority). And so it has been said: "A father, a friend, and others may be *āpta*s in some respects because they possess uncorrupted causes; if the Veda is indeed unauthored, then the Omniscient One is *āpta* regarding objects beyond the senses. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī is the supreme *āpta* due to his union with unsurpassed knowledge, compassion, and skillful means. He who possesses such a one is "one who has an *āpta*" (*āptavān*).

"Liberation (*mukti*), release (*mokṣa*), the limb of liberation (*vimokṣāṅga*), freedom (*vimukti*), tranquility (*śāntatā*), and auspiciousness (*śiva*)" (MNS 8.19cd). In this context, "liberation" refers to the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As it was said by Dharmakīrti: "Liberation, however, arises from the vision of emptiness; its purpose is the cultivation of everything [necessary for that]. Consequently, the Blessed One himself is liberation, because he exists inseparably from emptiness. "Release" (*mokṣa*)...

In that yogin who has entered upon dispassion, who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises; in one who is joyful, rapture is born; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he experiences happiness; in one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, he knows things as they truly are; he sees things as they truly are; knowing things as they truly are, and seeing things as they truly are—

"One becomes weary; being weary, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated. Thus, for one who sees things as they truly are, the state of liberation of mind has been established by the Blessed One, because of his seeing reality (*bhūtadarśitvāt*).
