And so it has been said: "With a body that is not cowering, one should endure sensations; like the extinguishing of a lamp, such is the liberation of his mind. It has also been said by the Master Kambala: "The mind defiled by passion and the like is *saṃsāra*; its separation from those [defilements] is [liberation]."

"Thus, liberation has been briefly described by the Victors who have abandoned all obscurations. In this way, such liberation as that of the Śrāvakas and others was established by the Blessed One within their respective vehicles; and that Blessed One should be understood as Mañjuśrī himself, because he is omnipresent.

Regarding "factors of liberation" (*vimokṣāṅga*): the factors of liberation are the limbs of liberation. Liberation is awakening (*bodhi*). Its factors are the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eight factors of the path (*aṣṭamārgāṅga*). Namely: the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of awakening of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of awakening of tranquility (*prasrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhisaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of awakening of energy (*vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga*), and the factor of awakening of equanimity (*upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅga*).

And because these are limbs—that is, constituent parts—of enlightenment, they are called "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*). Immediately following these, which serve as the antidotes to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there are the eight limbs of the path, distinguished by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for the sake of abandoning the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). They are as follows: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

That very [path] is both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, because they are the limbs of liberation and awakening. Thus, that Blessed One Mañjuśrī is called the "limb of liberation," since he has that as his intrinsic nature.

"Liberation" (*vimukti*) means [freedom] from the bonds of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. And thus: there are three bonds (*bandhana*): passion is a bond, delusion (*moha*) is a bond, and hatred (*dveṣa*) is a bond. These are called "bonds" because those bound by them cannot transcend the triple world (*traidhātuka*). Because one is liberated from them, it is called "liberation."

And thus, in this context, he will state regarding the benefits: "Liberation from all bonds. Regarding "quiescence" (*śāntatā*): it is called "quiescence" because of the quiescence of all mental disturbances (*cittopaplava*), that is, of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as the apprehending subject and so forth. Regarding "auspiciousness" (*śiva*):

That dependent origination which is free from the eight points of dispute, such as cessation and so forth, and which is characterized by the pacification of all conceptual proliferation—that is the Auspicious (śiva). And that Blessed One, the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) of all Tathāgatas, is called "Auspicious" because his intrinsic nature is the knowledge of emptiness. Thus it has been said by the Noble One (Āryadevapāda): "No cessation, no arising; no annihilation, no permanence; No unity, no plurality; no coming, no going."
That which is dependent origination, the auspicious cessation of conceptual proliferation, and so forth.

“Nirvāṇa, cessation, peace, the supreme good, the departure, the end, the maker of an end to pleasure and pain, the finality, dispassion, and the destruction of the substrates. (MNS 8.20) In this context, “nirvāṇa” is the designation; the remaining terms are its explanations according to their different aspects. [The nature of nirvāṇa is stated in the *Ratnāvalī*: “Nirvāṇa is not even non-existence; how much less could it be existence? The exhaustion of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is called nirvāṇa. Regarding “cessation” (*nirvṛti*):

Nirvāṇa is cessation (*nivṛti*); it is so called because its object of focus consists of those [elements] alone (*tanmātrāvalambanatvāt*). It is peace (*śānti*); "peace" means the act of calming (*śamana*). And that belongs to the Śrāvakas. It is the supreme departure (*niryāṇa*); "departure" means going forth with certainty (*niścayena yānam*). It is the excellent Nirvāṇa [of the Pratyekabuddhas]; it is the departure of the Pratyekabuddhas.

[82!!! *Antaga* means "one who goes to or reaches the end"; that is, one who goes to destruction (*anta*), meaning *antaga*. He is Akṣobhya, because he completely purifies those whose conduct is dominated by hatred through the gateway of his own liberation. *Sukhaduḥkhāntakṛt* (the maker of an end to pleasure and pain) refers to Ratnasambhava; for, by means of his nature of bestowing the purity of generosity, he brings about the end of the pleasure and pain of those beings whose conduct is dominated by stinginess.

"Perfection" refers to Amitābha; for, by means of revealing the nature of reality as the purification of passion (*rāga*), he reaches the culmination of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) for those beings who are characterized by passion. "Dispassion" refers to Amoghasiddhi; for, by generating dispassion in those beings characterized by indolence through his own form of liberation, and by engaging their minds in the side of virtue, he reveals the path to *nirvāṇa*. "The destruction of the substratum" refers to Vairocana; "substratum" (*upadhi*) is latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), and its "destruction" (*kṣaya*) is its eradication.

It is the destruction of the substrata (*upadhikṣaya*). This is because, for beings whose conduct is dominated by delusion, there is an illumination of the knowledge of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) by means of revealing the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as it is. Furthermore, liberation is twofold: with remainder of the substrata (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and without remainder of the substrata (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Among these, that of the outsiders and others is with remainder; that of the perfectly awakened Buddhas (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is without remainder. For this very reason it was said: "Those faults, along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), do not exist in the one Protector."
And therefore, since that very Blessed One Mañjuśrī alone is to be approached even by way of the nature of both types of nirvāṇa, he says "nirvāṇa," and so forth.

"Unconquerable, incomparable, unmanifest, without appearance, and stainless" (MNS 8.21ab). Regarding that, "unconquerable" (*ajaya*) means he is not conquered by others. "Incomparable" (*anupama*) means because he is devoid of all points of comparison. "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) means because he lacks forms such as those of women and so forth. "Without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*) means because he is free from appearances. "Stainless" (*nirañjana*) means because he is without defilement. Since that very Blessed One is the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*), he is grasped by these five qualifying terms.

"Partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed, and untainted" (MNS 8.21cd). Regarding these: "partless" because it is devoid of parts (*kalā*); "all-pervading" because it has gone everywhere; "omnipresent" because it is the intrinsic nature of all things, both stable and moving; "subtle" because it is subtler than even the minute and subtle; "the seed" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, which is inlaid with the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that cannot be seen as either merit or demerit; and "untainted" because its intrinsic nature is the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*). Thus, it is fourfold.

Because its intrinsic nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is fourfold: space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and suchness (*tathatā*). [This is because] it is stated that the untainted (*anāsrava*) Truth of the Path is threefold, and these are also unconditioned. Due to the distinctions of emptiness and so forth, it is the untainted; that very Blessed One is [the Tathāgata], because he has that as his intrinsic nature.

"Free from dust, stainless, immaculate, with faults vomited out, and free from affliction" (MNS 8.22ab). In this context, "free from dust" (*araja*) means being devoid of the dust of passion and so forth. "Stainless" (*viraja*) means that because of the purity of suchness (*tathatā*), there is no alteration of its state. "Immaculate" (*vimala*) means that because all phenomena are empty, defilements are merely adventitious; thus, the Blessed One himself is called "immaculate. "With faults vomited out" (*vāntadoṣa*) means one by whom the faults of passion and so forth have been vomited out—that is, cast away. For this very reason, he is "free from affliction" (*nirāmaya*).
He from whom all illness and disease have departed is "the one free from illness" (nirāmaya). And it is that very Blessed One who is distinguished by such qualities.

"Suprabuddha, Viśuddhātman, Sarvajña, Sarvavit, Para. (MNS 8.22cd) Regarding these: "Suprabuddha" means perfectly and pre-eminently awakened (*suprabuddha*), because of his non-erroneous realization of things as they truly exist. "Vibuddhātman" means specially awakened (*vibuddha*) compared to the Śrāvakas and others; his "self" (*ātman*) is the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*). He whose self is that very [emptiness] is the "Vibuddhātman. "Sarvajña" means...

He is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) because he knows all that is to be known without exception; he is "all-seeing" (*sarvavid*) because he knows the mental conduct, the inclinations, and the latent tendencies of all sentient beings. For this very reason, the Blessed One is supreme and preeminent.

"Transcending the nature of consciousness, wisdom maintains a non-dual form. (MNS 8.23ab) Regarding that, "transcending the nature of consciousness": there exists an *ālayavijñāna* distinct from [the consciousnesses of] the eye and so forth; and it is precisely this that contains all seeds, not the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the others. Why is this so? Because of scripture and because of reasoning. As for the reasoning, it has been explained there at length through many approaches, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

The scripture (*āgama*), however, should be stated because it is free from dispute and because there is little to be said regarding it. Thus it is said in the *Abhidharmasūtra*: "The element (*dhātu*) is beginningless and the common support of all phenomena; since it exists, all states of existence (*gati*) exist, as does the attainment of nirvāṇa. Its true nature (*dharmatā*) is the true nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatā*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); he has transcended and passed beyond that, because even that is non-apprehendable. And the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is used everywhere because it is characterized by sovereign power (*adhipatya*).

The wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). For this very reason, it is said to "assume a non-dual form," because its nature consists of both vastness and profundity.

"Non-conceptual, effortless, and the creator of the bodies of the Buddhas of the three times. (MNS 8.23cd) Regarding that, "non-conceptual" means because he is without conceptualization even with respect to ultimate conceptualization. And so it has been said: "The wise person does not sink even into ultimate conceptualization; for what difference is there between a conceptualization of the beautiful or even the ugly? Therefore, that very Blessed One is non-conceptual. "Effortless" means...

"Without effort" (*nirabhisaṃskāra*) means that exertion (*ābhoga*) has departed; thus, it is "effortless" (*nirābhoga*). Consequently, this is the meaning: in the previous state where wisdom proceeded with effort, one should maintain the resolve (*praṇidhāna*)—like a wish-fulfilling gem—that "even though I am free from conceptual construction, the welfare of sentient beings will be accomplished for me according to their capacity. That former resolve, being projected by that [wisdom], becomes constant, perpetual, and effortless.

Instead, [there is] the activity that has proceeded effortlessly (*anābhoga*), free from the desire for reward, which is the work for others; he who is the Wisdom-Being (*jñānasattva*) of all the Tathāgatas is called "effortless. By these two terms, it is stated that the Blessed One consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*). And so it has been said: "The work for others proceeds constantly and effortlessly, established by former vows. Thus: "He performs the work of the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the three times."

Those who are perfectly awakened in the three times are the "Perfectly Awakened Ones of the Three Times" (*tryadhvasambuddha*); their activities are the "activities of the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the Three Times" (*tryadhvasambuddhakārya*). One who performs those is the "performer of the activities of the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the Three Times. That indeed is the Blessed One.

"The Buddha is without beginning or end; he is the primordial Buddha, without causal succession. (MNS 8.24ab) Regarding this, "without beginning or end" (*anādinidhana*): beginning (*ādi*) and end (*nidhana*) are "beginning-and-end"; that which has no beginning-and-end is "without beginning-or-end," because for that Blessed One there is an absence of arising and cessation. Regarding "Buddha": now, how does this term "Buddha" apply to the Blessed One? And why might it not [so] apply? Because the root *budh* has the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Therefore, the suffix *-kta* [is applied].

The usage [of the word *buddha*] should be understood in both the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). In the sentences "the teaching was learned by Devadatta" (*buddhaṃ devadattenādhītam*) or "the treatise was learned by Devadatta" (*buddhaṃ śāstraṃ devadattena*), the word *buddha* is intended in the sense of the object (*karman*). For here, [it means] "he has awakened to all phenomena" (*buddhavān sarvadharmān*); thus, *buddha* refers to the agent (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, it means "one whose intellect (*buddhi*) awakens to all categories of things"; here the suffix *-a-* has the sense of the abstract noun (*matvartha*), or rather, it expresses excellence. Or else, because the root *budh* has the meaning of "understanding," and understanding is a form of "comprehension" (*gati*).

Since the suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "to go" (*gaty-artha*) in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*), let it be here in the sense of the agent: he is the Blessed One, the Buddha, because he has awakened to all phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the term *Ādibuddha*: he is the Buddha from the very beginning (*ādi*), thus the Ādibuddha; and he consists of the nature of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*). If one asks how so, it is said here: the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) is characterized by the powers (*bala*). Therein, the powers are five, characterized by faith, vigor, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Because it is manifested by these, there is the excellence of its realization within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) has the characteristic of fearlessness (*viśāradya*).

In that regard, the grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya) are: confidence regarding knowledge, confidence regarding abandonment, confidence regarding the teaching on the causes of affliction, and confidence regarding the teaching on the causes of purification. Thus, it is because of the attainment of the knowledge of equality through these four grounds of self-confidence.

Because it is purified by subtle conceptualization through the signless (*animitta*), the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) has the nature of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). In that regard, there are four analytical knowledges, due to the application of meaning (*artha*), phenomena (*dharma*), etymological definition (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*); for through them, one attains the wisdom of discernment. Because of the realization of the essence of all phenomena through the *dharmadhātu*, as well as the state of possessing the intention [to benefit others], there arises from that the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), which takes the form of loving-kindness and compassion. Because it is produced by the sovereignty over all things, it is called the "wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*."

Thus, this Blessed One consists of five gnoses and consists of five colors; he is to be viewed as having a single object of focus by way of the equality of all phenomena. And that Blessed One is Mañjuśrī for this very reason. He is "without lineage" (*niranvaya*); "lineage" (*anvaya*) means sequence. He is "without lineage" because no sequence exists in him, due to the absence of arising and ceasing.

"The Tathāgata is the one whose sole eye is gnosis, stainless, and whose very form is gnosis" (MNS 8.24cd). Regarding that, "one whose sole eye is gnosis" means he for whom gnosis alone is the eye; thus, he is "stainless," because of the absence of stains such as passion (*rāga*). "Whose very form is gnosis" means he for whom gnosis alone is the form, not [the aggregates] such as form (*rūpa*); he is the Tathāgata. The meaning is already explained.

"Lord of Speech, great debater, king of debaters, bull among debaters, best of speakers, most excellent, lion of debaters, unconquered. (MNS 8.25) In this regard, the existence of the fruit should be explained through the causal relationship between the eight terms beginning with "Lord of Speech. Therefore, he says: "Lord of Speech. He is the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśvara*) because he is the master of speech; for this very reason, he is the best among those who speak. "Great debater" means he is both great and a debater, thus a "great debater" (*mahāvādī*); for this very reason, he is the most excellent (*variṣṭha*).

"King of Speakers" (*vādirāṭ*): he is called *rāṭ* because he shines; the king of speakers is the "King of Speakers. For this very reason, he is the "Lion of Speakers" (*vādisiṃha*). "Bull among Speakers" (*vādipuṅgava*): *puṅgava* is said to mean "preeminent" or "foremost"; he is the bull among speakers, thus "Bull among Speakers. For this very reason, he is "Unconquered" (*aparājita*): he is unconquered because he is not defeated by others. And such is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, distinguished by these qualities.

"Samantadarśī, Prāmodya, Tejomālī, and Sudarśana. (MNS 8.26ab) Regarding that, "Samantadarśī" means one whose nature it is to see everywhere; this is because he has attained the wisdom (*jñāna*) of Samantabhadra. For this very reason, the Blessed One is the radiance that pervades everywhere. "Prāmodya" [means] because of his analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding meaning and phenomena (*dharma*). "Tejomālī" means a garland or row of splendors, that is, of rays; he who possesses such a garland of splendor is Tejomālī. "Sudarśana" means...
He whose good character, vision, and knowledge are excellent is Sudarśana; it is "excellent" because of its being endowed with reason.

"Śrīvatsa, Suprabha, Dīpti, Bhābhāsvarakaradyuti. Regarding that, "Śrīvatsa" refers to the Tathāgata mark (*lakṣaṇa*) in the heart of all Tathāgatas, which has the form of a śrīvatsa; it is not shared by any of the śrāvakas and others, serves as the seed of omniscience, is the cause for the arising of the entire world, and is the essence of non-delusion. It is so called because it is the receptacle for engraving [the teachings]. The Blessed One is indeed the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*) of all Tathāgatas, because he dwells within that heart. "Suprabha" means...

"Beautiful radiance" (*śobhanā prabhā*) because it is established through the application of a magnificent circle of light (*suprabhā-maṇḍala*). "Luster" (*dīpti*) because it illuminates all world-systems without exception or remainder. Regarding "the splendor of rays that produce brilliant light" (*bhābhāsvarakaradyuti*): the word *bhā* is a synonym for "ray" (*raśmi*) and also exists in its form ending in the vowel *ā*. Those rays are "brilliant" (*bhāsvara*); thus, they are "brilliant rays" (*bhāsvarakarāḥ*), meaning the rays of the wrathful deities (*krodha-dīdhitayaḥ*). The "brilliant rays of lights" (*bhānāṃ bhāsvarakarāḥ*) are [thus] "rays that produce brilliant light" (*bhābhāsvarakarāḥ*). The splendor of these is "the splendor of rays that produce brilliant light" (*bhābhāsvarakaradyutiḥ*).

And therefore, for the sake of disciplining those beings who are to be disciplined through wrath—by means of the radiance of rays issuing from his own [wrathful] form—that very Blessed One is called "the one whose hand-radiance is luminous."

"The supreme great physician, the best, the unsurpassed remover of thorns" (MNS 8.27ab). Regarding that, "great physician" (*mahābhiṣag*): he is both great and a physician, thus a "great physician"; the meaning is "the king of great physicians," because he eradicates all diseases such as passion (*rāga*). "Supreme" (*vara*): he is called supreme because he bestows the medicine of unerring instruction for the sake of pacifying the disease of ignorance. For this very reason, he is "best" (*śreṣṭha*), because he uplifts the entire world.

"Extractor of thorns" (*śalyahartā*) means one who removes thorns; he is an extractor because his nature is to remove the thorns of the heart—such as passion and so forth—from all sentient beings by means of revealing the reality of the dharmas that serve as the antidotes to those [afflictions] exactly as they are. For this very reason, this Blessed One Mañjuśrī is unsurpassed.

"The tree of all medicines, the great enemy of the disease of the afflictions" (MNS 8.27cd). Regarding that, "the tree of all medicines": "all medicines" (*aśeṣabhaiṣajya*) refers to medicines without exception (*niravaśeṣa*). The "tree of all medicines" is the tree of those [medicines]. For this Blessed One appears as the Great King of Medicines for the sake of favoring the entire world. And so it has been said: "They become great trees in the forests. Regarding "the great enemy of the disease of the afflictions": [it means he is the one who destroys the disease of the afflictions.]

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are passion (*rāga*) and so forth; these themselves are the diseases, hence "affliction-diseases. He is their great enemy because he reveals the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) which serves as their antidote.

"The beloved ornament of the three worlds, the glorious one, the circle of stars" (MNS 8.28ab). In this context, "ornament of the three worlds" (*trailokyatilaka*) means that he is so called because he is the unique ornament of the entire world—the three worlds—acting as the crest-jewel upon their crowns. "Beloved" (*kānta*) has already been explained. "Glorious" (*śrīmān*) is likewise [to be understood]. "Circle of stars" (*nakṣatramaṇḍala*) means the circle (*maṇḍala*) of the stars (*nakṣatra*).
Thus, for that Blessed One who is of such a nature, he is the "Circle of Stars" because his intrinsic nature is that very [circle].

"Extending to the limits of the sky in the ten directions, the great and lofty banner of Dharma" (MNS 8.28cd). In this context, "the sky in the ten directions" (*daśadigvyoma*) means the sky of the ten directions (*daśadiśāṃ*). "The limit of that" is "extending to the limits of the sky in the ten directions. Dharma itself is the banner; thus, it is the "banner of Dharma" (*dharmadhvaja*). It is both "great" (*mahān*) and "lofty" (*ucchraya*); [thus it is the "great and lofty"].

(Mahocchrayaḥ): And thus, this is the meaning: he whose great height (*mahān ucchrayaḥ*) extends as far as the limits of space in the ten directions in the form of the Banner of Dharma (*dharmadhvaja*); because that Blessed One has surpassed the merit and knowledge of the entire world, [his fame] being widespread, since he stands out like a banner.

"Extremely vast as the sole umbrella over the world," because he removes the heat of all afflictions (*kleśa*). "The mandala of loving-kindness and compassion": *maitrī* and *karuṇā* are *maitrīkaruṇau*; he is their mandala, because he takes up their essence.

"The glorious Padmanarteśvara, the great lord Ratnacchatra" (MNS 8.29cd). Regarding that, "Padmanarteśvara" refers to the Blessed One who has attained the well-known samādhi. "Glorious" (*śrīmān*) has its meaning already explained. "Ratnacchatra" [is so called] because he consists of all jewels. "Great lord" (*mahāvibhu*): he is both great and all-pervading, thus a "great lord," because he is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

"The Great King of all Buddhas, who maintains the embodiment of all Buddhas" (MNS 8.30ab). Regarding "the Great King of all Buddhas": he is both great and a king, thus a "Great King. He is the Great King of all Buddhas belonging to the three times; he is the Great King of all Buddhas because his intrinsic nature is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Regarding "who maintains the embodiment of all Buddhas": the self of all Buddhas is the "Self of All Buddhas," which is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*). Its "embodiment" (*bhāva*) is its existence (*sattā*). One who maintains that is "the one who maintains the embodiment of all Buddhas."

"The great yoga of all Buddhas, the single teaching of all Buddhas" (MNS 8.30cd). Regarding that, "the great yoga of all Buddhas": it is a great yoga (*mahāyoga*) because it is both great (*mahat*) and a yoga; thus, the great yoga of all Buddhas is the "great yoga of all Buddhas. For the Blessed One Vajrasattva Tathāgata is indeed the great yoga, because he dwells in the heart of all Tathāgatas; therefore, he is so called. As for "the single teaching of all Buddhas":

The teaching and vehicle of all Buddhas existing in the three times is one and the same; he who possesses this is "one whose teaching is the single teaching of all Buddhas. For it is said: "There is indeed only one vehicle, namely, the Mahāyāna."

"The glory of the Vajra-jewel consecration, the sovereign lord of all jewels, the lord of the lords of all worlds, the sovereign of all Vajra-holders, the great mind of all Buddhas. (MNS 8.31–32a) In this context, "Vajra-jewel" refers to Akṣobhya; his "glory of consecration" is Sattvavajrī. "Sovereign lord of all jewels": "all jewels" is Ratnasambhava, and his "sovereign lord" is Ratnavajrī. "Lord of the lords of all worlds": [refers to Amitābha].

The Lord of All Worlds is Amitābha; his consort is Dharmavajrī. "Lord of all Vajra-holders" refers to Amoghasiddhi, the bearer of the Vajra-banner of all; his consort is Karmavajrī. "Great Mind of all Buddhas" refers to Vairocana, the Universal Buddha; his consort is Vajradhātvīśvarī.

Consequently, this is the meaning: by virtue of the nature of those five family mothers associated with the five Tathāgatas—Vajra, Ratna, and so forth—the Blessed One Mañjuśrī attains the Vajra, Ratna, Padma, Viśvavajra, and Cakra.

"The movement of the minds of all Buddhas; the great body of all Buddhas; the eloquence of all Buddhas. (MNS 8.32bcd = 108bcd). In this context, "the movement of the minds of all Buddhas" is because [he] has the nature of mind (*citta-svabhāvatvāt*). "The great body of all Buddhas" is because [he] has the nature of body (*kāyātmakatvāt*). "The eloquence of all Buddhas" is because [he] has the nature of speech (*vāk-svabhāvatvāt*). Therefore, in the *Śrīsamāja*, he is called "the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas," for that Blessed One is the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*) of all Tathāgatas.

"Vajrasūrya, the great light; Vajracandra, of stainless radiance" (MNS 8.33ab). [... [Something is missing... Vajracandra is the moon of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Its "stainlessness" (*vimalā*) is due to the removal of all afflictions (*kleśa*), latencies (*vāsanā*), and so forth. "Radiance" (*prabhā*) is its brilliance, because it illuminates the world-systems (*lokadhātu*) without decay. He who possesses this is so described. By these two phrases, the following is stated:

The oral tradition (āmnāya) is as follows: a son of noble family (kulaputra) or others who practice the conduct of the mantra-entrance (mantramukhacaryācārī), having stabilized a sun-maṇḍala or a moon-maṇḍala within his own heart, and having visualized upon it either the letter Ā or one or another of the individual names and their meanings, should recite the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti*.

"Great passion beginning with dispassion, blazing with light of universal color" (MNS 8.33cd = 109cd). Here, by the phrase "great passion beginning with dispassion," he speaks of the distinction in the natures of yogins. [... One who has entered into dispassion, one who practices the conduct of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and one who practices the conduct of the mantra-entrance—these three natures are that very Blessed One. "Blazing with light of universal color": "universal color" means a color of manifold forms.

He is one whose radiance possesses a brilliant splendor that destroys all the darkness of gloom; for it is thus that the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, in a single very moment, [acts] through various gateways for those to be trained who have gathered from various world-systems, and who possess various names, lineages, dispositions, conducts, inclinations, and faculties.

By way of the distinctions of impermanence, suffering, non-arising, non-cessation, primordial peace, natural nirvana, and so forth; by way of the distinctions of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the noble truths (*āryasatya*); by way of the distinctions of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to the faculties (*indriya*) and so on; and by way of the distinctions of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the intrepidities (*vaiśāradya*), and other qualities of a Buddha—through various languages, various gateways, various exits (*niryāṇa*), various approaches, and various vehicles.

Because [the Buddha], through various vessels and the attainment of various fruits, teaches [the Dharma] by means of a single teaching at that very moment, it is said: "He illuminates the Dharma with the knowledge of a single teaching. Therefore, it says: "Possessing a blazing radiance of all colors. Furthermore, the explanation of this name-mantra phrase is according to the guru’s instruction: "The Blessed One (bhagavān) is the essence of all Tathāgatas" (sarvatathāgatagarbha); this should be applied to the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) of all Tathāgatas.

"The Perfectly Awakened One in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, the upholder of the Dharma of the Buddhas' assembly" (MNS 8.34ab). Regarding that, "the Perfectly Awakened One in the vajra-paryaṅka posture" means: the vajra-paryaṅka of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened Śākyamuni, [is the] vajra-paryaṅka; by means of which that Blessed One, having defeated the four Māras, directly realized the gnosis of exhaustion and non-arising. And he is the Blessed One himself. "The upholder of the Dharma of the Buddhas' assembly" means:

The communal chanting (*saṅgīti*) of the Buddhas is the "Buddha-communal-chanting" (*buddhasaṅgīti*). For it is said: "We shall chant together; we shall not dispute. That very Dharma upholds it; thus, the Buddha-communal-chanting is the upholder of the Dharma, and that indeed is the Blessed One.

"The glorious Buddha-padmodbhava, the bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom" (MNS 8.34cd). Regarding that, "Buddha-padmodbhava": the Buddhas themselves are the lotuses (*padma*), namely the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*); because he arises from them—[freeing them] from the afflictions—he is Buddha-padmodbhava, who is the Blessed One himself. "Glorious" (*śrīmān*) means [endowed with splendor]. "Bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom" (*sarvajñajñānakośadhṛk*): the wisdom of the Omniscient One is "omniscient wisdom"; that itself is the treasury or storehouse, and he who maintains it is the "bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom."

"The King who holds the universal illusion, the great holder of the Buddhas' knowledge" (MNS 8.35ab). Regarding that, "holder of the universal illusion" (*viśvamāyādhara*) means he holds the universal illusion, which is emanation in various forms; thus he is the "holder of the universal illusion. "King" (*rāja*) means he is the very one who delights the world through well-spoken teachings on the ten paths of wholesome action. "Holder of the Buddhas' knowledge" (*buddhavidyādhara*) means the knowledge of the Buddhas is "Buddha-knowledge," which refers to the four *dhāraṇīs* characterized by dharma, meaning, mantra, and patience.
"He who upholds them is that great Buddha-vidyādhara," because he is omnipresent.

"Vajratīkṣṇa, the great sword, pure, the supreme syllable" (MNS 8.35cd). In this context, "Vajratīkṣṇa" refers to the form of the *mahāmudrā*; "the great sword" refers to the nature of the *karmamudrā*; "pure" refers to the book of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is by way of the *samayamudrā*; and "the supreme syllable" refers to the gateway of the *dharmamudrā*. Therefore, this Blessed One is indeed the *Ādibuddha* himself; he is called Vajratīkṣṇa because he is sealed with the four *mudrās*.

"Great weapon of the Vajra-dharma of the Mahāyāna that cuts through suffering" (MNS 8.36ab). In this context, "suffering" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). The "cutting through" of these is the "cutting through of suffering. That itself is the "Mahāyāna," because it is the truth of the path. Its "Vajra-dharma" is the dharma of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Because it cuts through all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*), that very dharma is a "great weapon. Thus, the Blessed One is the "Great Weapon of the Vajra-dharma of the Mahāyāna that cuts through suffering."

Jinajig, Vajragāmbhīrya, Vajrabuddhi, the knower of things as they truly are. (MNS 8.36cd) Regarding this, "Jinajig" means *rdo rje zab mo 'dzin* (Holder of the Profound Vajra). "Vajrabuddhi" means the one who knows the meaning as it is. Here, "vajra" refers to the profound [vajra]; this profound primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) is the "profound vajra. Alternatively, it is so called for one who possesses the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) that is free from conceptual constructions such as subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

*Dzin* refers to the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya and the rest. Because he is the master who triumphs over and surpasses them, he is *Dzindik*, namely the Blessed One Vairocana; and that, moreover, is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī himself. As for *Vajramati*, one who possesses an intellect (*mati*) that is like a vajra—indestructible—is *Vajramati*.

This is because it cannot be divided by anything comprised within conceptual constructions such as subject and object. "Cognizing the object as it is" means that through the representation of the object exactly as it exists, one cognizes the object as it is.

Regarding the phrase "complete in all perfections and endowed with the ornaments of all the stages": "complete in all perfections" means that all perfections are those such as generosity (*dāna*) and the rest; one who possesses the manner of completing them is described in that way. "Endowed with the ornaments of all the stages" means that all the stages are those beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*) and so forth.

This refers to what has been taught regarding that very ornament, which is the maṇḍala. As for the phrase "the pure phenomenon of selflessness, the moonlight of authentic gnosis": here, the "pure phenomenon" is the established characteristic of pure individual investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā*); "selflessness" is that which renders [appearances] non-manifest. That very authentic gnosis is the moon.

It is the generation of the mind of Samantabhadra, because it is the very body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*) of all the Tathāgatas; that itself is the Blessed One. "Possessing excellent light" refers to the gnosis that is naturally luminous, having the form of the lunar mandala; one who possesses that is described as such. "The great-endeavoring net of illusions" is the supreme lord of all tantras.

Regarding that, "The Great Exertion, the Net of Magical Illusion" means that the "Net of Magical Illusion" (māyājāla) is a collection of emanations; thus it refers to one who possesses such great exertion. "The Lord of all tantras" means the sovereign of all tantras, such as the Yoga Tantras and so forth, because he is their very nature. "Supreme" has already been explained.

"Vajrāsana possesses them all without exception; he bears the bodies of gnosis without exception. This means that he who possesses the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) which is the nature of samādhi, complete and without remainder, is "Vajrāsana possessing them all without exception. For that very reason, it says, "he bears the bodies of gnosis without exception," meaning he bears the bodies of the five gnoses (*pañca-jñāna*) without exception.
"Samantabhadra, of noble intelligence, the womb of the earth, who sustains the world"—in this regard, "Samantabhadra" refers to that which is excellent and virtuous in every respect.

He is Samantabhadra because he is the nature of the vajra of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). "Sudhī" means one of excellent intellect, for he is free from the entire web of conceptual construction. Regarding "the womb of the earth": the element of earth there is the receptacle world; that which produces it is the "womb of the earth."

Regarding "the holder of the world" (*jagaddhṛk*): "world" (*jagat*) refers to the realm of sentient beings. It is called "the holder of the world" because it holds [that realm]; thus, the meaning is that it is the support of all worlds. This is because, through these two phrases, it is shown that this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all things, both moving and non-moving. 87a3

[81] Thus it has been explained. Regarding the term *jagaddhṛti*: "world" (*jagat*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). Its "support" (*dhṛti*) means its sustenance; thus, *jagaddhṛti* means the support of the entire world, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of both stable and mobile entities.

"The great womb of all Buddhas, bearing the wheel of manifold emanations" (MNS 8.39cd). Regarding that, "the great womb of all Buddhas": because he is the cause of the arising of all Tathāgatas existing in the three times, and since this Blessed One has the nature of the vajra of bodhicitta, he is called "the great womb of all Buddhas. For this very reason, [he is] "bearing the wheel of manifold emanations."

The "universal emanation" (*viśvanirmāṇa*) refers to the emanation that consists of the manifestation of various kinds of worldly and supramundane deities. The "wheel of universal emanation" (*viśvanirmāṇacakra*) is its maṇḍala; he who bears that is the "Bearer of the Wheel of Universal Emanation" (*viśvanirmāṇacakradhṛk*).

"The foremost of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the upholder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" (MNS 8.40ab). Regarding that, "the foremost of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena": "all phenomena" (*sarvabhāva*) refers to all things, both stable and moving. Their intrinsic nature is the "intrinsic nature of all phenomena. That which is both the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and the foremost is the "foremost of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. If one asks why this is so, it is because the Blessed One has as his intrinsic nature the body of the Tathāgata’s gnosis, which is utterly pure in its form as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

"Holder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena": for this very reason, because he maintains—that is, upholds—the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is the selflessness of all dharmas, he is the "holder of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena," since his own nature is the great emptiness of all aspects.

"Having the nature of non-arising, for the sake of the universe, and upholding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" (MNS 8.40cd). Regarding that, "having the nature of non-arising": non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the state of being impermanent; he whose nature is such is "one having the nature of non-arising," because from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), he is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*). "For the sake of the universe": because, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyā*), he accomplishes the purpose of benefiting the entire world. "Upholding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena": therein, what are "all phenomena"?

Namely: the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-fields (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), perfections (*pāramitā*), stages (*bhūmi*), emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*), truths (*satya*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), concentrations (*samādhi*), doors of dhāraṇīs (*dhāraṇīmukha*), powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the unique qualities of a Buddha (*aveṇikabuddhadharma*), the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*ānimitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—all these are "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*). Of these:

The intrinsic nature is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; and that is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are. Because he maintains that, he is the "Upholder of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena."

And so it has been said by Jñānapāda: "Having generated the mind of complete enlightenment through the application of great loving-kindness, and having realized that all phenomena are without self, one is liberated."

"One who possesses the realization of all phenomena through great wisdom in a single moment" (MNS 8.41ab). This "single moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) is that which is both one and a moment. This "greatly wise one" (*mahāprājña*) is both great and wise; he is characterized by the discernment of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaviveka*). Consequently, this meaning is established: by means of a single moment alone, through his great wisdom and through the realization of all phenomena as they have been described, he possesses the realization of all phenomena through great wisdom in a single moment;
thus, he is "one who possesses the realization of all phenomena through great wisdom in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇamahāprājñasarvadharmāvabodhadhṛk*).

"The realization of all phenomena, the Sage who has reached the limit of reality, the one of supreme intelligence" (MNS 8.41cd). Regarding that, "realization of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmābhisamaya*) means: the realization (*abhisamaya*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is the realization of all phenomena; he who possesses such a correct awakening (*samyagavabodha*) is the "realizer of all phenomena. "The Sage who has reached the limit of reality" (*bhūtāntamuni*): "reality" (*bhūta*) means truth, that is to say, *tathatā* (suchness); its "limit" (*anta*) is the "limit of reality," and he is both that [limit] and a sage (*muni*), thus he is the "Sage who has reached the limit of reality. For this very reason, he is "of supreme intelligence" (*agradhī*). This is because the yogic knowledge has reached the ultimate pinnacle of the cultivation of the true object.

"Stable, with a perfectly serene self, he who holds the awakening of the Perfectly Awakened One" (MNS 8.42ab). In this context, "stable" means being free from both lethargy and agitation; for this very reason, his self is "perfectly serene," which refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because of the absence of both the steady and the moving states. "He who holds the awakening of the Perfectly Awakened One" means that because he maintains the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, the Blessed One is called "the holder of the awakening of the Perfectly Awakened One."

"Directly perceived by all Buddhas, the flame of gnosis is brilliantly radiant. (MNS 8.42cd) In this context, "directly perceived" means that its characteristic is to be personally experienced (*svasaṃvedya*). "By all Buddhas" refers to those existing in the three times. "Flame of gnosis" means the lamp of wisdom (*prajñāpradīpa*). "Brilliantly radiant" means because it pervades ineffably ineffable Buddha-fields.

For this very reason, the Blessed One, who is the Gnosis-Body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas, desiring to favor sentient beings to be trained—whether they possess dull, middling, or superior faculties—manifests even through his nature as the welfare of the world.

By means of manifesting all mundane and supramundane meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), through the sequence of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, the stages (*bhūmi*), and the perfections (*pāramitā*), [the Buddha] appears in some places as a physical body (*ātmabhāva*), in some as a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*samyaksambuddha*), in some as the nature of mundane and supramundane gnosis, in some in the form of a "wishing-jar" (*bhadraghaṭa*) and so forth for the sake of favoring poor sentient beings, and in some in the form of great medicine and so forth for sentient beings afflicted by great diseases—thus, by means of the natures of all stable and moving phenomena.

For the sake of favoring the world, having followed [the sequence] by expanding two hundred and seventy-five name-mantra syllables and words, and having divided that into five parts according to the distinctions of the *kulas*, he assigned fifty-five name-mantra syllables to each *kula*. These name-mantra syllables, having fulfilled the activity of all Tathāgatas for infinite and boundless Buddha-fields in the ten directions, illuminated the assemblies of all Tathāgatas and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas.

Having purified beings of passionate temperament by means of his own gate of liberation, and having returned [to them] adorned with the colors of his own family, one should visualize them established in due order within the third wheel outside the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu. Then, the son of noble family or daughter of noble family who practices the conduct of the mantra-gate, by taking as his object the threefold form previously explained and reciting the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti*, attains the multitude of qualities as described; such is the oral tradition.
There are forty-two verses; the syllables of the name-mantra are two hundred and seventy-five, both by calculation and as a numeral.
In the *Āryanāmasaṅgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the eighth chapter, concerning the praise by way of the wisdom of discerning investigation, is concluded.

Now, with reference to the praise of the Lord’s Gnosis-Body (*jñānakāya*), which is the [essence] of all Tathāgatas by way of the entrance of the Gnosis of Equality, he says: “The supreme accomplisher of desired aims, the purifier of all miserable states, the highest of all beings, the Protector, the liberator of all beings” (MNS 9.1). In this context, “desired aim” (*iṣṭārtha*) means that which is both desired (*iṣṭa*) and an aim (*artha*). Its accomplisher, its producer, is Ratnasambhava.

For those overcome by stinginess, [he acts] through the gateway of the purification of giving; for this very reason, he is "the initiator of the gift purified of the three extremes. He is the "purifier of all miserable states" because, by purifying the karma that leads to the three miserable states—namely, the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm—he closes the doors to those miserable states. He alone is "the supreme among all sentient beings."

For this very reason, because he exerts himself for the sake of the supreme [awakening] of all sentient beings, he is therefore called the protector (*nātha*) of those sentient beings who are without a protector. He is called the "liberator of all sentient beings" because he brings about their liberation by means of the doors of [bestowing] the lineage (*gotra*), conduct (*carita*), disposition (*āśaya*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), inclinations (*adhimukti*), faculties (*indriya*), and so forth, for those who are to be trained (*vineya*).

"The sole hero in the battle against the afflictions, who destroys the pride of the enemy of ignorance; the glorious one who bears the grace of wisdom, yet assumes the forms of the heroic and the loathsome. The "afflictions" (*kleśa*) are attachment and the rest. The "battle with the afflictions" (*kleśasaṃgrāma*) is the conflict together with them. In that [battle], he is the "sole hero," unique and without a second, [surpassing] all the equipment for the combat of the primary and secondary afflictions. "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is delusion (*moha*).

Doubt regarding the [Four] Truths and so forth is itself the enemy, because it acts as an obstacle to the side of virtue (*kuśalapakṣa*). His pride is egoism; he destroys that, thus he is "the destroyer of the pride of the enemy that is ignorance. He is the seed of [all things], and he alone is the bearer of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). He is the "bearer of the erotic" (*śṛṅgāradhara*) because he bestows (*rāti*) semen (*śukra*) everywhere (*samantāt*); he is so called because he pervades all the sense faculties. He maintains that, thus he is "one who has removed suffering" (*gatārta*). He assumes the forms of the heroic and the loathsome.

Those specific forms of wrath which are endowed with the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsarasa*), he who bears their form—that is, the form of the heroic and the loathsome—is [the one] designated as *dhṛk*.

"Dancing with the casting of hundreds of staff-like arms and the placement of steps; possessing the magnificent expanse of a hundred arms; dancing across the expanse of the sky. (MNS 9.3) In this context, "casting of hundreds of staff-like arms" refers to the outward whirling of hundreds of staff-like arms. "Placement of steps" refers to positions such as *ālīḍha* and others. "Placement" (*nikṣepa*) refers to the distance of five spans (*vitasti*) and so forth. He who possesses these—namely, the casting of hundreds of staff-like arms and the placement of steps—is described as such.

Having displayed the dance of the earth-practice (*bhūmicaryā*), he spoke in order to further display the dance of the sky-practice (*gaganacaryā*): “The Lord of Dance (*narteśvara*) whose glorious hundred arms possess the expanse of the sky; his ‘glorious hundred arms’ (*śrīmacchatabhujāḥ*) are those hundred arms, and their ‘expanse’ (*ābhogaḥ*) is the extension of those glorious hundred arms. By means of that, there is an ‘expanse’—that is, a movement—in the sky, in the atmosphere. He who possesses hundreds of such arms is thus described.”

"Standing with the sole of one foot pressing upon the surface of the earth's mandala, and standing with the toenail of his big toe pressing upon the peak of the universe. (MNS 9.4) Regarding that, "standing with the sole of one foot pressing upon the surface of the earth's mandala": it is both "one" (*eka*) and "foot" (*pāda*), thus "one-foot" (*ekapāda*). Its "sole" is "the sole of one foot" (*ekapādatala*). "The surface of the earth's mandala" (*mahīmaṇḍatala*) is stated here by eliding the letter *l* (*lakāra*), or according to the recension of the *Saddharma* [Pundarīka Sūtra].

"One who stands with the surface of the earth's orb (*mahīmaṇḍatala*) stepped upon by the sole of one foot" means he is situated there, having the surface of the earth's orb stepped upon by the sole of one foot. He describes the activity of the second [foot] with the words beginning "the Brahmāṇḍa," and so forth. The big toe of the foot is the "toe of the foot" (*pādāṅguṣṭha*); its nail is the "nail of the toe of the foot. The summit of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is the "summit of the Brahmāṇḍa" (*brahmāṇḍaśikhara*).

He upon whose big toe-nail the [entire] Brahma-egg rests, having been stepped upon by him—that is, one whose foot and big toe-nail rest upon the summit of the Brahma-egg. By these two words, his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is demonstrated. Of that Blessed One; for the purpose of winning over those people who were to be disciplined by him.

"Having a single meaning, having the meaning of non-dual phenomena, having the meaning of the ultimate, and being indestructible; it is the object of various representations and forms, and the continuum of mind and consciousness. (MNS 9.5) In this context, "having a single meaning" means that its intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). For this very reason, it is said to "have the meaning of non-dual phenomena," because the apprehended object and the apprehending subject are untenable. It is called "the ultimate" because the ultimate truth is threefold, according to the distinctions of the object (*artha*), attainment (*prāpti*), and realization (*pratipatti*). It is "indestructible" because it is equal to space.

"The stream of various representations of forms and objects, and of mind and consciousness. Regarding "various representations of forms and objects": these are the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*). From this, the sequence is as follows: from the mind characterized as the storehouse consciousness arises the afflicted mind; and from that arise the six evolving consciousnesses, which are characterized by the representation of objects.

Furthermore, those latencies are perfumed within the *ālayavijñāna*, and from that *ālayavijñāna* arises again the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and from that, in turn, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). In this way, the subtle wheel of dependent origination revolves. Thus it has been said: "The maturation, that which is called mentation, and the representation of objects. And what does this mean? That which consists of the six types of object-representations, as well as the mind and the afflicted mind—all that is indeed the Blessed One himself.

"Delighting in the meaning of all phenomena without exception, delighting in emptiness, one of supreme intelligence" (MNS 9.6ab). Regarding that, "delighting in the meaning of all phenomena without exception" means: delight (*rati*) or joy in all those meanings of phenomena (*bhāvārtha*), such as abiding and so forth, by virtue of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). As it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna: "Abiding, arising, and ceasing; existence and non-existence; inferior, equal, or superior— The Buddhas speak [of these] by virtue of worldly convention, not by virtue of ultimate reality (*tattva*). Regarding "delighting in emptiness":

Delight in emptiness and joy in emptiness is "delight in emptiness. Because its intrinsic nature is the suchness of all phenomena, it is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, also unapprehendable. For this very reason, he is called "the one of supreme intelligence."

"And having transcended craving for existence and so forth, he possesses great delight in the three realms of existence" (MNS 9.6cd). Regarding "having transcended craving for existence and so forth": therein, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) constitute the three realms of existence (*trayo bhavāḥ*). Craving for the realm of desire is *kāmarāga*. Craving for the realms of form and the formless is *bhavarāga*; it is not *kāmarāga*. Thus it is said in the *Abhidharma*: "Craving for existence arises from two realms. Therefore, because he has transcended—that is, gone beyond—desire and the other [afflictions], he is called "one who has transcended craving for existence and so forth."

He is indeed the Blessed One Mañjuśrī. Regarding the phrase "one who finds great delight in the three states of existence": although this is so, he is called "one who finds great delight in the three states of existence" because, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the sons of the gods born in those respective levels within the three states of existence—namely the desire realm and so forth—he manifests births here and there.

"Pure, white as a bright cloud, with the beautiful luster of the autumn moon’s rays; possessing the radiance of the orb of the rising sun, with the glow of great red nails; with a fine crest like the tip of a sapphire, bearing hair-tips as dark as a great blue gem; possessing the splendor of the rays of a great jewel—he is adorned with the Nirvāṇa of the Buddha. (MNS 9.7–8) Regarding that, "pure" means due to the removal of the stain of ignorance. As for the remaining words, they have been explained in the context of the primordial union (*ādiyoga*) of the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas residing within the wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*);
they are not denoted by those [remaining] terms here.

"Shaking a hundred world-systems, possessing the great stride of the bases of miraculous power; the bearer of great mindfulness, the reality, the sovereign of the fourfold mindfulness and meditative concentration. (MNS 9.9) Regarding that, "shaking a hundred world-systems": "hundreds of world-systems" means *lokadhātu-śatāni*. He whose nature it is to shake those is "the shaker of a hundred world-systems. This demonstrates the majesty of the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of a bodhisattva established in the stage of *muditā* (joy). And so it was said by the venerable Candrakīrti:

He is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and all three fetters have been destroyed by him; for that Bodhisattva bears supreme joy, his attachment having arisen from the shaking of a hundred world-systems.

"Great stride of the bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda-mahākrama*) means that, relying upon the seclusion of body and mind, there are four bases of psychic power characterized by zeal, energy, mind, and investigation; these culminate in the non-conditioned activity (*anabhisaṃskāra-pravṛtti*) which has as its ultimate end the complete exhaustion of aversion toward opposing factors. He who possesses the great stride—the great prowess—of those bases of psychic power is "one of great stride of the bases of psychic power. "Possessor of great mindfulness" (*mahāsmṛtidhara*) means that his mindfulness is great.

And that great mindfulness (*mahāsmṛti*) has the characteristic of non-forgetfulness regarding a familiar object; he is "such" because he maintains that [mindfulness]. Regarding "reality" (*tattva*): because of the nature of the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). What is intended here as reality within these three natures? It is said: "That which is eternally non-existent, that which exists yet not in reality, and that which exists and does not exist in reality"—thus the three natures are intended. The characteristic of the imagined is eternally non-existent.

This is the reality (*tattva*) in the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because its nature is non-erroneous. The dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) both exists and does not exist in reality, because it is mere illusion; this is the reality in the dependent nature. The perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is both existence and non-existence in reality; this is the reality in the perfected nature due to its connection with reality (*tattva-yogāt*). That Blessed One himself is called "Reality. Regarding the phrase "the king of the samādhis of the four applications of mindfulness" (*catuḥ-smṛti-samādhi-rāj*), these are the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

For example, there is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). This body, which consists of an arrangement of various parts, has the characteristic of being devoid of [the notions of] "grasper" and so forth; thus it is the application of mindfulness. Likewise, there are the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), and the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Because of its conjunction with diligence, concentration, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, it shines; thus it is a "king" (*rāṭ*). The concentration of the four applications of mindfulness is the "King of Concentration," the *catuḥsmṛtisamādhirāṭ*, and that indeed is the Blessed One.

"The fragrance of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, an ocean of the qualities of the Tathāgata, one who knows the method of the eightfold path, and one who knows the path of the perfectly awakened Buddha" (MNS 9.10). In that regard, "the fragrance of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment" refers as follows: from the unconditioned [dharmas] beginning with faith that flow forth spontaneously, there arise the seven factors of enlightenment—characterized as previously described—which have the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as their object and are included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). These very factors are called "flowers. They are called "flowers of the factors of enlightenment" because they serve as the cause for the fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Their "fragrance" refers to that which is attained through knowledge consisting of hearing. Because one directly realizes the world—which is characterized by being like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflection in space—on the path of seeing that [truth], a great fragrance, a joy of the mind, arises; thus it is called the "fragrance of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment. Regarding the phrase "ocean of the qualities of the Tathāgatas": the qualities of the Tathāgatas are the *tathāgataguṇas*.

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) and so forth are themselves the oceans, because of their vastness and because they are the source of other jewel-like qualities; thus, the Blessed One is the ocean of the Tathāgata’s qualities. Regarding the phrase "knower of the method of the eightfold path": the eight factors of the path, which are manifested through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), have been explained previously. Their "method" (*naya*) means the path or the means (*upāya*). He who knows—that is, understands—that [method] is the "knower of the method of the eightfold path. Regarding the phrase "knower of the path of the perfectly awakened one" (*samyaksambuddhamārgavid*): [this refers to the same].

Regarding the term *samyaksambuddha*: because he has realized for himself, without instruction from another, that which is desired, and because he has realized the true path, he is the *samyaksambuddha*. The "path" (*mārga*) of the *samyaksambuddha* is the *dharmadhātu*; one who knows that is the *samyaksambuddhamārgavit*, namely, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).

"Greatly attached to all beings, yet unattached like the sky; born from the minds of all beings, with the speed of the minds of all beings. (MNS 9.11) In that regard, "greatly attached to all beings" (*sarvasattvamahāsaṅga*) means: it is both great and an attachment, thus a "great attachment" (*mahāsaṅga*). A great attachment toward all beings is a "great attachment to all beings" (*sarvasattvamahāsaṅga*). In this context, there are four bases of sympathy (*saṅgrahavastu*): generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavacana*), purposeful conduct (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*). Through generosity, one knows what is beneficial; through pleasant speech, one knows the proper time.

Through beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), he knows the welfare of others; through common purpose (*samānārthatā*), he knows the Dharma. By virtue of his knowledge of the superior and inferior capacities of sentient beings, the means of attraction (*saṅgrahavastu*) are accomplished. Because he brings all sentient beings into direct union with himself by means of these means of attraction, he is called the "Great Attachment to All Sentient Beings. Conventionally (*saṃvṛtitaḥ*), he is indeed the Blessed One. However, ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*), that very Blessed One is without attachment, because his intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). For this very reason, he is like space, because his intrinsic nature is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"Born from the minds of all sentient beings": born in the mind is "mind-born"; born from the minds of all sentient beings is "born from the minds of all sentient beings. And so it has been said: "All sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*. "Swift as the mind of all sentient beings": the speed of the mind is called the speed of the *Tathāgata*. Swift as the minds of all sentient beings is "swift as the minds of all sentient beings," because he conforms to the mental activities of the hearts of all sentient beings.

He who knows the faculties and objects of all sentient beings, he who captivates the minds of all sentient beings; he who knows the reality of the meaning of the five aggregates, and who maintains the purity of the five aggregates. (MNS 9.12) In that regard, "he who knows the faculties and objects of all sentient beings" means: the faculties of all sentient beings are weak, middling, or superior; their "object" is the state of those faculties, which is "the object of the faculties of all sentient beings. He who knows that is "he who knows the faculties and objects of all sentient beings"—that is the Blessed One himself. "He who captivates the minds of all sentient beings" means:

He is so called because he captivates the minds and hearts of all sentient beings through the gateway of teaching the Dharma according to their respective capacities. Regarding the phrase "knower of the reality-meaning of the five aggregates": therein, the five aggregates (skandhas) are characterized by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Among these, the aggregate of form has as its characteristics the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and non-informative matter (avijñapti). The aggregate of sensation [... has the nature of the three [types of feeling].

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) consists in the grasping of the signs of objects. The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists in those factors associated with or dissociated from the mind. The eight groups of consciousness constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). These are the five aggregates; their meaning is the "meaning of the five aggregates. That [meaning] is the sense of a "heap" (*rāśi*). The reality (*tattva*) of that is the realization of the meaning of discernment (*viveka*). In this context, the reality of the meaning of the five aggregates is characterized by the cessation of the grasping at oneness and so forth.

The cessation of that [self-grasping] is selflessness (*nairātmya*); from that, one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Thus, one who knows the reality of the meaning of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in such a manner is "one who knows the reality of the meaning of the five aggregates. That very person is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).

And so it has been said by the venerable Vasubandhu: "Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions other than the discernment of phenomena," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the bearer of the purification of the five aggregates": the five aggregates are themselves purified; thus they are the "purified five aggregates," characterized by ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. One who upholds these is the "bearer of the purification of the five aggregates"—that is, the Blessed One himself.

"Abiding at the limit of all deliverance, skilled in all deliverance, standing on the path of all deliverance, and the teacher of all deliverance. (MNS 9.13) Regarding that, "abiding at the limit of all deliverance" (*sarvaniryāṇakoṭistha*) means: whatever worldly forms of nirvāṇa there may be, their limit is their finality; he abides therein, and thus he is "abiding at the limit of all deliverance. "Skilled in all deliverance" (*sarvaniryāṇakovida*) means: he is skilled—that is, proficient—in the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas, and thus he is "skilled in all deliverance. "Standing on the path of all deliverance" (*sarvaniryāṇamārgastha*) means:

He stands on the path to the nirvāṇa of the pratyekabuddhas; he stands on all paths of deliverance; he is the teacher of all paths of deliverance. The nirvāṇa of the perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas) is the "all-deliverance"; he is its teacher and proclaimer—namely, the Blessed One himself.

"Uprooted from the twelvefold existence, bearing the twelvefold purity; having the form of the method of the four truths, and possessing the realization of the eightfold knowledge. (MNS 9.14 = 132) Regarding that, "uprooted from the twelvefold existence": there are twelve factors, namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). [Ignorance is so called] because it conceals reality and obstructs vision according to one's [erroneous] inclinations.

By "implanting" (*ropaṇa*), because the latent impressions of karma are established in consciousness (*vijñāna*) by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). By "leading" (*nayana*), because one is brought to the place of rebirth by consciousness. By "appropriating" (*saṃparigraha*), because the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is grasped by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). By "filling" (*pūraṇa*), because it is completed by the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). By "discriminating" (*tripariccheda*), because of contact (*sparśa*). By "experiencing" (*upabhoga*), because of feeling (*vedanā*). And by "attracting" (*karṣaṇa*), because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) binds the renewed existence (*punarbhava*) scattered by karma; and by "grasping" (*upādāna*), because consciousness is directed toward desires and so forth conducive to rebirth.

Because of "facing toward" (ābhimukhyāt), there is the turning toward the ripening of karma performed in a previous existence so that it may yield its fruit in a future existence. Because of "suffering" (duḥkhanāt), by means of birth, aging, and death—since existence characterized by the five aggregates of clinging has been uprooted and eradicated by these twelve factors in their reverse order of dissolution—he is called "one who has uprooted existence consisting of the twelve factors."

And so it is said in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*: "Because of concealing, because of planting, because of leading, because of grasping, because of filling, because of the threefold discrimination, because of enjoyment, and because of dragging along; because of binding, because of facing toward, and because of causing suffering, the world is afflicted."

"Holder of the twelvefold pure aspects" means that the twelve aspects are the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*); they are pure because they are devoid of the forms of apprehended object and apprehending subject. He who holds these is the "Holder of the Twelvefold Pure Aspects. "Having the aspect of the method of the four truths" means that there are the four noble truths known as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. The method (*naya*) or path of those four truths is itself the aspect (*ākāra*), the form; he whose [form] is such is the Blessed One, the "One Having the Aspect of the Method of the Four Truths. "Holder of the realization of the eight knowledges" means:

In this context, there are eight knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). He who upholds their realization—that is, their direct manifestation—is "the one who upholds the realization of the eight knowledges. That indeed is the Blessed One.

"One who possesses the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects, who knows reality in sixteen aspects, whose awakening consists of twenty aspects—he is the Fully Awakened One, the Supreme Knower of All. (MNS 9.15 = 133) In that context, "the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects" means the meaning of the truths (*satyārtha*). Having analyzed it into twelve aspects, the Wheel of Dharma has three turnings and twelve aspects; namely, [the first turning] as impermanent, suffering, and empty—this refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). [The second turning] as cause, origin, and production...

[He turns the wheel] of the truth of origination by way of its arising; of the truth of cessation by way of its being cessation, peace, and excellence; and of the truth of the path by way of its being the path, the method, and the practice. Since he thus turns the wheel of Dharma whose meaning consists of the truths in these twelve aspects, according to the capacity [of beings], that Blessed One is said to be "twelve-aspected."

"One who knows the reality of the sixteen aspects" refers to this: when one attends to the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, there arise the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*). Through these two, all ten afflictions belonging to the desire realm are abandoned. When one attends to the truth of suffering belonging to the form and formless realms in the same manner, there arise the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*).

By those two [paths], those very same [afflictions]—excluding those associated with aversion (*pratigha*)—namely the nine belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and the nine belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), totaling eighteen, are abandoned. Thus, through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) within the three realms by means of the four moments of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through the vision of suffering.

Of these same ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), when one attends to the remaining seven underlying tendencies in the desire realm—excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the misapprehension of rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarṣa*)—as the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*) belonging to the desire realm, by way of cause, origin, production, and condition, those very [tendencies] are abandoned through the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding the origin.

Those same twelve latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the two realms—excluding those associated with aversion—which pertain to the form and formless realms, are abandoned through the vision of the truth of origin by means of the subsequent-knowledge-receptivity (anvayajñāna-kṣānti) and subsequent-knowledge (anvayajñāna) regarding origin; thus, nineteen latent dispositions are abandoned through the vision of the truth of origin.

Likewise, for one who attends to the truth of the cessation of suffering belonging to the desire realm through the four aspects of cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation, those same seven proclivities mentioned as [abiding in] the origin are abandoned by means of the receptivity to and the knowledge of the dharma-knowledge regarding cessation. In this way, the twelve proclivities belonging to the form and formless realms are abandoned by means of the receptivity to and the knowledge of the subsequent knowledge. Thus, nineteen proclivities are abandoned through the vision of the truth of the cessation of suffering in the three realms.

Likewise, for one who attends to the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering in the desire realm through the four aspects of the path—path, correctness, practice, and departure—there are the two moments of receptivity and knowledge of the dharma-knowledge regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣāntijñāna*). By adding the eighth, namely the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), to the seven previously mentioned [fetters], these eight are abandoned through the vision of the truth of the path. Through the receptivity and knowledge of subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣāntijñāna*), the fourteen [fetters] belonging to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path are abandoned.

Thus, these twenty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are to be abandoned through the vision of the path; in this way, for one who brings the four noble truths before their mind through sixteen aspects, there is an absence of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Likewise, through the mental engagement with the fourfold aspects of the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering pertaining to the desire realm—as a path, as reason, as definitive emergence, and as accomplishment—there arises the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). Following those two [receptivities and knowledges], in the seven [moments] previously mentioned, there is morality (*śīla*) and...

By adding the adherence to supreme ascetic practices (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), eight are abandoned through seeing the truth of the path. Since the fourteen [afflictions] pertaining to the form and formless realms—consisting of the two types of patience and knowledge regarding the path—are abandoned through seeing the path, there are thus twenty-two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by seeing the truth of the path.

Therefore, by means of the sixteen aspects, one realizes the four noble truths; thus, there arises suchness—the realization of the non-erroneous reality that is free from the afflictions of the three realms.
