Because he knows and understands this, he is the knower of the sixteen aspects of suchness; he is the Blessed One himself.

Awakening by means of twenty aspects refers to the manifestation of perfect awakening through the mode of individually conceptualizing each of the five aggregates in twenty ways, as follows: "Form itself is the self; the self dwells in form; form belongs to the self; the self is possessed of form. "Feeling is the self; the self dwells in feeling; feeling belongs to the self."

"I possess feeling; perception is my self; I abide in perception; perception is mine. I possess perception. Formations are my self; I abide in formations; formations are mine. I possess formations. Consciousness is my self; I abide in consciousness; consciousness is mine. I possess consciousness."

Thus, by means of these twenty aspects, one thoroughly realizes non-conceptual primordial wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is said that "one awakens through twenty aspects. As the venerable Nāgārjuna stated: "When analyzed through reasoning, nothing exists apart from the aggregates; [those things] imagined by the non-Buddhists—"

"There is no self whatsoever; if it were the aggregates, it would be impermanent. That too is not the nature of a self. Because neither permanence nor impermanence exists, the support and the supported never exist either. Thus, the meaning of these three lines from the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra* has been explained.

"The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas, the creator of the immeasurable and infinite, who realizes all moments [of existence] in a single instant, and who knows the meaning of all things in a single moment of mind"—this means that the emanations of immeasurable Buddhas are the "immeasurable Buddha-emanations"; their collective embodiment is the "immeasurable Buddha-emanation body."

To the extent that sentient beings who are to be disciplined are brought to full maturity, he radiates an infinite limit of Buddha-emanations; since that very radiation is the Blessed One himself, it is said: "The emanation bodies of the Buddhas radiate infinitely and without limit."

The clear realization of all moments refers to that which is both a single moment and all [moments]; thus, "all moments" refers to those consisting of the nature of the sixteen moments. The knowledge of these is the clear realization of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and that itself is the Blessed One. Accordingly, it is stated in the Abhidharma: "Entering extensively in successive order..."

"By the path of seeing in sixteen moments, its fruit is abandonment. Thus it is said. "The moment of mind that cognizes all objects" refers to all the moments of all sentient beings. Because he knows their objects, he is "the moment of mind that cognizes all objects"; he himself is the Blessed One. "By means of various vehicles and methods, he radiates for the benefit of wandering beings."

"Through the three vehicles one attains liberation, yet through the single vehicle one abides in the fruit. Regarding this, "various vehicles" and so forth means that the vehicles which have become diverse are the "various vehicles," such as those of the śrāvakas and others. Their method is the path; the means for that is the "method of the various vehicles."

Therefore, "acting for the benefit of beings" refers to performing the welfare of migratory beings through that method of various vehicles and skillful means; because one discerns and extends [the teachings] therein, it is called "the method of various vehicles and skillful means."

...it radiates for the benefit of wandering beings. Regarding "definitive emergence through the three vehicles," because there is definitive emergence by means of the three vehicles according to the power of discipline, it refers to definitive emergence through the three vehicles. Ultimately, however, one abides in the fruit by means of a single vehicle; that which is only one vehicle is the "single vehicle" (ekayāna).

Its fruit is characterized by unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Because one abides therein, one abides in the fruit of the single vehicle; thus, the vehicle is indeed only one, namely, the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). This was also spoken by the venerable Kamalaśīla:

"Who would abandon the lordly elephant of contention and travel on the vehicle of a helpless donkey? Like one who abandons a noble, wealthy woman and desires a prostitute. "The master of the purity of the realms of affliction, who brings an end to the realms of karma, has crossed over all rivers and oceans; he has emerged from the wilderness of worldly application."

Regarding this, the "pure self of the afflictions" refers to the elements that constitute the nature of the afflictions; these are the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). Therefore, that which is the pure nature among those [elements] is the pure self of the afflictions.

"Exhausting the realms of karma" refers to the realms of karma such as the wholesome and so forth; these are the realms of karma known as the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Because they exhaust those [realms], they are called "exhausters," which means they destroy them, for they perform the action that brings about their disintegration.

"Having crossed all rivers and oceans": there are four rivers—the river of desire (*kāma*), the river of existence (*bhava*), the river of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the river of ignorance (*avidyā*). Among these, apart from views and ignorance, the outflows of desire themselves are the river of desire; they consist of twenty-nine entities. The outflows of existence themselves are the river of existence.

These are the twenty-eight substances. The views of the three realms are the river of views, consisting of thirty-six substances. Ignorance itself as an outflow is the river of ignorance, consisting of fifteen substances. That is it.

It is the ocean, because of its vastness. It is said that those who have truly crossed over those oceans of rivers have thereby reached the further shore of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Emerging from the wilderness of application, they enter into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in mere gnosis (*jñāna*); this is what is explicitly taught as "yoga."

This very thing is the "wilderness" (*kāntāra*), because it is difficult to know and difficult to cross. To emerge from that is "to have crossed"; because it is the state of complete perfection through all mundane and supramundane applications (*prayoga*), it is "emerged from the wilderness of application. That itself is the Blessed One.
Having thoroughly abandoned the afflictions, secondary afflictions, and all defilements along with their latent tendencies;
possessing wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion, he unfailingly accomplishes the welfare of the world.

"Having forever abandoned the afflictions and secondary afflictions along with their habitual tendencies; possessing great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means; acting for the benefit of beings so that it is never in vain"—in this regard, "afflictions" refers to the six [root afflictions] such as attachment and so forth, while "secondary afflictions" refers to the twenty-four [derivatives] such as anger and so forth.

The "thorough affliction" (*saṃkleśa*) consists of the seven types of suffering. That which possesses the permanent abandonment of those very phenomena—the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and thoroughly afflicted factors—along with their latencies (*vāsanā*), is what is described as: "the thorough abandonment of the primary and secondary afflictions along with their latencies. Alternatively, the "afflictions" refer to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Existence (*bhava*) and grasping (*upādāna*). The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). The others are as explained above.

[... [93] [approximately 18 akṣaras darkened] Great Compassion. He himself is the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "the one who accomplishes the purpose of the world unfailingly" (*amoghajagadarthakṛt*): "unfailing" (*amogha*) means not in vain; that which is both "the purpose of the world" (*jagadartha*) and "unfailing" is "the unfailing purpose of the world," and he who performs that is "the one who accomplishes the purpose of the world unfailingly."

"The meaning of the abandonment of all perceptions, the meaning of consciousness, the upholder of cessation; the object of the minds of all sentient beings, the assembly of all Buddhas. (MNS 9.xx = 138) In that regard, "the meaning of the abandonment of all perceptions" refers to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Furthermore, it refers to the first place of rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), namely the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). These three types [of states] are [to be understood] by means of those [perceptions].
He for whom the objects of mind and mental factors have been abandoned by means of these three is "one whose objects are abandoned of all conceptualizations"; he alone is the Blessed One.

"Vijñānārtha" means that consciousness itself is the object; thus, "vijñānārtha. This occurs specifically in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The second place of rebirth is the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); because consciousness alone is conceptualized there, it is that very thing which is the "object" (*artha*) of which there is cessation—thus, he is "Vijñānārtha," the Blessed One. Regarding "Nirodhadhṛk": in that same realm, the fourth place of rebirth is the cessation that is cultivated through the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). He is called "Dhṛk" because he maintains (*dhārayati*) that [cessation].

That very Blessed One is "the object of the minds of all sentient beings. This means that the mind of all sentient beings—[text partially obscured]—is precisely his object and sphere of activity; thus he is "the object of the minds of all sentient beings. That very Blessed One is "the range of the minds of all Buddhas. This means that the mind of all Buddhas existing in the three times is the thoroughly purified gnosis of the dharmadhātu, and he is its range; thus he is "the range of the minds of all Buddhas."
And so it has been said: "It is both afflicted and purified, with stains and without stains; its purity is held to be like the purity of the water-element, gold, and space."

"Abiding within the minds of all sentient beings, having attained equality with their minds; gladdening the minds of all sentient beings, delighting the minds of all sentient beings" (MNS 9.xx = 139). Regarding "abiding within the minds of all sentient beings": the mind (*manas*) is the consciousness (*citta*) of all sentient beings; he who dwells within (*antaḥsthaḥ*)—that is, in the midst (*madhye*)—of that is "abiding within the minds of all sentient beings. He is the Blessed One himself. For this very reason, it says "having attained equality with their minds": the mind of those sentient beings is "their mind" (*taccitta*).

Its equanimity is the equanimity of that mind, which is suchness (*tathatā*), that is to say, emptiness (*śūnyatā*). And so it is said in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*: "The suchness of ordinary beings, the suchness of śrāvakas, the suchness of pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of perfectly awakened buddhas—this suchness is one and the same. Having realized that suchness as the equanimity of all minds, he has gone to and attained it; thus he is "Tathā" (Thus-Gone).

Therefore, it is said: "the delight of the minds of all sentient beings. The delight of the minds of all sentient beings is *sarvasattvamanoratiḥ*. [The phrase *niṣṭhamanaḥprītiḥ* is missing. ... [Folio side is badly darkened; input provided later.]

Therefore, it is said: "It satisfies the minds of all sentient beings. This means that because those very sentient beings have transcended error, the mere fact that they generate the primordial wisdom of great bliss is described as "satisfying the minds of all sentient beings. For that very reason, it is further said: "It gladdens the minds of all sentient beings."

The delight of the minds of all sentient beings is the untainted bliss of the Tathāgata. Through the agitation of attachment to the essential nature, one enters into the state of "I alone am all things," whether moving or unmoving, solely through the mental formation (*manasaṃskāra*) of attachment. There is no error regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

"Having completely abandoned all sophistry, possessing an intellect free from doubt regarding the three goals, and being the master of the qualities that benefit all"—this refers to "being unerring regarding the tenets. That which is unerring regarding the tenets is the tenet itself; that which is free from an uncertain intellect and is unerring regarding those established conclusions is precisely what is meant by "being unerring regarding the tenets. For this very reason:

"Having completely abandoned all views" means that one has thoroughly understood the nature of reality as it exists. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the mind free from doubt concerning the three objects," one who possesses such a mind is "one with a mind free from doubt," because they have thoroughly understood the worldly and transcendent philosophical tenets (*siddhānta*).

The three objects are the past, the future, and the present. Mañjuśrī is their very nature, because the universal object is the nature of all things, whether mobile or immobile. He is the embodiment of the three qualities (*guṇa*), because he enters into *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus it has been said: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas, Because they serve the purpose of sentient beings."

"Therefore, I, whose nature is Samantabhadra, proceed according to the conduct of awakening. Thus it is said. "The five aggregates, in their meaning throughout the three times, are distinguished in every single instant; in a single instant, one attains perfect awakening, maintaining the very nature of all Buddhas."

Regarding this, the meaning of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the three times is as follows: because the meaning of the five aggregates consists of the nature of the various categories of the three times, it is said, "The meaning of the five aggregates is the three times themselves. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Abhidharma*: "Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are the five aggregates, beginning with form; these very [phenomena] are the four time-periods (*adhvan*)."

“Those which are associated with renunciation, together with the four [truths], and those contaminated aggregates that involve grasping—these are also ‘with conflict,’ ‘suffering,’ ‘origination,’ ‘the world,’ and ‘existence’ along with the gods. Thus it is said.

"Every moment is distinguished" means that during the stage of the cause, one has accumulated the roots of virtue consisting of the perfection of generosity and so forth; thus, because one understands all the phenomena of method and wisdom arising from hearing, reflection, and meditation, it is said: "Every moment is distinguished."

Regarding the stage of the fruit: one awakens to perfect enlightenment in a single moment. Because it is both a moment and singular, it is called "a single moment. One who, in that very same single moment, realizes the omniscient wisdom known as the wisdom of exhaustion and the wisdom of non-arising is "perfectly awakened in a single moment."

"Holding the nature of all Buddhas" means that this very nature belongs to all Buddhas residing in the three times; thus it is said: "Perfectly awakening in a single instant. Because one holds that, one "holds the nature of all Buddhas. As it is also stated: "The assembly of all Buddhas..."

"Because the Dharmakāya acts for the benefit of beings, it is equal [to all], yet its lifespan, lineage, and physical stature are not [identical]. Regarding the phrase "the bodiless body, the supreme body, the body that causes tens of millions to emanate, the teacher who displays all forms without exception, the great jewel, the crest-jewel": therein, "the bodiless body" means that which is not a body is the bodiless body.

One who possesses a non-existent body has a "bodyless body," because its very nature is that of the *dharmadhātu*. For that very reason, it is the supreme body (*kāyottama*), meaning it is the most excellent among the bodies such as the *saṃbhogakāya* and others; this is the sense of "supreme" (*pra*). "Bodies" (*kāyān*) refers to tens of millions of bodies—that is, countless millions of bodies. These are what cause [beings] to proceed.

Because he causes expansion, the body is "the one who expands ten million [forms]. For that very reason, it says: "The teacher who reveals all forms without exception. One who possesses the manner of correctly teaching those to be disciplined through forms that are without exception—that is, without remainder—is "the teacher who reveals all forms without exception"; that is the Blessed One himself.

The "Jewel Crest" (Ratnacūḍa) is a "jewel" in the sense that it causes all beings to be filled with attachment; it is a "crest" marked by that jewel. That itself is the mudrā, and the one who holds it is the Blessed One, because through the perfection of generosity alone, he completely fulfills all intentions.

Because he is definitively engaged in the perfection of generosity of all the Tathāgatas, Ratnaketu is called Mañjuśrī. Now, to summarize the teaching, the Blessed One is shown to have the nature of Ratnasambhava as well; thus it says, "The great jewel."
Because all Tathāgatas are infinite, it is thus spoken: since the Tathāgatas arise from the infinite great jewel, it is the wisdom of equality.

Furthermore, because all the Tathāgatas who have attained manifest, perfect enlightenment bestow the empowerment of the great Dharma King of the triple world through their own mudrās, it is therefore called the "Great Jewel"; it is the Blessed One Mañjuśrī himself.

Then, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, established in the Ākāśagarbha-samādhi, went to the infinite and boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions; having purified the realms of sentient beings afflicted by stinginess through his own gate of liberation, he divided the one hundred and four [deities] into five classes according to the distinctions of families such as the Śāśvata and so forth. Having assigned twenty-one names to each family and performed the activities of a Buddha by means of them, he returned once more to the exterior of the great Vajradhātu-maṇḍala.

In the fourth wheel, having become syllables colored by their own respective colors, they are established according to their sequence. Then, relying upon oneself as the aforementioned form of the triple world, a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family who practices the conduct of the mantra-entrance (*mantramukhacaryā*) and recites this *Nāmasaṃgīti* attains precisely those qualities previously mentioned; such is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*).

In the *Ārya-nāmasaṃgīti-ṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the ninth chapter, concerning the praise by way of the nature of the wisdom of equality, is concluded. There are twenty-four verses and one hundred and four syllables. 104.

Now, therefore, by way of the knowledge of the performance of rites, there is praise of the Blessed One, the Wisdom-Body of all Tathāgatas: “He who has awakened to all that is to be awakened to by all the Perfect Buddhas; he is the unsurpassed awakening of the Buddha, the syllable-less source of mantras, the great mantra of the three families. (MNS 10.1 = 143) In this context, “he who has awakened to all that is to be awakened to by all the Perfect Buddhas” means that which is to be realized—namely, that very Blessed One himself. Thus, he is “the one who has awakened to all that is to be awakened to by all the Perfect Buddhas.”

And so it is said in the *Śrītattvasaṅgraha*: "For perfect enlightenment depends upon you; you are the father of all seers. Having approached you, the Tathāgatas have come into being and will continue to do so."

"Buddha-enlightenment" (*buddhabodhi*) means the enlightenment of the three types of Buddhas, beginning with the *śrāvakas*; thus, it is "Buddha-enlightenment. For it is said: "There are three kinds: the enlightenment of the *pratyekabuddhas* and the perfect complete enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); all three are that very same thing. Regarding "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*): for this very reason, there is nothing superior to it; thus it is "unsurpassed. Or, it is "without syllables" (*anakṣara*), because in it there exist no syllables characterized as the signified (*vācya*) or the signifier (*vācaka*), since its intrinsic nature is the *dharmadhātu*.

"Mantrayoni" means that it is the source (*yoni*) of mantras because it is the place of their origin; thus, it is the cause. "The three great mantra families" (*mahāmantrakulatraya*) means: it is both "great" (*mahān*) and a "mantra" (*mantra*), hence a "great mantra" (*mahāmantra*); and the "three families" (*kulatraya*) refers to the three families of Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha. That which possesses these three families consisting of great mantras is "the one with the three great mantra families. This is because the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind is equal to space.
And so it is said in the Śrī-samāja-tantra: "Then those great bodhisattvas, having applied the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas to the form of space, uttered this inspired utterance."

The Great Bindu, which gives birth to the meaning of all mantras, is without syllables; it is the five-syllabled Great Void, the void of the bindu, and the six-syllabled one. (MNS 10.2 = 144) Regarding that, "the generator of the meaning of all mantras" means that the Blessed One himself is the generator—that is, the producer—of the meaning of all mundane and supramundane mantras. "The Great Bindu": the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, along with the consonants, are called the "Great Bindu. And that is the Blessed One himself. "Without syllables" (*anakṣara*): [This refers to the fact that] although he is designated by the conventional term "mantra," he is in reality free from the nature of syllables. He is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the unchanging (*nirvikāra*), and the indestructible (*avināśin*). Thus, he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the source of all syllables, he is also "without syllables. Moreover, because he transcends the nature of syllables, he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the non-dual syllable (*advayākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Mantra (*mahāyānamantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra (*vajrayānamahāyānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra (*vajrayānamahāmantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables.
