Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantrākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Also, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle (*vajrayānamahāmantrayānamantrayānamantrayānamantramantrayānamantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantramantrayānākṣara*), he is "without syllables. Furthermore, because he is the syllable of the Great Vehicle of the Vajra Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the Mantra Vehicle of the

Because its nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding "five-syllabled" (*pañcākṣara*): because it consists of the syllables *āḥ hūṃ oṃ hrīḥ aḥ*, which represent the eternal and so forth, it is called "five-syllabled. Regarding "great void" (*mahāśūnya*): because its intrinsic nature is the sixteenfold emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Regarding "void of the drop" (*binduśūnya*): the "drop" (*bindu*) is the seed-syllable; because even that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, has the nature of non-apprehension. Regarding "six-syllabled" (*ṣaḍakṣara*): [about six syllables damaged] ... *īśvara mur*; because it consists of six syllables.

"Possessing all forms and yet formless, holding the sixteen, the half, and the quarter-bindu; partless, beyond calculation, he holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna. (MNS 10.3 = 145) Regarding that, "possessing all forms and yet formless": "all forms" refers to the qualities such as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*); by means of these, he has emerged from all forms... [approx. 15 syllables damaged].

And so it is said in the *Āryatriśatikā*: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be perceived by means of the perfection of marks? Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Tathāgata is to be perceived by means of the perfection of the absence of marks. And why is that? Because that which was described by the Tathāgata as the 'perfection of marks' is itself the 'perfection of the absence of marks.'"

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, to the extent that there is perfection of characteristics, to that extent it is false; to the extent that there is perfection of the absence of characteristics, to that extent it is false. For it should be viewed from the perspective of both characteristics and the absence of characteristics, because that conventional reality has the nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha). He who holds the sixteen half-and-half drops, who is partless and beyond calculation, and who holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna. Here, the meaning of the verse (or the quarter-verse with its supplement) has not been explained [by me], because of the teacher’s word regarding this.

For it was thus stated by our own teachers: "Because [this teaching] brings about the realization of all phenomena for those who practice through the gateway of mantra, one must reveal this subsequent oral tradition (*uttarāmnāya*) concerning the awakening to the *Māyājāla*—transmitted through the lineage of ears—to one's own long-served disciples who are endowed with faith and possess a particular spiritual disposition. Therefore, out of fear that they might not understand it, I have not elaborated upon it in this commentary.

"Master of all the arts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), knower of the lineage and clan of *samādhi*, the body of *samādhi*, supreme among bodies, king of all *saṃbhoga-kāyas*. (MNS 10.4 = 146) In this context, "master of all the arts of meditative concentration" refers to the four meditative concentrations known as having applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*). Among these, the first *dhyāna* is characterized by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and accompanied by joy and bliss; the second is devoid of applied and sustained thought.

The third is devoid of joy and associated with equanimity and mindfulness; the fourth is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, characterized by equanimity and purity of mindfulness. This constitutes a fraction (*kalā*) of these four dhyānas—a portion (*aṃśa*). One who is skilled therein is an expert. That dhyāna is for the purpose of attracting those beings who are inclined toward it, through the application of its cultivation.

And so it has been said: Bodhisattvas bring the first and subsequent meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) to manifestation, yet they do not take rebirth under their influence because of their lack of concern for the welfare of sentient beings. Thus it will be stated later: "He will not be reborn among the long-lived gods," because they have attained mastery over rebirth.

"Holder of the family-lineage of meditative concentration (*samādhi-kulagotra-dhṛk*). Regarding "meditative concentrations": because they are characterized by supreme purity and one-pointedness, they consist of the first dhyāna and so forth; according to their actual nature, they follow the meaning of their names and possess infinite subdivisions. Therefore, their family-lineage is the "family-lineage of meditative concentration," which is fixed as that of the Śrāvakas and others. One who maintains that is a "holder of the family-lineage of meditative concentration. Regarding "the body of meditative concentration, the foremost of bodies (*samādhikāyakāyāgrya*)": the "body of meditative concentration" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Therefore, he is the foremost and most excellent among all emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth; he is the "Foremost Body of the Samādhi-Body," which is the Blessed One himself. He is the "King of All Enjoyment Bodies" (*sarvasambhogakāyarāṭ*). Having become the body of universal enjoyment, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī manifests within the midst of the entire assembly his own great majesty—the fruit of well-performed deeds—which is manifold, inconceivable, supramundane, and for the sake of bringing joy to all bodhisattvas. And because he shines and blazes through that very gateway of teaching, he is the "King of All Enjoyment Bodies."

And so it has been said: "I bow to that incomparable Saṃbhogakāya, which proclaims within the midst of the assembly its own transcendent, inconceivable, and manifold majesty—the fruit of hundreds of well-performed deeds—for the sake of delighting the wise; which is born from all the Buddhas of the world, whose noble sound of the True Dharma resounds without ceasing, and which is established in the sovereignty of the Dharma."

"The foremost of the nirmāṇakāyas, upholder of the lineage of the Buddha’s emanations, manifesting as various emanations throughout the ten directions, acting for the benefit of the world according to what is appropriate. (MNS 10.5 = 147) In this regard, concerning the phrase "the foremost of the nirmāṇakāyas": a body whose nature is emanation is a *nirmāṇakāya*. And because it is distinct from others [due to its supreme qualities], it is called "foremost" (*agrya*).

And thus it has been said: "For the sake of maturing sentient beings, he appears in some places like fire, blazing toward perfect enlightenment; and in other places, he is seen again as utterly tranquil. I pay homage to that Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Sages, which proceeds in manifold forms, removes the fear of the three realms through various means and diverse manifestations, pervades the ten directions, and accomplishes the great purpose."

"Bearing the lineage of the Buddha’s emanations" means: the emanations of the Buddhas residing in the three times constitute the "lineage of the Buddha’s emanations"; he who maintains that lineage is "one who bears the lineage of the Buddha’s emanations," because he ensures that the lineage of all the Tathāgatas is never interrupted. "One whose emanations in the ten directions are manifold" means: he whose emanations in the ten directions are manifold, that is, of various kinds, is "one whose emanations in the ten directions are manifold. "One who acts for the benefit of the world as it truly is" means:

For this very reason, by means of teaching the Dharma exactly as it is—that is, without error—he acts for the benefit of the world; thus, he is "the one who acts for the benefit of the world exactly as it is."

"The god beyond gods, lord of the gods, lord of the asuras, sovereign of the dānavas; lord of the immortals, preceptor of the gods, the Pramatha, and lord of the Pramathas. (MNS 10.6 = 148) In this context: "God beyond gods" is because he has the nature of Brahmā. "Lord of the gods" is because he has the essential nature of Viṣṇu. "Lord of the asuras" is because he takes the form of Bali, the son of Virocana. "Sovereign of the dānavas" is because he has the essential nature of Rāhu. "Lord of the immortals" is because he takes the form of Purandara. "Preceptor of the gods" is because he has the essential nature of Bṛhaspati.

"Pramatha" [is used] because of his nature as the leader of the Gaṇas. "Pramatheśvara" [is used] because of his nature as Tryambaka. By means of [epithets] such as "Devātideva," that very Blessed One is designated.

"The sole Teacher, the Guru of the World, who has crossed over the wilderness of existence (*bhava*), is renowned throughout the worlds of the ten directions as the Great Lord of the Gift of Dharma. (MNS 10.7 = 149) Regarding the phrase "who has crossed over the wilderness of existence": *bhava* is *saṃsāra*. Because it is difficult to cross, it is itself a wilderness; thus, it is the "wilderness of existence" (*bhavakāntāra*). He by whom this wilderness of existence has been crossed is "one who has crossed over the wilderness of existence" (*uttīrṇabhavakāntāra*). "He is alone" means he is without a second, because there exists no one equal to him.

Therefore, regarding the term "Teacher" (śāstṛ): because he performs the task for all sentient beings and demonstrates it, [it is said] "the Teacher of all sentient beings. Without distinction, the Blessed One—[Mañjuśrī]—performs the task for all sentient beings by virtue of being their Teacher. For it is thus:

He causes those born in the states of woe to generate faith through his radiance and by manifesting the form of the Tathāgata, thereby establishing them in a happy rebirth. Furthermore, even among those born in happy rebirths who are of an unserviceable nature (*abhavyajātīya*), he establishes them in the path of the happiness of *saṃsāra*—such as generosity and so forth—by means of the previously described method when they approach him with their respective dispositions.

He effects the planting of roots of merit for those of a fortunate nature who have approached him with the two kinds of intention but have not yet planted such roots; he effects the ripening of the roots of merit for those who have already planted them; and he effects the liberation of those whose roots of merit are fully ripened, establishing them in the state of a *śrāvaka* or other [vehicles] according to their lineage (*gotra*). Because he thus carries out his duties for those born in miserable or happy states—whether they are of a fortunate or unfortunate nature—he alone is called the Teacher of all sentient beings.

"Jagadguru" (the Teacher of the World): for this very reason, he is the teacher of the worlds (*jagatām guruḥ*), thus "Jagadguru. "Renowned Lord of the Gift of Dharma throughout the Worlds of the Ten Directions": the worlds of the ten directions are the "worlds of the ten directions" (*daśadiglokāḥ*); those who are renowned in those worlds of the ten directions are the "renowned ones of the worlds of the ten directions" (*prakhyātadaśadiglokāḥ*). He who is the Lord of the Gift of Dharma among those renowned ones of the worlds of the ten directions is the "Renowned Lord of the Gift of Dharma throughout the Worlds of the Ten Directions" (*prakhyātadaśadiglokadharmadānapatiḥ*). For this very reason, he is "Great" (*mahān*): because he is pervasive (*vyāpī*), as he consists of all things, both moving and stationary.

And so it is said in the *Śrīsaṃvaratantra*: "In every place, from every source, everything, in every way, at all times, he himself (*svayam*) becomes this [all], consisting of all phenomena—both stable and moving—beginning with all the Buddhas."

"Clad in the armor of loving-kindness, armored with the mail of compassion, bearing the sword, bow, and arrows of wisdom, he abandons the battle against afflictions and ignorance. (MNS 10.8 = 150) In that regard, "clad in the armor of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) means: loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is friendliness (*maitratā*), affection (*snehatā*), and the love one feels for an only son directed toward all sentient beings. The "armor of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-saṃnāha*) is the donning of armor by means of that loving-kindness. One who has donned the armor of loving-kindness is "clad in the armor of loving-kindness. "Armored with the mail of compassion" (*karuṇā-varma-varmita*) means: compassion (*karuṇā*) is the state of wishing to remove the suffering of others. It is called "mail" (*varma*) because it protects against the cold wind of aversion (*pratigha*). Being protected by that mail is "armored with the mail of compassion. One who is thus armored is "armored with the mail of compassion."

Compassion (*karuṇā*) has the characteristics as previously described; that itself is the armor, hence "compassion-armor" (*karuṇā-varma*). One who is protected by that is "armored with compassion-armor" (*karuṇā-varma-varmitaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the sword of wisdom, the bow, and the arrows": "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; "sword" refers to the sword of wisdom (*prajñā-khaḍga*); "bow" refers to the vajra-bow; and "arrows" refers to those whose nature is the penetration of the subtle mind.

And what is meant by this? He is one who is girt with the armor of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), clad in the mail of compassion (*karuṇā*), protected, and accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other perfections. He abandons—that is, he casts off—the battle, that is, the encounter with afflictions (*kleśa*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*), such as passion (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*); such is the Blessed One. [The question: "Is the abandonment of the battle of afflictions and ignorance his very nature? [The answer: He is to be visualized as having the color of vermilion, four arms, and being established in the tradition of the *astamya* [or *astamyā*].

"The enemy of Māra, the conqueror of Māra, the hero who brings an end to the fear of the four Māras, the victor over the entire army of Māra, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Leader of the World. (MNS 10.9 = 151) In this context, "enemy of Māra" (*mārāri*) means the enemy (*ari*) of the Māras, that is, the obstacles (*vighna*); he is thus the "conqueror of Māra" (*mārajit*). He is called the "conqueror of Māra" because, seated upon the Vajra-throne, he conquers the Māras who are his adversaries. For this very reason, he is a "hero" (*vīra*), since he cannot be overcome by others who have become his adversaries. "He who brings an end to the fear of the four Māras": [this refers to...]

The four Māras are the "four Māras"; fear of them is "fear of the four Māras. He who brings about the end—the destruction—of that is the "one who has brought an end to the fear of the four Māras" (*caturmārabhayāntakṛt*). Regarding the phrase "conqueror of all the hosts of Māra": the host of all Māras is the "host of all Māras," which is their army. He whose nature it is to conquer that is the "conqueror of all the hosts of Māra" (*sarvamāracamūjetā*). With the word "Perfectly Awakened One" (*sambuddha*), he provides a summary of the names.

For instance, beginning from "the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One" and so forth, up until this point, the *Nāmasaṅgīti* has been recited for the most part. Regarding "the Leader of the World": he is the Leader of the World (*lokanāyaka*) because he uplifts the entire world.

"He is to be saluted, worshipped, greeted, and honored perpetually; he is most worthy of adoration, venerable, and to be prostrated to—the supreme Guru. (MNS 10.10 = 152) In this context, "to be saluted" (*vandya*) means that he is worthy of being saluted by the worlds including the gods. "To be worshipped" (*pūjya*) means that he has reached the ultimate limit of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; and that Blessed One Mañjuśrī is called "worshipful" because he has gone to the further shore of all philosophical systems (*siddhānta*). "To be greeted" (*abhivādya*) means that he is worthy of praise.

"And always to be honored" means that he is to be honored at all times by the *śrāvakas* and others. "Most worthy of worship" means because his qualities are perfectly complete. "Mañjuśrī alone is to be revered by all bodhisattvas" means because he is the most highly revered among all the Tathāgatas. "To be saluted" means because he is to be saluted by those who practice the conduct of the mantra-vehicle (*mantramukha-caryā*). For this very reason, he is "supreme" because of his excellence. "The Guru" means because he instructs all sentient beings.
And because he has manifested the heart of the wisdom of all the Tathāgatas, he alone is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).

"Whose stride traverses the three worlds alone, whose prowess is boundless as space, who possesses the three knowledges, who is a learned master of the Vedas, who is purified, who possesses the six superknowledges, and who possesses the six recollections. (MNS 10.11 = 153) Regarding that, "whose stride traverses the three worlds alone": the collection of the three worlds is the *triloka*; *triloka* itself is *trailokya*. He whose stride—that is, the range of a single step—extends across that *trailokya*, he is "one whose stride traverses the three worlds alone. By this, the greatness of the Blessed One’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is fully demonstrated.

"Whose prowess is boundless as space": "Space" (*vyoma*) means the sky (*ākāśa*); "boundless as space" means that which has no limit. He whose prowess (*vikrama*), that is, his valor, extends to that [boundlessness] is "one whose prowess is boundless as space. By this term, the Blessed One’s progression for the sake of sentient beings is indicated. Regarding "the one possessed of the three knowledges" (*traividya*): he states the view of those who know the Vedas. The three knowledges are characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas]. [The other three knowledges are] the triple science (*trayī*), logic (*anvikṣikī*), and economics (*vārtā*).

Or, one who studies or knows that [Veda] is "one possessed of the three knowledges" (*traividya*); he is of that very nature, and is thus the Blessed One himself. Alternatively, he is one who studies or knows the three branches of knowledge (*vidyā-traya*) whose nature is comprised within the three baskets (*piṭaka-traya*) included in the three vehicles (*yāna-traya*). Or again, he is "one possessed of the three knowledges" because he knows that which has as its nature the supernormal powers of psychic transformation, knowledge of the minds of others, and the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*). Regarding the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*): according to the view of those who know the Vedas, one who studies the *chandas* (the Vedic hymns) is called a *śrotriya*.

And the Blessed One Mañjuśrī is called a *śrotriya* because of his study of the immeasurable Mahāyāna scriptures; he is called "pure" (*pūta*) because he purifies by means of this, since he is the cause of purification.

And so it is said in the Mahābhāṣya: "Water is the first purifier on earth, and the supreme purifier of water is the mantras; and of those Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus mantras, the great seers have declared the grammars to be the purifiers. Because of his purity, that Blessed One is called "the Purified" (pūta). Regarding the phrase "possessing the six superknowledges" (ṣaḍabhijña): they are the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former abodes, supernormal power, and the superknowledge of the destruction of all outflows (āsrava).

He who possesses these six superknowledges (*abhijñā*) is "one who has the six superknowledges" (*ṣaḍabhijña*). Regarding "the six recollections" (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*): namely, the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Vajra, the recollection of the Family, the recollection of the Wrathful One, and the recollection of the Samaya. Thus, he who possesses these six recollections is so designated.

"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has transcended the world, possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), is established in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and has attained the state of the reality of wisdom. Regarding this, "Bodhisattva" means one whose being (*sattva*)—that is, whose intention (*abhiprāya*)—is directed toward enlightenment, which is non-attachment to all phenomena and the fulfillment of one's own welfare; thus he is a Bodhisattva. [One might ask: "In that case, would not a Śrāvaka also be so? Therefore, he says: "Mahāsattva."

One who possesses the courage (*sattva*) for the great accomplishment of the welfare of others is a *mahāsattva*. Since such greatness might otherwise belong even to non-Buddhist practitioners or virtuous people, the term "bodhisattva" is employed. For this very reason, it is that Blessed One alone who is characterized by these two terms.

And thus, he is "transcending the world" because he moves against the current of the great river of saṃsāra. He is "possessed of great supernatural power" because his equipment of merit and wisdom is fully perfected. He is "one who has reached the culmination of the perfection of wisdom": the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the perfection belonging to wisdom characterized by the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); he who has gone to its culmination, its final limit, is one who has reached the culmination of the perfection of wisdom. "The reality of wisdom" (*prajñātattva*): the reality of wisdom is the reality of wisdom; it is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).
He is indeed the Blessed One. "Having attained reality" means that he who has reached or arrived at that very non-dual gnosis is so described.

"Knowing himself and knowing others, he is all, for he is the most excellent person; having transcended all comparisons, he is to be known as the supreme Lord of Wisdom. (MNS 10.13 = 155) In this context, "knowing himself" (*ātmavit*) means he knows the self (*ātmānaṃ vetti*). "Knowing others" (*paravit*) means he knows what is other (*paraṃ vetti*). "All" (*sarva*) refers to his manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena without exception. "The most excellent" (*sarvīya*) means he is beneficial to all (*sarveṣāṃ hitaḥ*).

Because he is the sole son of the entire world and desires its welfare—for this reason, the Blessed One is the foremost person (*agrapudgala*). "Transcending all comparisons" means that comparison is the mental faculty regarding all things; he who has transcended—that is, surpassed—that faculty of comparison is "one who has transcended all comparisons. "The object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) is because he possesses the nature of the apprehended (*grāhya*). "Lord of knowledge" (*jñānādhipa*) is because he possesses the nature of the apprehender (*grāhaka*). "Supreme" (*para*) is because of his excellence.

"The Lord of the Gift of Dharma is supreme, the teacher of the meaning of the four mudrās; he is most worthy of being venerated by the worlds of those who proceed toward the three vehicles of liberation. (MNS 10.14 = 156) In this context, "Lord of the Gift of Dharma" means that he bestows the Dharma without error according to the spiritual capacity [of beings]. For this very reason, among all those worthy of being approached, that Blessed One alone is supreme. "Teacher of the meaning of the four mudrās" means...

The "meaning of the four mudrās" refers to the meaning of the four mudrās, beginning with the *mahāmudrā*. He is the teacher and elucidator of that, because his intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of the Tathāgata. Regarding the term "most worthy of being attended upon": those whose nature it is to go by means of the three vehicles—that is, the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and so forth—are called "those who travel by the three vehicles. Therefore, for all those beings who travel by the three vehicles, this Blessed One is the most worthy of being attended upon, because his intrinsic nature is the liberation of all.

"Mañjuśrī, the glorious one, is the supreme among the glorious; he is the great one, fortunate throughout the three worlds, who brings about all prosperity, and whose glory is purified in the ultimate sense. (MNS 10.15 = 157) In this context, he is "one whose glory is purified in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthaviśuddhaśrī*) because his glory is purified by the *dharmadhātu* in the ultimate sense, owing to his nature as both wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*). For this very reason, he is "fortunate throughout the three worlds" (*trailokyasubhaga*); he alone is fortunate within the three worlds because he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings. Thus it is said in the *Śrīsamvaratantra*:

The Blessed One, the Vajrī, is fortunate because he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings; all the Śrāvakas are unfortunate, as they have attained ultimate parinirvāṇa. "Great" means because he is all-pervading. "The maker of all prosperity" means because he is the foundation of all excellence. "Glorious" means because he is endowed with good fortune. "Mañjuśrī" is his designated name. "The best among the glorious" means the most excellent among those who possess such glory.

Now, this very Blessed One Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Being of all Tathāgatas, by means of the nature of the knowledge for accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), fulfills all the hopes of the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, because he performs all manifold deeds having attained mastery over all the mudrās of all Tathāgatas. Having gone to the infinite and boundless world-systems in all ten directions, he divides each of the ninety-five names, mantras, syllables, and phrases—according to the classification of the five families—into nineteen parts each, making five groups, and by means of those...

Having removed the laziness of all sentient beings and established them in the factors of virtue, and having illuminated the assembly of all Tathāgatas with the light of his own gate of liberation, he returns; then, having formed those previously mentioned characteristics into the syllables and words of the name-mantras, he is stationed in due order in the fifth wheel outside the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu. Furthermore, the son of noble family or daughter of noble family who practices the conduct of the mantra-gate, taking himself as the object of focus in the three aforementioned forms, [proceeds].
The traditional teaching is that by reciting the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti*, one attains the aforementioned qualities.

In the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti-ṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the tenth chapter, the "Praise of the Knowledge of the Performance of Duties," is concluded. There are fifteen verses and ninety-five mantra-words, as indicated by the numerical figure.

Now, the five Tathāgatas, Mahāvairocana and the others, praised the Blessed One, the embodiment of gnosis residing within the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, with verses consisting of the five gnoses. They are as follows: "Homage to you, the bestower of boons," and so forth, by way of the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*). "O Buddha-love," and so forth, by way of the nature of the gnosis of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātujñāna*). "O Buddha-smile," and so forth, by way of the gnosis of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "Arising from the non-arisen," and so forth, by way of the essence of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*).
"By means of the *māyājāla*," and so forth; [this is] by way of the intrinsic nature of the gnosis of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Thus.
In the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti-ṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, the eleventh chapter, the Section on the Praise of the Conclusion, is completed. [There are] five verses.

Now, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having addressed Vajradhara because he had been requested by him, and having thus addressed him, spoke concerning the *Nāmasaṅgīti* together with its benefits, for the sake of inspiring those possessed of faith: "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara! This is that very *Nāmasaṅgīti*. [He addresses him] as "Vajrapāṇi" by way of the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), and as "Vajradhara" by way of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

The *Nāmasaṃgīti* belongs to Mañjuśrī-jñānasattva, who is the embodiment of wisdom (*jñānamūrti*) and the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Tathāgatas, because he was authorized as the compiler by virtue of possessing both qualities.

What is its specific characteristic? It is "unmixedly pure" (*āveṇika-pariśuddhā*). In this context, *veṇi* means "intermingling" with the afflictions (*kleśa*); that which is not *veṇi* is *aveṇi*. That which exists there, having a pure intrinsic nature, is *āveṇika*; by that, the *Nāmasaṅgīti* is "completely pure. This is the connection with what will be said later: "that [Nāmasaṅgīti] has been taught by me. For what purpose? He says: "for the sake of generating unsurpassed joy, serene faith, and great exhilaration."

In this context, supreme joy is gladness and clarity, which is faith; and that is conviction regarding the fruits of action, the truths, and the jewels. Great exultation is vigor, and that is the enthusiasm for what is wholesome.

O Vajrapāṇi, for the sake of generating and producing these [beings], for the sake of purifying the secrets of body, speech, and mind, the secret of body, speech, and mind has the nature of the *bodhicitta-vajra*. For the sake of its purification—for the sake of fulfilling and purifying the accumulations of merit and wisdom belonging to the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*) that are incomplete and unpurified—the stages are incomplete and the perfections are unpurified; thus, they are called "incomplete and unpurified stages and perfections."

It is for the sake of the fulfillment and purification of their equipment of merit and knowledge; for the attainment of the unsurpassed goal not yet attained. That which is both "not yet attained" and the "unsurpassed goal" is the "unattained unsurpassed goal"; it is for the sake of the attainment of that.

It is for the sake of attaining the Buddha-qualities and so forth not yet attained, up to the sake of maintaining the guidance of the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas. The word "up to" (yāvat) refers to the sequence [of goals]. The "guidance of the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas" is the *prajñāpāramitā*. And it is for the sake of correctly upholding that by way of its nature as non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). "Taught by me" means by way of the intrinsic nature of the vajra of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*). "Clearly revealed" means by way of the gateway of the knowledge of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). "Expounded" means...

"By way of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). "Discriminated" means by way of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). "Made manifest" means by way of the nature of the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "Empowered" means by way of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). "This is indeed the *Saṅgīti*, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, within the mind that is the continuum of existence, through the empowerment of the reality-nature (*dharmatā*) of all mantras. The reality-nature of all mantras is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); its empowerment is its stabilization—by means of that empowerment.
This is the praise of the first wheel; there are eleven words even by calculation. || 11 || o ||

Then, concerning the praise of the second wheel, he says: "Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, this *Vajradhara-nāmasaṅgīti* is the secret of the body, speech, and mind of the perfectly pure and completely cleansed omniscient gnosis-body (*sarvajñajñānakāya*). Here, "perfectly pure" means thoroughly purified, and "completely cleansed" (*paryavadāta*) means cleansed on all sides; thus, it is both perfectly pure and completely cleansed, and that is the omniscient gnosis.

The omniscient gnosis (sarvajñajñāna) is perfectly pure and completely cleansed; his body, speech, and mind are secret because they are of a nature that cannot be revealed. "The awakening of all Tathāgatas" means the awakening of the Buddhas; it is "Buddha-awakening," meaning it is not the awakening of the Śrāvakas.

"The realization (*abhisamaya*) of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksambuddha*). Realization is knowledge; it is the knowledge of the omniscient one. It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) for all Tathāgatas because there is nothing superior (*uttara*) to it; hence it is "unsurpassed. "The movement into the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) of the Sugatas," because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "The defeat of the power of all Māras by the Jinas," because they are not defeated by the powers of the four Māras. "The possession of the power of the ten powers (*daśabala*) by all those who possess the ten powers," refers to the ten powers whose characteristics have already been described.

That *Nāmasaṅgīti* in which these [qualities] exist is "possessing the power of the ten strengths" (*daśabalabalini*). Its state is "the possession of the power of the ten strengths" (*daśabalabalitā*). Regarding "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) as "the knowledge of the omniscient": one who knows everything is "omniscient" (*sarvajña*); its state is "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*).

"Scripture (*āgama*) is [the source] of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). It is called scripture because it comes from another (*parasmād āgacchati*). And it is of two kinds: characterized by scripture (*āgamalakṣaṇa*) and characterized by realization (*adhigamalakṣaṇa*). "The full attainment (*samudāgama*) is [the source] of all Buddhas. This is because Śrāvakas and others realize [the state of] all Buddhas through their respective forms as Śrāvakas and so forth. "The fulfillment of the accumulations of stainless and perfectly pure merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*) is [the source] of all great Bodhisattvas. It is both stainless (*vimala*) and perfectly pure (*supariśuddha*), thus "stainless and perfectly pure."
And that is the equipment of merit and wisdom; it is the stainless and perfectly pure equipment of merit and wisdom. Its fulfillment is found in this *Nāmasaṅgīti*; therefore, it is so described.

It is the source (*prasūti*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; "source" because it is their place of origin. It is the field (*kṣetra*) for the prosperity of all gods and humans; "field" because it is the mine of all excellences. It is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Mahāyāna; because it is the mode of abiding of the Mahāyāna whose characteristics have been described. It is the birthplace (*sambhava*) of the bodhisattva’s conduct; "birthplace" because it is the locus of its arising. It is the culmination (*niṣṭhā*) of the perfect noble path; "culmination" means the final end.

"It is the touchstone of the liberations. *Nikaṣa* means a place of examination, just as there is a touchstone for gold. "It is the origin of the path to deliverance" because it serves as the cause for the means to *nirvāṇa*. "The non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas": "non-interruption" here means absolute non-interruption, because it performs the work of a Tathāgata. "The increase of the family and clan of the great Bodhisattvas": for this very reason, there is an excellent growth. "The subduing of all opposing disputants": *nigraha* is that by which one is subdued.
And so it is said in the Śrīsaṃvara: "In some cases, there is the suppression of those of other sects in accordance with the Dharma."

"The destruction of all non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*). Regarding "destruction": it is the refutation by means of demonstrating one's own greatness, as in the case of the Descent from the Gods (*devāvatāra*). "The defeat of the army and host of the four Māras. Regarding "army" (*bala*): it refers to the fourfold army (*caturaṅgabala*). "Host" (*camū*) refers to the arrangement of battle formations. "Host" (*senā*) refers to the multitude. Therefore, the meaning is this: the *Nāmasaṃgīti* is that which constitutes the defeat—the refutation—of the army, host, and multitude of the four Māras.

"Comprehending all sentient beings" means "comprehension," which is characterized by generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency of purpose. It is called "comprehension" because they are gathered together by it. "The ripening of the noble path for all those who proceed toward liberation" means the ripening of the noble path; that is, the state of full maturity of the noble eightfold path.

"Concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to those who dwell in the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Concentration is the one-pointedness of mind upon an object that has been examined; and that [one-pointedness] pertains to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. "Meditation (*dhyāna*) belongs to those whose minds are one-pointed. Meditation is what is termed initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*). "Yoga belongs to those who are devoted to body, speech, and mind. Yoga is the attainment (*samāpatti*) consisting of mere knowledge (*jñānamātra*). "Dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) from all fetters (*saṃyojana*). Dissociation means being free from the nine fetters.

There are nine fetters (*saṃyojana*): the fetter of attachment (*anunaya*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarṣa*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*). "Abandonment" refers to the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). "Abandonment" means relinquishment; [it is the relinquishing] of passion and so forth, as well as anger and so forth.

"Quiescence of all obscurations" means the absolute non-existence of the obscurations consisting of the knowable, afflictions, karma, and their maturation. "Liberation from all bonds" means that it is the cause for liberation from the bonds of attachment, aversion, and delusion. "Release from all acquisitions" means that its intrinsic nature is the liberations characterized by both those with remainder and those without remainder. "Peace of all mental disturbances" means that peace is the act of calming, because it dwells in a state of tranquility. "The source of all prosperities" means...
Because it is the source of all mundane and supramundane prosperities; and "the abandonment of all misfortunes" because it consists in the abandonment of all defects.

"The closing of all doors to the lower realms" means that it serves as a lid for the doors to the lower realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. "The true path to the city of liberation": it is a true path because it is both real (*sat*) and a path (*panthā*). "The non-functioning of the wheel of saṃsāra": functioning is *pravṛtti*; the absence of functioning is non-functioning (*apravṛtti*). "The turning of the wheel of Dharma": because the wheel of Dharma is turned according to one's spiritual capacity (*yathābhavyatayā*).

"Having raised up the parasols, banners, and flags of the Tathāgata’s teaching": surpassing the merit of the external Śrāvakas and others, the *Nāmasaṅgīti* is like a raised parasol, banner, and flag. "The empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the teaching of all dharmas": "empowerment" means stabilization. "Swift accomplishment for the Bodhisattvas who practice the path of mantra-observance": "swift accomplishment" means rapid attainment independent of preliminary ritual service (*puraścaraṇa*).

"The realization through cultivation belongs to those devoted to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, "realization" (*adhigama*) refers to the direct manifestation (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) resulting from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) of cultivation. "It is to be penetrated as emptiness by those devoted to the cultivation of the penetration of non-duality. "Penetration" (*prativedha*) means comprehension (*avagama*). The penetration of emptiness is "penetration of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-prativedha*). "It is the fulfillment of the equipment for all the perfections (*pāramitā*). Regarding "fulfillment" (*niṣpatti*), it means accomplishment (*sampādana*).

Pariśuddhi (complete purity) means purity that is thorough and all-encompassing for the sake of fulfilling all the stages (*bhūmi*). *Prativedha* (penetration) refers to the correct penetration of the four noble truths; the term *prativedha* is as explained previously. *Sarvadharmaikacittaprativedha* (penetration of all phenomena with a single mind) refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). "All phenomena" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); "single mind" means having a single object of focus (*ekālambanatā*) regarding them. "Penetration of that" has its meaning already established. The word "up to" (*yāvat*) indicates completion. "The completion of all the qualities of a Buddha is this *Nāmasaṅgīti*"—thus it is concluded.
These are the fifty-two verses of praise for the second great Vairocana-cakra, even by way of their numerical count. || 52 ||

Now, concerning the praise of the third wheel, he says: "Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara! This *Saṅgīti* is the pacifier of the sins of all sentient beings' entire conduct of body, speech, and mind. It is the pacifier of whatever sin exists within the entirety of the movements of body, speech, and mind—that is, within all bodily, vocal, and mental actions. It is the purifier of all miserable states; it is the purifier of all miserable states.

It wards off all three miserable destinies; thus, it is the "warder-off of all miserable destinies. Because it utterly cuts off hells and the like, it is the "utter destroyer of all karmic obstructions," the "destroyer of all karmic obstructions. [107]

It is that which prevents the arising of all the eight inopportune conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*). Regarding "all inopportune conditions": a *kṣaṇa* is an opportunity; "occasion" (*avasara*) is a synonym. They are called "inopportune" (*akṣaṇa*) because there is no opportunity for clear realization (*abhisamaya*). And these are eight, namely: rebirth in hell; rebirth as an animal; rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*); rebirth among the border tribes or barbarians; rebirth in the formless realm or among those without perception; and being blind, deaf, mute, or the like.
False view and birth in a world-system devoid of a Buddha; [namely,] being one who holds false views and being born into a family where no Buddha has appeared.

It brings about the pacification of the eight great fears; it is the pacifier of the eight great fears. It is the destroyer of all bad dreams; it is the maker of their destruction. It is the destroyer of all bad dreams (it is the destroyer of all bad dreams). It brings about the removal of all ill omens; it is the remover of all ill omens. It brings about the pacification of all evil portents and obstacles; it is the pacifier of all evil portents and obstacles. It is that which distances all the activities of the enemy Māra.

It is that which brings about the accumulation of all roots of merit and virtue; it is that which brings about the gathering of all roots of merit and virtue. It is that which prevents the arising of all improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) that is antagonistic to meditative concentration; it is that which prevents the arising of all improper mental attention. It is that which eradicates all intoxication, pride, arrogance, and egoism.

In this context, "intoxication" (*mada*) is the elation of a mind attached to its own prosperity, which is a state of mental obsession. "Pride" (*māna*) is loftiness. "Arrogance" (*darpa*) is the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*). "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*) is the thought "I am. She is described as such because she brings about the destruction of these.

It is that which prevents the arising of all physical and mental suffering and dejection; it is that which prevents the arising of all physical, vocal, and mental suffering and dejection. It is the heart of all Tathāgatas because it is born from them; it is the secret of all Bodhisattvas because it is to be guarded; it is the mystery of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas because it is not to be disclosed. All mudrās are the four mudrās; all mantras are the heart-mantras and near-heart-mantras.

The mantras are those beginning with the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra), because she has that as her essence. She is the embodiment of all mudrās and mantras. She generates mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) for those who proclaim that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are ineffable. "All phenomena" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth. Their "ineffability" is their inexpressibility. Those whose nature it is to speak of that are described in such a way. Therefore, [she is]... [due to] non-forgetfulness through verbal expression.

Therefore, their mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the state of the mind’s non-forgetfulness and verbal expression regarding a familiar object; their clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) is the state of remaining well-restrained and alert in body and speech; and it is the producer of those two. Wisdom (*prajñā*) and intelligence (*medhā*) constitute wisdom-and-intelligence (*prajñāmedhā*); since its nature is to produce unsurpassed wisdom and intelligence, it is called "that which produces unsurpassed wisdom and intelligence" (*anuttaraprajñāmedhākarī*).

Health is freedom from disease. Strength is physical capacity. Sovereignty is the abundance of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as wealth and grain. [She who] has such a nature—that is, she whose nature is to perform all this, bringing about the excellence of health, strength, and sovereignty—is thus described. "Śrī" means Lakṣmī. "Auspiciousness" (śubha) means welfare. "Peace" (śānti) means a rite for well-being. "Benevolence" (kalyāṇa) means auspiciousness. For this very reason, she is the one who causes their increase. "Fame" is [attained] through the giving of material gifts.

"Renown" (*kīrti*) is through the gift of Dharma; "fame" (*śloka*) is through the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*); "praise" (*stuti*) is through the gift of consecration (*abhiṣekadāna*). [It is] the illuminator of these gifts; that is to say, the thorough illuminator of these four kinds of gifts.

"All diseases" refers to all illnesses. "Great terrors" refers to the great terrors that are all diseases; she is the one who brings about their pacification, thus "the pacifier of all diseases and great terrors. The terms "pūtatarā" (more purified) and "pavitratarā" (more pure) employ the comparative suffix *tara* to indicate that she is more purified than those already purified and more pure than those already pure. "Dhanyatamā" (most blessed) means she is the most blessed among those who are blessed. "Māṅgalyatamā" (most auspicious) means she is the most auspicious among all auspicious things. The meaning is established through the nature of the superlative suffix *tama*.

The meaning has been demonstrated by means of the superlative suffix (*tamap*). "Refuge" (*śaraṇa*) means the state of being one worthy of refuge; [he is] for those seeking refuge. "Abode" (*layana*) means a place of rest; [he is] for those seeking an abode. "Protection" (*trāṇa*) means preservation; [he is] for those seeking protection. "Ultimate resort" (*parāyaṇa*) means being intent upon that; [he is] for those who have no other resort. Regarding the phrase "become an island" (*dvīpabhūta*): an island (*dvīpa*) is that in which the waters are divided into two parts. Having become such [an island], he is for those seeking an island. For those who have no way of going, he has become the unsurpassed way of going, because his intrinsic nature is the unsurpassed way of going.

"She has become a vessel for those traveling across the ocean of existence," because she has become a vessel for the Dharma-vehicle. "She has become the great king of medicines" by virtue of her eradication of all diseases. "She has become wisdom" through the discernment of phenomena that are to be abandoned and those to be adopted; that is, the discernment of phenomena to be abandoned and adopted. By means of that [wisdom] acting as the cause, "she has become the light of knowledge" because she removes all darkness, gloom, and false views (i.e., because she removes all darkness, gloom, and false views). She is described in that way.

"Having become a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) for the sake of fulfilling the intentions of all sentient beings as they desire, because it fulfills the mental aspirations of all sentient beings. Having become the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) for the sake of attaining the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of Mañjuśrī, because of being endowed with that wisdom."

It is the realization of pure knowledge and vision for the sake of attaining the five eyes; through the possession of that eye, it is the fulfillment of the six perfections by way of bestowing the gift of material goods, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma—namely, by reaching the culmination of the perfection of generosity and the other perfections—and it is the attainment of the ten stages through the complete fulfillment of the accumulations of merit, wisdom, and meditative concentration.

Because of reaching the ultimate limit of merit and so forth; because of the absence of duality in the non-dual dharmatā (due to being free from the duality of dharmas, i.e., the absence of the grasped and the grasper); suchness-nature (because of being free from the superimposition of other dharmas); and thus, because of the absence of the extremes of superimposition and denial.

Because there is an absence of extreme views due to the non-superimposition [of conceptual constructs]. "Having the nature of the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭirūpa*) means having the nature of the Tathāgata’s body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*) which is purified as the limit of reality; because it has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

The nature of the great emptiness in all its aspects; because it destroys the thicket of all erroneous views without exception; [due to the fact that all phenomena are inexpressible in form... it is the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. That is to say, it is the emptiness of the non-dual reality (*advayadharmatā*). For the purpose of introducing [beings] to that, there is the retention of the names, which is its manifestation. By means of that [retention], acting as the cause... [the benefits of the third wheel consist of fifty-two words]. || 52 ||

[109–110 are missing; henceforth from 81, last line onwards: Regarding the benefits of the fourth wheel, he says: "Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara," and so forth. When there is a connection with a contemptible person, that which dissolves is the *kula* (family), such as the Kṣatriya caste and so on. He purifies—that is, makes holy. Because he protects [others] from *saṃsāra*, he is a *putra* (son); thus, a *kulaputra* (noble son). A *kulaputra*.

Whosoever—whether a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family—who practices the conduct of the mantra-entrance, shall daily—that is, every day—at the three times of the day, uphold this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the crest-jewel of names, which is the non-dual ultimate reality, the embodiment of gnosis, and the gnosis-body of the Blessed One Mañjuśrī-Jñānasattva, who is the essence of all Tathāgatas; [uphold it] in its entirety, complete, without deficiency, and without breakage, by means of these very verses, phrases, and syllables just mentioned, according to both the text and the meaning.

He will recite it by way of reading from a book; he will master it through reflection; and he will attend to it with wise cultivation (*yoniśo-bhāvanā*). Furthermore, he will proclaim it to other disciples at the appropriate time and occasion, according to the words and without error. And each one, having taken as an object the Mañjuśrī-jñānakāya under whichever name [is preferred], shall cultivate it with a one-pointed mind and a concentrated mind.

"Adhimukti is likewise"—this is the restriction. Because it is the reality (*tattva*) and the non-erroneous view, one dwells in the "dwelling of the universal gate" (*samantamukha-vihāra*) by means of those two mental attentions (*manaskāra*). [This is done] by means of that which has the penetration of all phenomena as its nature—that is, by means of purity, the supreme, the most excellent, the untroubled, the faultless, and the purity permeated by wisdom (*prajñānuviddhā*). And so it is said: "Because of faith, one resorts to the Dharma; because of wisdom, one knows it according to reality."
Of these two, faith is primary; yet for one whose wisdom is preceded by [faith], it is wisdom that is foremost.

For one who is thus endowed and practices the conduct of the mantra-entrance, throughout the three times—those very three times—all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are bound together, having girded their loins. Being united and assembled, they will manifest all the gateways of the dharmas—the gateways of liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and they will also manifest their own physical forms and essential natures.

And the great wrathful kings (*mahākrodharāja*), the tamers of the difficult-to-tame—the great Vajradhara kings (i.e., Mahāvajradhara and others)—who have become the protectors of the world through various emanated form-bodies, [bestow] "vitality and strength" (*ojobala*). "Strength of vitality" (*ojaso bala*) means capacity. "Splendor and invincibility" (*tejo 'pradhṛṣyatā*): "splendor" (*tejas*) refers to invincibility, that is, the state of being unconquerable. They will demonstrate all mantras, the maṇḍalas of the realization of mudrās, such as the Vajradhātu and others.

"Without exception" means entirely without remainder; these are the kings of mantra-knowledge (*mantravidyārāja*), the enemies of all obstacles, obstructors, and Māras, namely the *Pratyaṅgirās* and the great *Mahāparājitās*. "All of them, night and day, at every moment" means: that which exists together with the night is "night-and-day" (*sarātridiva*); "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*) means at each and every instant (*kṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇaṃ prati*). "Protection, defense, and concealment in all modes of conduct" (*sarveryāpatheṣu rakṣāvaraṇaguptam*): protection (*rakṣā*) and defenses (*āvaraṇa*) are "protection-and-defenses" (*rakṣāvaraṇa*); their concealment (*gupti*) is "protection-and-defense-concealment" (*rakṣāvaraṇagupti*).
They will perform that [rite], and through the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they will correctly empower his mental continuum with their entire body, speech, and mind.

And by the grace of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they will be graced; they will bestow upon them the eloquence that is confidence regarding all phenomena—that is, the eloquence of confidence regarding all phenomena—and also [the grace] of all Arhats, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. With love, affection, intention, and purpose toward the noble qualities—the Buddha-qualities—they will manifest their own person, that is, their true nature.

And those who are Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, Sanatkumāra, Maheśvara, Kārtikeya, Mahākāla, Nandikeśvara, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Hārītī, and the world-protectors of the ten directions—[they watch] constantly and perpetually, always, day and night, whether he is walking, standing, lying down, sitting, sleeping, waking, composed, or uncomposed, whether he is alone or in the midst of a great crowd, even as far as a village, city, or market town.

Outside the city is the settlement; a district or kingdom is the territory. Within the royal capital are the Indra-pillars, carriage-roads, main streets, city gates, market-streets, royal highways, crossroads, junctions of three roads, and junctions of four roads. Inside the city are the marketplaces, the shops, the merchandise for sale, the warehouses for that merchandise, and whatever is situated therein, up to empty houses, mountain caves, thickets, rivers, and forests.

For one who has entered that dense forest thicket— whether they are impure, pure, intoxicated (due to the transformation of pride), or heedless (due to the transformation of power)— they will always, in every way, and by all means, provide supreme protection, defense, and guardianship.

Day and night they will perform the highest rites of well-being. And there are others: gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas—namely, the eight families of nāgas; humans and non-humans, such as the pretas and so forth; and others such as the lords of the planets, constellations, and the hosts of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇapati), the Seven Mothers, and the yakṣiṇīs, rākṣasīs, and piśācīs—all of them assembled together.

Gathered together, complete, and fully assembled—with their armies, forces, retinues, and followers—all of them will provide protection, defense, and guardianship. Furthermore, they will infuse his body with vitality and strength; they will bestow upon him health, vigor, and an increase in lifespan, and they will present these gifts to him.
This is the benefit of the fourth wheel; its words are twenty-one, even by calculation. || 21 ||

Now, concerning the praise of the fifth wheel, he says: "Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara," and so forth. Whoever shall daily, every day, recite this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the crest-jewel of names—having undertaken it without interruption, three times [a day], and having multiplied it by three—and shall cause it to revolve as if it were upon their throat, or reading it from a book, shall set its recitation in motion.

Taking as his object the form of the Blessed One, Mañjuśrījñānasattva, reflecting upon it and meditating on that very form, he will—by means of that form-body, and by virtue of the power of discipline—soon, indeed swiftly, behold him according to the inclinations of sentient beings; and he will behold all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas situated in the expanse of the sky, accompanied by various emanated form-bodies.

That great being shall never, at any time, or in any way, fall into the miserable states of existence or the lower realms. Nor shall there be rebirth in a low family; therein, a "low family" refers to those such as the caṇḍālas and so forth.

A border region refers to a place of barbarians and the like where the word "Buddha" is not known; there, rebirth will not occur. "Having impaired faculties" means that one will not be born blind, mute, deformed, or the like. "A family of wrong views": wrong view is the nihilistic view; it is the uprooter of all [right] views. A family of such [a view] is a family of wrong views; there, rebirth will not occur. One will not be reborn in Buddha-fields where no Buddha resides.

And as for being turned away from the arising of a Buddha and being remote from the Dharma taught by him: there shall be no turning away from the arising of a Buddha, nor shall there be remoteness from the Dharma taught by him.

One will not be reborn among the long-lived beings in the formless realms or the state of non-perception (or among the gods). There are three intermediate kalpas of famine, disease, and weapons. As it is said in the Abhidharma: "The kalpa comes to an end through weapons, disease, and famine, for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively. One will not be reborn during those [periods].

The five degenerations (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*)—characterized by the degeneration of sentient beings, views, eons, lifespan, and requisites—are called "degenerations" (*kaṣāya*) because they are derived from the verbal root *kaṣ* (meaning "to rub away") through both its sense of "grinding" and "impressing as a latent tendency" (*vāsanā*). One will not be born during those times; there will be no fear of kings, enemies, or thieves. Furthermore, there will be no fear of poverty—that is, the deficiency of all necessities such as clothing and so forth.

[84] There is the fear of ill-repute, defamation, censure, and infamy. The meaning of "ill-repute" and so forth is already understood; by combining it with that [fear], one will no longer have such fear.

He will be endowed with a noble birth, family, and lineage; he will possess a form and complexion that are pleasing from every side and in every respect. He will be possessed of these qualities: he will be "dear" because of his sweet disposition (or sweet speech); he will be "pleasant to dwell with" because of the absence of suffering; and he will be "lovely to behold" because of his gladdening appearance. Thus he will be for the sake of the people and sentient beings.

His speech will be auspicious, fortunate, and authoritative, and he will be one whose words are accepted by the world. Wherever he is reborn, in each and every birth, he will possess the memory of his former lives (*jātismara*). He will have great enjoyments, meaning great wealth and grain; he will have a great retinue, meaning an abundance of many servants and attendants; and he will have inexhaustible enjoyments and an inexhaustible retinue, such that these will remain in an inexhaustible state for as long as he lives.

He will be a leader, a precursor for all sentient beings, endowed and joined with supreme qualities. By his very nature and inherent essence, he will be endowed with the qualities of the six perfections. He will dwell in the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). He will be endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, skillful means, power, aspiration, and primordial wisdom. In every respect, he will be confident in the treatises, expansive, and eloquent; he will be one whose speech is clear and whose expression is lucid.

"He is not dull-witted" because he is endowed with wisdom and intelligence. "He is clever" because he will be possessed of inspired eloquence (*pratibhāna*). "He is skillful" because he is possessed of enthusiasm. "He is not indolent" because there is no laziness regarding the factors conducive to the wholesome. "He is contented" because he dwells in fewness of desires. "He is of great purpose" because he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings. And he will be free from craving because he does not turn his face toward any [sensual] objects. Furthermore, he will be supremely trustworthy to all sentient beings because he is non-deceptive.

He will be esteemed and favored by teachers and gurus. Furthermore, crafts, arts, technical sciences, and treatises never heard before will appear to him in their meaning and their textual form. Because his livelihood and conduct—his way of life and behavior—are based on that morality which is perfectly pure and utterly refined, he will be one whose conduct and practice consist of such perfectly pure morality and livelihood. This is because he is free from wrong livelihood.

He will be one who has set out well, because his ethical discipline (*śīla*) is unbroken; and he will be one who is well-perfected, because his ethical discipline is faultless. He will be one whose resolve for the awakening of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bodhicitta*) is never lost. Furthermore, he will never—at any time—enter the fixed course (*niyāma*) of the Śrāvakas, Arhats, or Pratyekabuddhas, but will remain inclined toward that [supreme] awakening.

Thus, by way of conclusion, he speaks of the infinity of qualities: "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, that person who practices the conduct of the mantra-vehicle will be endowed with immeasurable qualities; he will be endowed with other immeasurable multitudes of qualities of this kind and this nature. O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara, before long, that bull among men who upholds the *Paramārthanāmasaṃgīti* [will be so]. The meaning is that he will be preeminent.

Therefore, having fully accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom, he will very swiftly and most rapidly bring forth the qualities of a Buddha; having grasped them, he will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Possessing the dharma of no small, auspicious parinirvāṇa, he will be the teacher of the unsurpassed dharma for all sentient beings, an empowered King of Dharma whose drum of the true dharma resounds throughout the ten directions.

This is the praise of the fifth wheel. Its words are fifty-one, even by calculation [51]. Beginning with "O Vajrapāṇi, O Vajradhara" and ending with "O Dharmarāja," these five praises are taken together. This concludes the twelfth chapter on Praise in the *Āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*.

Now, concerning the arrangement of the mantra for this wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*) of the sixth Bodhicittavajra, which is permeated by the heart of the Ādibuddha, he says: *oṃ sarvadharmā bhāvabhāvaviśuddhavajra a ā aṃ aḥ*. This is the root mantra of this *Nāmasaṅgīti*.

"All phenomena are pure by nature" means they are pure by their very nature, effortlessly and spontaneously; "all phenomena" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. That is to say, it is because one takes as a basis and accepts the purity of Mañjuśrī—the wisdom-body of all Tathāgatas—and its having the *dharmadhātu* as its intrinsic nature.

ĀḤ AḤ! Heart of all Tathāgatas, take away, take away! OṂ HŪṂ HRĪḤ! Blessed One, embodiment of primordial wisdom, Lord of Speech, Great Word, essence of the wisdom of the dharmadhātu—utterly pure and stainless as the sky regarding all phenomena—ĀḤ! This is the garland mantra of the Noble Nāmasaṃgīti.
In the *Āryanāmasaṅgītiṭīkā*, titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*, this is the thirteenth chapter, concerning the arrangement of the mantras of the Wisdom Wheel.

Now, by way of dissolution, the Lord Vajradhara, through various forms of Vajrapāṇi, paid homage to Śākyamuni—who is the embodiment of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as "Sarvanātha," who is the form of the equality-wisdom (*samatājñāna*) as "Saṃbuddha," who is the nature of the discerning-wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) as "Bhagavān," and who is the essence of the all-accomplishing-wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) as "Tathāgata"—and having bowed to him who is thus constituted of the four wisdoms, he spoke these words aloud; such is the connection.

Therefore, it is said: Then the glorious Vajradhara, joyful and satisfied, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down to the Lord, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Blessed Tathāgata. (MNS 163) Together with many other Lords, the Indras of Secrets who hold the vajra, and the Kings of Wrath, he spoke these words aloud: “We rejoice, O Lord! Excellent, excellent is this well-spoken [teaching]. A great benefit has been wrought for us, which leads to the attainment of perfect awakening. (MNS 164)

In this regard, O Protector, we truly rejoice; well spoken, very well spoken! A great benefit has been conferred upon us. To the question of what kind of benefit it is, he says: "that which brings about perfect enlightenment," meaning that which leads to Buddhahood.

And for the world that is without a protector and yearns for the fruit of liberation, this pure path to excellence has been proclaimed through the method of the *māyājāla* (the Net of Illusion). (MNS 166) In this regard, it is not only for the world that is without a protector, but also for those who yearn for the fruit of liberation; this great meaning proclaimed through the method of the *māyājāla* is distinguished as "pure" because its intrinsic nature is the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the phrase "the path to excellence": it is because it is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. "It is the domain of the Buddhas, taught by all the Perfectly Awakened Ones; profound, vast, extensive, and of great significance, it accomplishes the welfare of the world. (MNS 167) In this context, "this significance" refers to the fact that because it is profound, vast, extensive, and of great significance, it is the domain and sphere of activity of the Buddhas alone, and not of others such as the *śrāvakas* and so forth. It "accomplishes the welfare of the world" because it is embraced by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
It was taught by all the perfectly awakened ones existing in the three times; it is taught by all the perfectly awakened ones.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Conclusion, in the *Ārya-nāmasaṅgīti-ṭīkā* titled *Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī*. || 0 ||
Having composed this commentary on the *Nāmasaṅgīti* according to the power of my own intellect— though it is difficult for those of impure minds to grasp—
whatever incomparable merit has been acquired by me, may sentient beings through that [merit] reach the far shore.
May those who have pacified the passion for existence attain supreme enlightenment. ||o||

The Commentary on the *Āryanāmasaṅgīti* is completed. O || The measure of this work is two thousand plus four hundred verses. O || This is the composition of the master Vilāsavajra, a resident of Ratnadvīpa, the illustrious nephew of Agrabodhi, whose name was Pra...śvarūpa. [115] In the year numbered by the horses (7), the earth (1), the mountains (7), and the arrows (5)—that is, 7175—in the month of Śuci, on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight, the commentary on the glorious *Nāmasaṅgīti* was composed by Pavibhṛta(?). O || Verses.
By means of this extensive transcription, whatever merit has been acquired by me, Śrī Sarvamitra—may the entire world become a son of the Buddha. May there be auspiciousness! Om!
The Commentary on the *Āryanāmasaṅgīti* is completed. Oṃ. This is the work of the master Vilāsavajra. Oṃ.
